{"comments":[{"id":"42a1a953-977a-4f1e-ba2e-2875f693e954","body":"**Two E1 line items inherited from Track D's migration kickoff (2026-08-14):**

1. **Fleet-side timing-envelope invariant:** the cmd/worker migration carries an app-side test pinning `MaxDeliver × syncTimeout + scheduled waits < mirror_git_v1 maxAge` (measured 5h04m vs 6h), but mirror-pipeline cannot import fleet's CR, so the maxAge is a mirrored named constant — the app test catches app-side erosion only. The fleet-side half belongs here: an admission check in fleet CI asserting `mirror_git_v1` maxAge stays ≥ the documented worker give-up envelope (pointer comments on both sides reference each other). Generalizes to any workqueue whose consumer's wall-clock envelope approaches its maxAge.

2. **Tooling dependency for config-level checks:** the entire MCP NATS toolset exposes consumer *runtime state* only (floor, pending, redelivered) — not consumer *config* (AckWait, MaxDeliver, BackOff, InactiveThreshold, MaxAckPending, policies). Track D's per-PR stored-vs-rendered diffs are human-gated (`nats consumer info -j` by hand) until a consumer-config read exists; E1's admission/verification work will hit the same wall. Candidate small ticket: add consumer-config read to the MCP nats tools.","createdAt":"2026-08-14T11:36:19.128Z","updatedAt":"2026-08-14T11:36:19.114Z","parentId":null,"resolvedAt":null,"quotedText":null,"author":{"id":"76f6927c-ac03-4620-9454-a3acd751fbd7","name":"Andrea Nodari"},"onBehalfOf":null},{"id":"a6ce66ec-64d2-40f3-a58a-921d2852c489","body":"**Ladder-arithmetic trap for the admission lint (2026-08-12, found during the A1 ladder-ownership cutover):** JetStream **repeats the last `backOff` rung** when the array is shorter than `maxDeliver` — a short array under a larger maxDeliver is the *common* CR shape, and summing the array as written under-counts real time-to-dead-letter, i.e. a naive checker passes ladders that breach the bound in production. Fixed in go-nuts' `Schedule.TimeToDeadLetter` with boundary tests.

**Counting rule, stated precisely (an off-by-one lives here):** the repeat covers **rungs served before delivery N** — i.e. deliveries `1..DeadLetterDelivery−1`. Example: 3-rung array `[5m,10m,30m]`, MaxDeliver 7, capture reserve 1 → dead-letter at delivery 6 → sums **five** rungs (5+10+30+30+30 = 1h45m), not six. Say "rungs served before delivery N", never "rungs up to N".

Standing rule for E1: the lint must call go-nuts' exported validation (`jsconsumer.Schedule`), never re-implement the arithmetic — this trap and its off-by-one are exactly why.","createdAt":"2026-08-12T13:19:07.499Z","updatedAt":"2026-08-12T13:23:55.627Z","parentId":null,"resolvedAt":null,"quotedText":null,"author":{"id":"76f6927c-ac03-4620-9454-a3acd751fbd7","name":"Andrea Nodari"},"onBehalfOf":null},{"id":"6ca0ded5-3492-4f02-bac6-cad4c22e04ee","body":"**E1 admission-control mechanism, sharpened by the A1 scope change (2026-08-12):** with the enforcing breaker demoted to an observe soak (see ENT-1601), the M1 stall-safety property is now "validated bounded ladders" — and once Track D lands Consumer CRs in fleet, that property is **fully computable at merge time**: `backoff`, `maxDeliver`, `ackWait` all live in the CR, so the lint can compute cumulative ladder time per consumer per rendered cell overlay, plus cross-resource checks against the stream CR (ladder vs `maxAge` redelivery envelope, DLQ pairing).

Implementation note to prevent drift: **do not re-implement the arithmetic**. go-nuts is exporting its schedule validation as a pure function (requested of the A1 session); the fleet CI checker should compile that same function over rendered CRs. One source of truth, three enforcement points: fleet CI refuses the merge (admission), NACK makes the server match the CR (generation), and bind-only jsconsumer refuses to start if its client-side expectations (`RecoverBy`/`FloorAge`) don't match the durable's actual server-side ladder (library). Client-side knobs stay app-config and are validated at bind time against real server state — no inference anywhere in the chain.","createdAt":"2026-08-12T13:09:35.314Z","updatedAt":"2026-08-12T13:09:35.285Z","parentId":null,"resolvedAt":null,"quotedText":null,"author":{"id":"76f6927c-ac03-4620-9454-a3acd751fbd7","name":"Andrea Nodari"},"onBehalfOf":null}],"hasNextPage":false}

{"id":"COR-1255","title":"Track E — Guardrails & cell industrialization: admission control, generation, fault injection (wk 4–12, ~22.5 pd)","description":"## Problem

Stream invariants are enforced by comments (`webhooks_github_v1 maxAge ≥ 48h` vs the ~41h redelivery envelope); NATS users/grants are hand-written per cell — how five consumers shipped without `$JS.ACK` grants (<issue id="33e005d5-f925-4d4a-b46c-d423ec5ac549" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1224/five-webhooks-github-v1-consumers-lack-an-explicit-dollarjsack-publish">COR-1224</issue>); monitors are hand-added per durable, so a consumer can ship unmonitored; deploys race the shared fleet branch with no ordering guard (a prod schema rollback already happened, <issue id="fbd6173d-349e-42f7-9a38-856d62fa4ef6" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1046/deploy-pipeline-race-out-of-order-promotedeploy-lets-an-older-build">COR-1046</issue>); and the cell layer has zero fault-injection coverage — NATS is exempt in Antithesis, so every NATS failure mode has been discovered in production.

## Proposed solution

{"id":"COR-1009","title":"go-nuts Phase 5: migrate remaining consume/admin surfaces to the modern JetStream client","description":"## Context

Follow-up to <issue id="ba4a571f-d55f-45f2-9b1a-696c23eb4324" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1004/go-nuts-phase-4-retire-the-legacy-jetstream-publishing-bridges">COR-1004</issue>, which removed the legacy `nats.JetStreamContext` **publishing** surface everywhere. What remains on the legacy client is consume/admin-side:

* **mirror-pipeline**: the six explicit pull loops (worker, fanoutengine's serial + worker-pool loops, webhook-forwarder, meta-fanout lifecycle, the two meta-fanout backfills), the KV fail-index, ConsumerInfo gauges, the webhookdlq advisory backstop's stream reads, the admin CLIs (rekicker, mirror-pipeline-admin), and the backfill/rekick raw enqueuers.
* **entiredb**: repoops `EnsureStream`/StreamInfo gauges (dev/standalone bootstrap; fleet nack owns the streams in prod), the verified-email ConsumerInfo probe, and the email outbox relay's publish transport.
* **entire-api**: nothing (fully modern since <issue id="ba4a571f-d55f-45f2-9b1a-696c23eb4324" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1004/go-nuts-phase-4-retire-the-legacy-jetstream-publishing-bridges">COR-1004</issue>).

## Design constraints

* The pull loops keep their **explicit-fetch pacing** — port to modern `jetstream.Consumer.Fetch(batch, FetchMaxWait(…))`, NOT the `Consume()` client-buffer shape. AckWait must keep starting only when the process holds the message; the fanoutengine pool keeps `FetchBatch ≤ Concurrency`; `NumPending` stays honest for KEDA.
* The worker's `InProgress` heartbeat (AckWait/3), publish-before-ack ordering, disposition trees, hooks, and route memo stay byte-identical in behavior.
* **Test-coverage gate**: mirror-pipeline's loops have no broker-level tests today (interface fakes only). Embedded-NATS coverage for fetch-loop semantics (fetch timeout/no-messages classification, batch delivery, drain-during-shutdown, heartbeat extension) is part of this ticket — landed before or with the loop ports, so wire-level semantic differences between legacy and modern Fetch can't hide.
* `nuts.Connect`/`Drain` (core NATS connection lifecycle) are unaffected.

## Scope

### 5a — mechanical admin/probe/transport swaps (low risk, first PRs)

* entiredb: `EnsureStream`/`applyContract` + StreamInfo gauges → modern stream APIs; verified-email ConsumerInfo probe → `Consumer.Info`; email outbox relay transport → ctx-native publish over a local narrow interface (still no span/inject — outbox semantics unchanged).
* mirror-pipeline: fail-index KV → `jetstream.KeyValue`; worker/forwarder ConsumerInfo gauges → `Consumer.Info`; advisory backstop stream reads → `Stream.GetMsg`; admin CLIs and rekicker.

After 5a, entiredb has no legacy JetStream API use at all.

### 5b — the fetch loops (the substantial half)

1. Embedded-NATS test harness + loop-semantics coverage in mirror-pipeline.
2. Port the six loops to modern `Consumer.Fetch`; serial loops that fit jsconsumer's shape (webhook-forwarder, lifecycle, backfills) may converge onto `jsconsumer` instead where that does not change behavior.
3. `ensureInactiveThreshold` reconciles → `CreateOrUpdateConsumer`.
4. Remove the last legacy contexts and the dual-handle wiring from <issue id="ba4a571f-d55f-45f2-9b1a-696c23eb4324" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1004/go-nuts-phase-4-retire-the-legacy-jetstream-publishing-bridges">COR-1004</issue>.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] No `nc.JetStream()` call remains in entiredb, entire-api, or mirror-pipeline.
- [ ] All consumer contracts preserved: durables, filters, AckWait, MaxDeliver, batch bounds, heartbeat cadence, dispositions, DLQ order, metrics, spans, logs.
- [ ] mirror-pipeline gains embedded-NATS coverage for its fetch loops; `go test -race` passes in all repos.
- [ ] Lint, `go mod tidy -diff`, vendoring, `git diff --check` clean.

## Out of scope

Changing any consumer's delivery semantics (no move to the `Consume()` buffer shape for the pull loops); KEDA/fleet scaling {"id":"COR-1257","title":"go-nuts: embedded real-broker test suite — verify JetStream semantic beliefs against nats-server, not a fake","description":"## Problem

Every major bug found in the A1 review cycle was a **model error** — code faithfully implementing a wrong belief about JetStream semantics: Term doesn't settle on limits streams (<issue id="96688401-2b2d-48dd-8a77-a4400bd1bb45" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1492/entire-search-exhausted-ref-events-are-termed-which-does-not-settle">ENT-1492</issue>); `NumDeliver` increments on AckWait expiry with no handler involvement; the server stretches NAK delays by consumer BackOff increments; the last `backOff` rung tail-repeats under a larger `maxDeliver` (with an off-by-one — see <issue id="ef0f3a5a-67e4-48db-849c-8aafe12e38b0" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1255/track-e-guardrails-and-cell-industrialization-admission-control">COR-1255</issue>); pedantic mode requires `ackWait = backoff[0]`. The unit suite runs against `natsmsgtest`'s fake, which encodes *the same model as the code* — so it stays green precisely when the model is wrong. The only step in the pipeline that consults reality is human review, which is why review keeps finding P1s.

## Proposed solution

An integration suite in go-nuts running an **embedded in-process nats-server** (pinned to the go.mod version), asserting every semantic belief the library encodes:

* ack-floor behavior with an unacked head-of-line message (floor stationary; later messages ack past it out of order)
* `NumDelivered` inflation on AckWait expiry / client death
* tail-repeat arithmetic: rungs served **before** delivery N, incl. the <issue id="ef0f3a5a-67e4-48db-849c-8aafe12e38b0" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1255/track-e-guardrails-and-cell-industrialization-admission-control">COR-1255</issue> boundary cases
* capture-then-Ack settles and advances the floor; Term behavior on limits streams
* pedantic-mode rejections (`ackWait ≠ backoff[0]`, `maxDeliver ≤ len(backoff)`, stream `consumerLimits` interactions)
* regression assertions for **each P1 found in the current review rounds** (list from the review thread)

The fake (`natsmsgtest`) is demoted to library-logic tests only; the real-broker suite joins the merge gate. Also serves D0 bind-only later (expectations vs real `ConsumerInfo`) and <issue id="0a63017b-ca4e-4999-83c5-e558afcca5e1" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1256/non-lossy-poison-message-break-glass-quarantine-nats-poison-ref-event">COR-1256</issue>'s quarantine tool (read-by-seq / publish / remove ordering); re-runs on every nats-server bump so upgrades re-verify the whole belief set instead of surprising us via incident.

**Acceptance:** suite green against embedded nats-server at the pinned version; every historical model-error P1 has an assertion; the A1 merge (<issue id="57d2a8d9-c2a6-49c4-8014-8a67857ef1b0" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1535/entire-search-the-ent-1492-dlq-doesnt-prevent-the-stall-a-poison-ref">ENT-1535</issue>) is gated on this {"comments":[{"id":"a3de7924-77d3-40a1-bcca-da5cfd51298e","body":"**Suite complete and green (2026-08-13).** Branch `nodo/cor-1257-go-nuts-embedded-real-broker-test-suite-verify-jetstream` off main@143ec67, two commits (committed, not yet pushed): `3b6f979` — the suite (`internal/brokersemantics`, **21 tests**) + `natsmsgtest` demotion + README; `f6f999f` — doc corrections from review. **All assertion classes pass against the embedded broker:** the seven model-errors, plus normalization-vs-pedantic asserted in *both* modes (pedantic driven via raw `$JS.API` request — nats.go exposes no pedantic option), the 10116 boundary (`len > maxDeliver` rejected, `len == maxDeliver` accepted), and `backOff` with `maxDeliver -1` accepted.

**Four NEW findings neither list had:**
1. **`Ack`/`Nak`/`Term` return `nil` while the server rejects them for want of a `$JS.ACK` grant** — the COR-1224 grant-gap class is *silent at the client*. (Ticket-worthiness flagged to Andrea — this is the detection side of what E7's generated grants prevent.)
2. `NumAckPending` is 0 on an exhausted message.
3. Stream `ConsumerLimits` silently fill a consumer's zero fields.
4. **The ack floor advances on stream-side message removal** — directly relevant to COR-1256's quarantine semantics (remove does un-pin the floor).

**Shipping shape: the split is clean and entirely category (a)** — the suite imports only symbols on main, nothing from the A1 branch; it merges independently. Stated plainly: merging it gates the *beliefs underneath* the A1 work, not the A1 code paths themselves. Overlap with the A1 branch's `f4e160a` is two doc-only files; **suite-first merge order is cheaper** (the A1 branch then resolves mechanically — keep the suite's ConsumerLimits doc block, drop the 7-line duplicate).

Open (non-gating) decisions: where the requested-vs-stored config read-back check lives (jsconsumer at Start vs COR-1255 admission); whether findings 1/3 get their own tickets.","createdAt":"2026-08-13T07:59:03.149Z","updatedAt":"2026-08-13T07:59:03.084Z","parentId":null,"resolvedAt":null,"quotedText":null,"author":{"id":"76f6927c-ac03-4620-9454-a3acd751fbd7","name":"Andrea Nodari"},"onBehalfOf":null},{"id":"dca978ca-8615-400f-9518-63ad52853e0b","body":"**The assertion list, from the A1 review history + a fresh empirical probe (2026-08-12).** Seven P1 model errors — each was invisible to the `natsmsgtest` fake because it encodes the same wrong belief:

1. **Term does not settle** (ENT-1492's root): floor stays pinned after Term; capture-then-Ack advances it.
2. **Blocker identity is not derivable from `ConsumerInfo`**: `AckFloor.Stream+1` is wrong after a drain (floor jumps to the delivered high-water mark; measured floor 2, blocker at 6); `AckFloor.Consumer+1` pins to the blocker's *first* delivery and goes stale across redeliveries (measured floor 1 vs redeliveries 4, 5, 6). Assert both, on a filtered consumer, before and after a drain.
3. **`NumDelivered` is not a ladder counter** — increments on AckWait expiry with no handler involvement (measured 4 deliveries in 68 ms).
4. **`BackOff` does not govern Nak — it governs ack timeouts.** Measured on 3s/3s/3s: plain `Nak()` redelivers in 0 s; `NakWithDelay(3s)` in 3 s; no-ack in 3 s. This is why "do nothing" is the correct failure disposition under server-owned ladders.
5. **Absent `BackOff` ≠ absent ladder** — redelivery continues on AckWait repeated.
6. **Short `BackOff` array ≠ short ladder** — last rung repeats, counted over rungs served *before* delivery N (see COR-1255 for the off-by-one).
7. **Non-positive `MaxDeliver` means unlimited, not invalid** — a `-1` consumer must start and consume.

**Empirical corrections to the original scope (probe, 2026-08-12):**
- `ackWait ≠ backOff[0]` is **silently normalized** by the server on the ordinary client path (AckWait 30s + BackOff [1m,2m] → stored AckWait 1m), *not* rejected. In **pedantic** JS-API mode (what NACK's controller uses) the same mismatch *is* a rejection — assert both modes, or at minimum normalization + label the pedantic case as NACK-context.
- `len(backOff) > maxDeliver` rejected (400 / err 10116); `len == maxDeliver` **accepted** — the server's own error text ("required to be >") overstates its rule.
- `backOff` alongside `maxDeliver = -1` accepted.

**Build note:** no build tag — the suite runs in default `go test ./...`. A tag CI can forget is a gate that silently doesn't run. Harness partially exists (`runJetStreamServer`/`runTestEnv`, seven real-broker tests in tree); estimate is hours, not days.","createdAt":"2026-08-12T16:07:45.837Z","updatedAt":"2026-08-12T16:07:45.795Z","parentId":null,"resolvedAt":null,"quotedText":null,"author":{"id":"76f6927c-ac03-4620-9454-a3acd751fbd7","name":"Andrea Nodari"},"onBehalfOf":null}],"hasNextPage":false}

{"id":"COR-1270","title":"webhook-forwarder and fanout run a 41h orphaned BackOff ladder no code declares (live ENT-1535, prod)","description":"## What was found

Measured 2026-08-14 during Track D's loop-1 pre-flight, via `natsctl -- consumer info webhooks_github_v1 <durable> --json` on **prod us-east-2** and **staging us-west-2** (identical on both):

| durable | code declares | server actually stores | real envelope |
| -- | -- | -- | -- |
| `webhook-forwarder` | no `BackOff`, client `NakWithDelay(30s)` | `backoff: [30s, 2m, 10m, 1h, 4h, 12h, 24h]` | **41h12m30s** |
| `fanout-us-east-2` / `fanout-us-west-2` | no `BackOff`, client `NakWithDelay(30s)` | same 7 rungs | **41h12m30s** |
| `core-fanout` | no `BackOff` | absent | 3m30s — agrees |
| `meta-fanout` | no `BackOff` | absent | 3m30s — agrees |
| `trails-fanout-push` | no `BackOff` | absent | 3m30s — agrees |
| `trails-fanout-pull-request` | no `BackOff` | absent | 3m30s — agrees |

Two of the seven `webhooks_github_v1` consumers carry a server-side redelivery ladder that **no source file declares**, alongside a client-side `NakWithDelay(30s)`. That is mixed ownership — the <issue id="57d2a8d9-c2a6-49c4-8014-8a67857ef1b0" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1535/entire-search-the-ent-1492-dlq-doesnt-prevent-the-stall-a-poison-ref">ENT-1535</issue> defect — live in production.

Because the requested Nak delay equals `BackOff[0]` (both 30s), the server's stretch term is zero on the first rung and redeliveries then follow the **server** ladder exactly. So the real give-up envelope is **41h12m30s**, against `cmd/webhook-forwarder/forwarder.go:48-52`, which states: *"No* `nats.BackOff` *is set, so this is a free choice — not clamped to a schedule."*

## How it got there

`consumerMaxDeliver`'s own comment names the mechanism without drawing the conclusion: *"dropping* `nats.BackOff` *is tolerated (BackOff is not part of that comparison)."* It is tolerated by nats.go's `checkConfig`, which is exactly why the ladder survived its deletion from the source — legacy `PullSubscribe` **binds** to an existing durable and never updates it. So a ladder removed from code stays on the server forever.

The four durables that never carried a ladder never acquired an orphan. This is a history artefact, not a config decision — nobody chose 41 hours.

## Why it matters, independent of Track D

A delivery that keeps failing (entire-web 5xx, network error) holds the `webhooks_github_v1` **ack floor for up to 41 hours**. That stream is interest-retention with seven consumers, and a pinned floor is the <issue id="57d2a8d9-c2a6-49c4-8014-8a67857ef1b0" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1535/entire-search-the-ent-1492-dlq-doesnt-prevent-the-stall-a-poison-ref">ENT-1535</issue>/Aug 5–6 shape: the stall signal cannot distinguish one pinned message from a throughput collapse.

It is a **stall, not a loss**: 41h12m30s < the stream's 96h `maxAge`, so the delivery still reaches DLQ capture on delivery 8.

**Second finding — nothing observes this today.** The only per-consumer monitor on this stream (`monitor_ingest_consumer_backlog.tf`) fires on `num_pending + num_ack_pending > 5000` sustained over 20m — a *volume* signal, sized for the 2026-06-01 orphaned-durable starvation. A single message pinning the floor for 41h leaves `num_ack_pending` at 1 and never trips it. Unlike `repo_refs_v1`, `webhooks_github_v1` has **no ack-floor-age monitor at all**, so this behaviour is not merely undocumented — it is unmeasured.

## Proposed work

1. **Decide the intended envelope.** Options span 3m30s (a declared flat 30s ladder), ~42m (the entire-search shape `[5m, 5m, 5m, 12m, 15m]`), and ~4h (bounded but patient). The real question is how long an entire-web outage should be absorbed automatically versus dead-lettered for manual replay — `webhooks_github_dlq` retains 7 days in prod, and replay is a manual `mirrorctl` operation.
2. **Make it declared, not inherited.** Whichever envelope is chosen, it has to be written where the code says it is. Reconciling an existing durable's `BackOff` needs `CreateOrUpdateConsumer` (the modern client) — which is precisely what the Track D migration of these two loops does, so the fix and the migration can be the same change if the timing suits.
3. **Close the observability gap** — an ack-floor-age monitor on `webhooks_github_v1`, sized under whatever envelope is chosen.

## Relationship to Track D

Found by <issue id="3b85cbc3-db3f-422f-acf9-aa89bc5e47c8" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1254/track-d-consumer-standardization-jsconsumer-everywhere-durables-as">COR-1254</issue>'s pre-flight and it changes that plan (loop 2 and loop 9 are no longer envelope-preserving migrations — see the correction on mirror-pipeline trail #100), but it is **not** created by the migration and should not wait on it. The migration is the natural vehicle for item 2; items 1 and 3 stand on their own.

COR-1254 Track D — Consumer standardization: jsconsumer everywhere, durables as fleet Consumer CRs (wk 2–9, ~18 pd)

## Problem mirror-pipeline — the service whose whole job is consuming JetStream — has **zero** `jsconsumer` adopters; every fetch loop is hand-rolled. That's the failure class behind the 48h backlog (an app backoff config silently overriding AckWait) and it means no consumer inherits library fixes (circuit breaker, DLQ capture, telemetry). Consumer config is imperative, per-app, undiffable, and identical across cells whether that fits or not. ## Proposed solution * **Harden go-nuts first:** reject invalid configs at startup (backoff ladder > AckWait unrepresentable; DLQ policy required; no bare `Term()`); add bind-only mode (+ dev mode for local/CI); publish stream contracts as a module so `refevents`-style hand copies die. * **Migrate one loop at a time** ([COR-1009](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1009/go-nuts-phase-5-migrate-remaining-consumeadmin-surfaces-to-the-modern) ph. 5): mirror-pipeline's 4 loops, then entiredb `permssweep`, entire-api `ingest`/`analysis`. * **Per loop, durables become fleet-managed NACK** `Consumer` **CRs** (extends nats-streams "Option A"): snapshot `nats consumer info -j`, author a full-mirror CR (`preventDelete: true`, explicit `ackPolicy`, `ackWait = backoff[0]`, live maxAckPending/maxWaiting stated), canary-adopt verifying ack floor/delivery counts unchanged, then switch the app to bind-only in the same change (single-writer rule). Go/no-go checkpoint after the first canary durable; fallback is app-owned consumers with library validation. * Durable advisory capture for the live index queue ([COR-997](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-997/durable-advisory-capture-for-job-stream-dead-lettering-close-the-repo)). **Exit:** 0 hand-rolled fetch loops; 0 app-side create/update calls; legacy consume-surface list empty; migrated durables are fleet CRs with delivery state untouched.

The cross-region resource_lifecycle_v1 fan moves off its hand-rolled PullSubscribe/Fetch(1) loop onto jsconsumer.Run + Process, and its redelivery ladder moves server-side. Same durable name, so no recreation and no redelivery storm; behaviour is preserved except where noted below. WHAT MOVES - jsconsumer.Run + Process replace the subscribe/backoff loop, the Fetch loop, the shutdown-error classification and the span prologue. MaxMessages 1 preserves the Fetch(1) pacing: AckWait runs from server delivery into the client buffer, not from callback dispatch, so anything queued behind a slow fan would age unprocessed. - The ladder is now the durable's. lifecycleBackOff derives consumerFailureDelay x (consumerMaxDeliver-1) from the two constants rather than restating them, so the numbers that must agree cannot drift. The app's disposition for a failed fan is DO NOTHING — the ack timeout brings the delivery back on that ladder. A client NakWithDelay beside a server ladder is the ENT-1535 defect (the server stretches each NAK by the BackOff increments, so redeliveries follow neither); a plain Nak would redeliver immediately and skip the ladder. - Every field CreateOrUpdateConsumer sends is now stated, because a field omitted in code is not "unchanged on the durable" — it is reset to a default. WHAT DOES NOT MOVE Give-up semantics. No Term path, no Retry, no DLQ: the event is republished verbatim so nothing about it can be permanently unprocessable, and resource_lifecycle_v1 is limits-retention — it holds every event for its full max age whatever this consumer does, so the replay path is the source stream. Adding capture would need a DLQ stream and a meta-fanout publish grant that do not exist. InactiveThreshold stays unset, and now says so explicitly. The 2026-06-01 reaping valve is for interest streams where an abandoned durable pins deliveries for ALL consumers; on limits retention an idle durable pins nothing. All seven cells carry no threshold today and none is added. The timing envelope is unchanged — 8 deliveries, give up at t+3m30s — which the pre-flight is what licenses claiming: snapshots of all 7 cells showed this durable has NO server-side backoff, so the effective ladder really was the client's flat 30s. (webhook-forwarder and fanout are NOT like this; they carry an undeclared 41h ladder, COR-1270. Loop 2 cannot make this claim.) ONE DELIBERATE CONFIG CHANGE MaxAckPending 65536 -> 1000. The 65536 in all seven cells was never chosen: nats.go's legacy PullSubscribe copies its own client-side subscription-channel capacity into the server config. jsconsumer sends the field on every start, so leaving it zero would have rewritten all seven silently; this makes it a recorded decision instead. Generous either way at a one-message prefetch. TWO KNOWN DELTAS - /readyz is narrower. The old loop held a `subscribed` bool set after each successful PullSubscribe, so a RETRYABLE boot failure (stream absent, no responders) also read NotReady. jsconsumer.Run exposes no start-success signal, so Ready() now reports only that the configuration was accepted — which does cover this migration's likeliest failure, an immutable-field disagreement. In exchange Run recreates a consume loop that closes mid-run, as the old outer loop did. Closing the gap needs go-nuts to expose readiness from Run; recorded beside the Runner.Drain and FloorMonitor-attach gaps entire-search #131 logged. - The fan-failure log drops redeliver_in and gains max_deliver. The app no longer schedules the redelivery, so printing a delay would be a claim about someone else's config — true only while the two agree, which is the drift this track exists to remove. Position in the ladder is what a responder can act on; the ladder is on the durable. outcome=nak is kept verbatim on the metric: dashboards key on it and its meaning is unchanged (this delivery failed and will come back). What changed is who schedules the redelivery, which the metric never described. The local ackableMsg seam and numDelivered helper are gone — jetstream.Msg is already an interface, natsmsgtest.FakeMsg is the double, and backoff.NumDelivered is the library's own reading of the delivery count. Ready() reflected only configRejected — set when jsconsumer.Run RETURNS, which it does only for a permanently rejected config. Run retries everything else and logs a warning per attempt, so through the outages a readiness gate exists for (stream not provisioned yet, JetStream unreachable while the TCP connection is up: no responders, meta-leader election, a CONSUMER.CREATE permission rejection surfacing as a timeout) configRejected never flips and /readyz stayed green while nothing was consumed. I checked whether the pre-existing gate covered it. It does not: natsregions.Health.Status() asks Local.IsConnected() only, so a live connection to a JetStream that cannot answer passes it. Run joins it on the way out, so no ConsumerInfo can be in flight on a connection the caller is about to drain. What the probe proves: the stream and durable exist and the JetStream API answered. The first probe races Run creating the durable, so a single 5s interval left a healthy pod NotReady for seconds after it was already consuming — visible as a 5.10s test runtime, now 0.36s. It polls at 250ms until the first success, then settles to 5s, so a sustained outage is not hammered with four ConsumerInfo requests a second at the moment the server is already struggling. THE PROBE JOIN DEADLOCKED ON A REJECTED CONFIG (lifecycle.go) I registered `defer stopProbe()` and then `defer func(){ <-probeDone }()`. Defers run LIFO, so the JOIN ran first and the cancel second — and the probe exits only on its context. A Run that returned while the parent context was still alive (the only such path: a permanently rejected config) therefore blocked in its own defer until whole-app shutdown: goroutine leaked, the caller's lifecycleDone never closed, and the probe kept polling — at the 250ms startup cadence if CONSUMER.INFO never succeeded. TestLifecycleRun_ReturnsOnRejectedConfig covers it, with the parent context deliberately left alive because that is the condition the bug needed. COR-1254 Track D — Consumer standardization: jsconsumer everywhere, durables as fleet Consumer CRs (wk 2–9, ~18 pd)

## Problem mirror-pipeline — the service whose whole job is consuming JetStream — has **zero** `jsconsumer` adopters; every fetch loop is hand-rolled. That's the failure class behind the 48h backlog (an app backoff config silently overriding AckWait) and it means no consumer inherits library fixes (circuit breaker, DLQ capture, telemetry). Consumer config is imperative, per-app, undiffable, and identical across cells whether that fits or not. ## Proposed solution * **Harden go-nuts first:** reject invalid configs at startup (backoff ladder > AckWait unrepresentable; DLQ policy required; no bare `Term()`); add bind-only mode (+ dev mode for local/CI); publish stream contracts as a module so `refevents`-style hand copies die. * **Migrate one loop at a time** ([COR-1009](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1009/go-nuts-phase-5-migrate-remaining-consumeadmin-surfaces-to-the-modern) ph. 5): mirror-pipeline's 4 loops, then entiredb `permssweep`, entire-api `ingest`/`analysis`. * **Per loop, durables become fleet-managed NACK** `Consumer` **CRs** (extends nats-streams "Option A"): snapshot `nats consumer info -j`, author a full-mirror CR (`preventDelete: true`, explicit `ackPolicy`, `ackWait = backoff[0]`, live maxAckPending/maxWaiting stated), canary-adopt verifying ack floor/delivery counts unchanged, then switch the app to bind-only in the same change (single-writer rule). Go/no-go checkpoint after the first canary durable; fallback is app-owned consumers with library validation. * Durable advisory capture for the live index queue ([COR-997](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-997/durable-advisory-capture-for-job-stream-dead-lettering-close-the-repo)). **Exit:** 0 hand-rolled fetch loops; 0 app-side create/update calls; legacy consume-surface list empty; migrated durables are fleet CRs with delivery state untouched.

Same durable name, so no recreation and no redelivery storm; behaviour is preserved except where noted below. WHAT MOVES - jsconsumer.Run + Process replace the subscribe/backoff loop, the Fetch loop, the shutdown-error classification and the span prologue. MaxMessages 1 preserves the Fetch(1) pacing: AckWait runs from server delivery into the client buffer, not from callback dispatch, so anything queued behind a slow fan would age unprocessed. - The ladder is now the durable's. lifecycleBackOff derives consumerFailureDelay x (consumerMaxDeliver-1) from the two constants rather than restating them, so the numbers that must agree cannot drift. The app's disposition for a failed fan is DO NOTHING — the ack timeout brings the delivery back on that ladder. A client NakWithDelay beside a server ladder is the ENT-1535 defect (the server stretches each NAK by the BackOff increments, so redeliveries follow neither); a plain Nak would redeliver immediately and skip the ladder. - Every field CreateOrUpdateConsumer sends is now stated, because a field omitted in code is not "unchanged on the durable" — it is reset to a default. WHAT DOES NOT MOVE Give-up semantics. No Term path, no Retry, no DLQ: the event is republished verbatim so nothing about it can be permanently unprocessable, and resource_lifecycle_v1 is limits-retention — it holds every event for its full max age whatever this consumer does, so the replay path is the source stream. Adding capture would need a DLQ stream and a meta-fanout publish grant that do not exist. InactiveThreshold stays unset, and now says so explicitly. The 2026-06-01 reaping valve is for interest streams where an abandoned durable pins deliveries for ALL consumers; on limits retention an idle durable pins nothing. All seven cells carry no threshold today and none is added. The timing envelope is unchanged — 8 deliveries, give up at t+3m30s — which the pre-flight is what licenses claiming: snapshots of all 7 cells showed this durable has NO server-side backoff, so the effective ladder really was the client's flat 30s. (webhook-forwarder and fanout are NOT like this; they carry an undeclared 41h ladder, COR-1270. Loop 2 cannot make this claim.) ONE DELIBERATE CONFIG CHANGE MaxAckPending 65536 -> 1000. The 65536 in all seven cells was never chosen: nats.go's legacy PullSubscribe copies its own client-side subscription-channel capacity into the server config. jsconsumer sends the field on every start, so leaving it zero would have rewritten all seven silently; this makes it a recorded decision instead. Generous either way at a one-message prefetch. TWO KNOWN DELTAS - /readyz is narrower. What changed is who schedules the redelivery, which the metric never described. A Run that returned while the parent context was still alive (the only such path: a permanently rejected config) therefore blocked in its own defer until whole-app shutdown: goroutine leaked, the caller's lifecycleDone never closed, and the probe kept polling — at the 250ms startup cadence if CONSUMER.INFO never succeeded. The distinction is not available from the error value, so it does not belong in a predicate over error values. natslog goes back to keeping a missing consumer loud (ErrJetStreamNotEnabled stays transient — a 503 from a server still starting), and the PROBE makes the call, because only the probe knows which side of the first successful bind it is on: - before any bind + consumer missing -> debug, no failure run. Honest limit, stated in the code: at a 5s cadence this probe can miss a delete that Run recreates before the next tick, so it is a backstop, not a detector. The phase is now bounded by attempts as well: 20 at 250ms (~5s, orders of magnitude more than creating a durable takes), then the steady 5s cadence whether or not it ever succeeded. COR-1254 Track D — Consumer standardization: jsconsumer everywhere, durables as fleet Consumer CRs (wk 2–9, ~18 pd)

## Problem mirror-pipeline — the service whose whole job is consuming JetStream — has **zero** `jsconsumer` adopters; every fetch loop is hand-rolled. That's the failure class behind the 48h backlog (an app backoff config silently overriding AckWait) and it means no consumer inherits library fixes (circuit breaker, DLQ capture, telemetry). Consumer config is imperative, per-app, undiffable, and identical across cells whether that fits or not. ## Proposed solution * **Harden go-nuts first:** reject invalid configs at startup (backoff ladder > AckWait unrepresentable; DLQ policy required; no bare `Term()`); add bind-only mode (+ dev mode for local/CI); publish stream contracts as a module so `refevents`-style hand copies die. * **Migrate one loop at a time** ([COR-1009](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1009/go-nuts-phase-5-migrate-remaining-consumeadmin-surfaces-to-the-modern) ph. 5): mirror-pipeline's 4 loops, then entiredb `permssweep`, entire-api `ingest`/`analysis`. * **Per loop, durables become fleet-managed NACK** `Consumer` **CRs** (extends nats-streams "Option A"): snapshot `nats consumer info -j`, author a full-mirror CR (`preventDelete: true`, explicit `ackPolicy`, `ackWait = backoff[0]`, live maxAckPending/maxWaiting stated), canary-adopt verifying ack floor/delivery counts unchanged, then switch the app to bind-only in the same change (single-writer rule). Go/no-go checkpoint after the first canary durable; fallback is app-owned consumers with library validation. * Durable advisory capture for the live index queue ([COR-997](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-997/durable-advisory-capture-for-job-stream-dead-lettering-close-the-repo)). **Exit:** 0 hand-rolled fetch loops; 0 app-side create/update calls; legacy consume-surface list empty; migrated durables are fleet CRs with delivery state untouched.

WHAT MOVES - jsconsumer.Run + Process replace the subscribe/backoff loop, the Fetch loop, the shutdown-error classification and the span prologue. MaxMessages 1 preserves the Fetch(1) pacing: AckWait runs from server delivery into the client buffer, not from callback dispatch, so anything queued behind a slow fan would age unprocessed. - The ladder is now the durable's. lifecycleBackOff derives consumerFailureDelay x (consumerMaxDeliver-1) from the two constants rather than restating them, so the numbers that must agree cannot drift. The app's disposition for a failed fan is DO NOTHING — the ack timeout brings the delivery back on that ladder. A client NakWithDelay beside a server ladder is the ENT-1535 defect (the server stretches each NAK by the BackOff increments, so redeliveries follow neither); a plain Nak would redeliver immediately and skip the ladder. - Every field CreateOrUpdateConsumer sends is now stated, because a field omitted in code is not "unchanged on the durable" — it is reset to a default. WHAT DOES NOT MOVE Give-up semantics. No Term path, no Retry, no DLQ: the event is republished verbatim so nothing about it can be permanently unprocessable, and resource_lifecycle_v1 is limits-retention — it holds every event for its full max age whatever this consumer does, so the replay path is the source stream. Adding capture would need a DLQ stream and a meta-fanout publish grant that do not exist. InactiveThreshold stays unset, and now says so explicitly. The 2026-06-01 reaping valve is for interest streams where an abandoned durable pins deliveries for ALL consumers; on limits retention an idle durable pins nothing. All seven cells carry no threshold today and none is added. The timing envelope is unchanged — 8 deliveries, give up at t+3m30s — which the pre-flight is what licenses claiming: snapshots of all 7 cells showed this durable has NO server-side backoff, so the effective ladder really was the client's flat 30s. (webhook-forwarder and fanout are NOT like this; they carry an undeclared 41h ladder, COR-1270. Loop 2 cannot make this claim.) ONE DELIBERATE CONFIG CHANGE MaxAckPending 65536 -> 1000. The 65536 in all seven cells was never chosen: nats.go's legacy PullSubscribe copies its own client-side subscription-channel capacity into the server config. jsconsumer sends the field on every start, so leaving it zero would have rewritten all seven silently; this makes it a recorded decision instead. Generous either way at a one-message prefetch. TWO KNOWN DELTAS - /readyz is narrower. The old loop held a `subscribed` bool set after each successful PullSubscribe, so a RETRYABLE boot failure (stream absent, no responders) also read NotReady. jsconsumer.Run exposes no start-success signal, so Ready() now reports only that the configuration was accepted — which does cover this migration's likeliest failure, an immutable-field disagreement. In exchange Run recreates a consume loop that closes mid-run, as the old outer loop did. Closing the gap needs go-nuts to expose readiness from Run; recorded beside the Runner.Drain and FloorMonitor-attach gaps entire-search #131 logged. - The fan-failure log drops redeliver_in and gains max_deliver. The app no longer schedules the redelivery, so printing a delay would be a claim about someone else's config — true only while the two agree, which is the drift this track exists to remove. Position in the ladder is what a responder can act on; the ladder is on the durable. outcome=nak is kept verbatim on the metric: dashboards key on it and its meaning is unchanged (this delivery failed and will come back). What changed is who schedules the redelivery, which the metric never described. The local ackableMsg seam and numDelivered helper are gone — jetstream.Msg is already an interface, natsmsgtest.FakeMsg is the double, and backoff.NumDelivered is the library's own reading of the delivery count. Ready() reflected only configRejected — set when jsconsumer.Run RETURNS, which it does only for a permanently rejected config. Run retries everything else and logs a warning per attempt, so through the outages a readiness gate exists for (stream not provisioned yet, JetStream unreachable while the TCP connection is up: no responders, meta-leader election, a CONSUMER.CREATE permission rejection surfacing as a timeout) configRejected never flips and /readyz stayed green while nothing was consumed. Ready() is now (config accepted) AND (durable reachable), the second refreshed by a slow probe that lives exactly as long as the consume loop. Run joins it on the way out, so no ConsumerInfo can be in flight on a connection the caller is about to drain. What the probe proves: the stream and durable exist and the JetStream API answered. What it does not: that THIS process is the one consuming (replicas share the durable), or that a delivery arrived. It is a strictly better proxy than configRejected for every case above, and it starts false — so a pod is NotReady until the first success, matching the old gate's boot behaviour. Two cadences, because startup and outage want opposite things. The first probe races Run creating the durable, so a single 5s interval left a healthy pod NotReady for seconds after it was already consuming — visible as a 5.10s test runtime, now 0.36s. It polls at 250ms until the first success, then settles to 5s, so a sustained outage is not hammered with four ConsumerInfo requests a second at the moment the server is already struggling. THE PROBE JOIN DEADLOCKED ON A REJECTED CONFIG (lifecycle.go) I registered `defer stopProbe()` and then `defer func(){ <-probeDone }()`. Defers run LIFO, so the JOIN ran first and the cancel second — and the probe exits only on its context. A Run that returned while the parent context was still alive (the only such path: a permanently rejected config) therefore blocked in its own defer until whole-app shutdown: goroutine leaked, the caller's lifecycleDone never closed, and the probe kept polling — at the 250ms startup cadence if CONSUMER.INFO never succeeded. Now one defer that cancels THEN joins. The join is still required: an in-flight ConsumerInfo must not outlive Run and land on a connection the caller is about to drain. TestLifecycleRun_ReturnsOnRejectedConfig covers it, with the parent context deliberately left alive because that is the condition the bug needed. The rejection is the real-world one this migration risks — a durable pre-existing with an immutable field set differently — and the broker supplies it verbatim: "ack policy can not be updated" (err_code 10012). Verified it catches the bug: with the two defers restored the test fails at its 20s guard; with the fix it returns in 0.04s. 2. SUSTAINED-OUTAGE TELEMETRY WAS LOST WITH natslog.Health Adopting jsconsumer.Run dropped the old subscribe loop's natslog.Health supervision, and Run is not an equivalent: it logs every retryable failure at WARN indefinitely, with no escalation and no counter. So the five-minute warn->error escalation and the restart-proof nats.consumer.recoverable_failures counter both went away. That matters most in US/default mode, where readiness DELIBERATELY excludes this consumer so a problem here cannot stall the live github_meta fan-out — which means a stopped lifecycle fan there shows up only in telemetry, and the telemetry had been removed. The readiness probe is the programmatic signal Run does not expose, so it now drives Health: SubscribeErr on a failed probe (the create/bind path, which absorbs a slow JetStream API and a not-yet-provisioned stream), Recovered on success. That required teaching natslog the modern client's errors first, and this is the part worth review attention. nuts.IsTransientSubscribeErr keys on the LEGACY nats.* values; the jetstream package defines its own distinct ones — jetstream.ErrStreamNotFound is a *jsError carrying an APIError, not nats.ErrStreamNotFound, so errors.Is finds neither across the two. Wiring the probe in naively would have classified every rollout-ordering failure as a FAULT and logged it at ERROR: the exact alert-eroding noise natslog exists to prevent (COR-1228), introduced by the package meant to prevent it. So SubscribeErr now also matches jetstream.ErrStreamNotFound (canonical "Stream not yet present, retrying", warn forever, excluded from escalation), and isTransientSubscribeErr extends the go-nuts predicate with ErrConsumerNotFound / ErrConsumerDoesNotExist (a supervised runner recreates a missing durable, so this is a race until escalation says otherwise) and ErrJetStreamNotEnabled (a 503 from a server still starting). ErrConsumerCreate and ErrBadRequest stay at ERROR — the migration's likeliest failure must page. TestSubscribeErrClassifiesModernClientErrors is the modern half of the existing severity table. Note on the fixture: its wantMsg column was initially never read, which is the same defect as no test — and it hid a wrong expectation, since the rollout-ordering case swaps in the canonical message rather than prefixing the caller's. Both fixed; the message is now asserted. This extension belongs in go-nuts beside the predicate it extends. Left here until the modern-client migration has more than one adopter to generalise from — recorded with the Runner.Drain / FloorMonitor-attach / Run-readiness follow-ups. A MISSING DURABLE MEANT TWO THINGS AND I CLASSIFIED IT AS ONE I demoted the modern ErrConsumerNotFound / ErrConsumerDoesNotExist to transient inside natslog. That is right during the initial create race and wrong afterwards, and natslog already had the contract I broke: nats.ErrConsumerDeleted stays at ERROR because a durable that disappears is recreated from the stream's DeliverPolicy, losing the cursor. For THIS consumer that is not abstract — DeliverPolicy is all and resource_lifecycle_v1 retains up to 96h, so a recreate re-fans the retained backlog cross-region, and the demotion would have let it happen under generic warnings. The distinction is not available from the error value, so it does not belong in a predicate over error values. natslog goes back to keeping a missing consumer loud (ErrJetStreamNotEnabled stays transient — a 503 from a server still starting), and the PROBE makes the call, because only the probe knows which side of the first successful bind it is on: - before any bind + consumer missing -> debug, no failure run. Expected: Run is concurrently creating it and logs its own attempts. - after a bind -> natslog.SubscribeErr, which is now ERROR for this class. - everything else (no responders, timeouts, stream missing) -> SubscribeErr from the first attempt, so a real outage at boot still escalates after five minutes. everBound is one-way on purpose: re-entering the startup posture after a real disappearance would both silence it and hammer the server at the fast cadence. Honest limit, stated in the code: at a 5s cadence this probe can miss a delete that Run recreates before the next tick, so it is a backstop, not a detector. The reliable signal is the runner's own recreate, which jsconsumer only logs. 2. THE FAST STARTUP PHASE WAS UNBOUNDED It ended on the first success only, so a pod starting while the stream or the API was unavailable never left it: four CONSUMER.INFO requests and — after the Health wiring — four log lines per second, indefinitely. That contradicted the comment directly above it and recreated the log-volume problem natslog exists to solve. The phase is now bounded by attempts as well: 20 at 250ms (~5s, orders of magnitude more than creating a durable takes), then the steady 5s cadence whether or not it ever succeeded. ON THE TESTS The disappearance test asserts LOG LEVEL, not just the boolean, because the level is what the finding was about — it deletes a bound durable under the consumer and requires ERROR. The burst test is worth noting: my first version re-implemented the cadence loop and counted its own probes over 8 wall-clock seconds. It passed — and would have kept passing with the bound deleted from production, which is the same defect as no test, and slow as well as useless. The decision is now a pure function (nextProbeInterval) that probeDurable actually calls, and the test drives that. Verified it fails with the bound removed: "interval = 250ms, want the steady 5s". Runtime 8.03s -> 0.00s. Gate: build, vet, go mod tidy -diff, git diff --check, gofmt -s, go test ./..., go test -race -count=2, golangci-lint (0 issues) — all clean. So a durable that bound on its first probe kept ~19 unspent attempts, and a genuine loss inside the following ~95s (19 spent one per 5s tick) returned 250ms — re-entering the fast cadence to hammer a server that had just lost the durable. The comment three lines above said that must never happen; the code did not implement it. Every single-call assertion I had written passed, because the broken property is about a SEQUENCE: end, and never resume. So the decision is now a small state machine (probeCadence) whose observe(bound) ZEROES the budget on success rather than leaving it to decay, and the test drives sequences — never-binds, binds-immediately- then-loses, binds-mid-startup-then-loses. CANCELLING AN IN-FLIGHT PROBE LOGGED A FALSE ERROR ON EVERY ROLLOUT Run cancels the probe context on the way out, so a CONSUMER.INFO in flight at that moment returns context.Canceled. That value is not in the transient set, so it reached Health as a fault: {"level":"ERROR","msg":"Lifecycle durable unreachable; reporting NotReady","error":"context canceled"} Self-inflicted shutdown noise — precisely what natslog exists to remove (COR-1228: 57 ErrNoResponders in 83ms during a deploy, three false alerts in forty minutes) — reintroduced by the probe added to report real outages. Guarded narrowly: BOTH the parent context being done AND the error being context.Canceled, the same discipline as nuts.IsShutdownFetchErr, which will only call a drain benign when ctx is already done. A context.DeadlineExceeded from the probe's own timeout leaves the parent alive and still reaches Health, as do consumer-deletion and stream-missing errors. The test asserts both directions — silence on a cancelled parent, and a complaint on a live one — so the guard cannot be widened into swallowing real failures without going red. Verified: removing it reproduces the exact ERROR record above. Gate: build, vet, go mod tidy -diff, git diff --check, gofmt -s, go test ./..., go test -race ./... {"id":"COR-1252","title":"NATS robustness & standardization: stop fixing per-app, enforce per-layer","description":"## Problem

Every NATS correctness fix this month landed in the app where it bit, and the bug class resurfaced in the next app: Term-without-settle was fixed three times (<issue id="96688401-2b2d-48dd-8a77-a4400bd1bb45" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1492/entire-search-exhausted-ref-events-are-termed-which-does-not-settle">ENT-1492</issue> → <issue id="61e680fd-b8da-4226-8d21-e703b0482d29" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1525/ci-webhooks-the-outbound-dispatcher-still-terms-poison-ref-events-on">ENT-1525</issue> → <issue id="2e3ba22f-563d-407f-a1c0-28e470b8fe06" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1496/entire-search-lifecycle-consumer-still-terms-exhausted-events-same-ent">ENT-1496</issue> still open); five consumers were missing `$JS.ACK` grants (<issue id="33e005d5-f925-4d4a-b46c-d423ec5ac549" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1224/five-webhooks-github-v1-consumers-lack-an-explicit-dollarjsack-publish">COR-1224</issue>); an app backoff config silently overriding AckWait caused a 48h indexer backlog. The Aug 5–6 P1s (12 auto-incidents, one 9h ack-floor stall cleared with a lossy `stream rmm`) showed the new DLQ doesn't prevent stalls. Detection today is production P1s. NATS correctness lives in per-app convention — whack-a-mole.

## Proposed solution

Move every invariant into a layer where divergence is structurally impossible or automatically visible:

1. **Library owns the discipline** — floor-age circuit breaker + invariant-rejecting configs in go-nuts `jsconsumer`; apps inherit via migration.
2. **Config is generated, not hand-written** — durables become fleet-managed NACK `Consumer` CRs (extending the nats-streams "Option A" decision); NATS users, grants, and per-durable ack-floor monitors generated from the CRs; stream contracts published as a module.
3. **Admission control** — CR safety lint + import-boundary lint (raw JetStream calls legal only inside go-nuts, ratcheted).
4. **Continuous verification** — weekly poison-message conformance canary; NATS as a chaos fault target.

Four tracks as sub-issues, ~60 pd total, target Oct 30. Milestones: **M1** stalls dead (Aug 22) · **M2** routing real (Sep 5) · **M3** loops retired (Oct 14) · **M4** guarded (Oct 30).

Out of scope by decision (2026-08-11): the wire-format program (<issue id="de67b2e7-cb22-4764-8bf7-afe42524e94c" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1087/shrink-webhook-nats-messages-with-raw-payloads-and-conditional">COR-1087</issue>) is parked; the payload-cliff risk is accepted with ops-side {"id":"COR-1255","title":"Track E — Guardrails & cell industrialization: admission control, generation, fault injection (wk 4–12, ~22.5 pd)","description":"## Problem

Stream invariants are enforced by comments (`webhooks_github_v1 maxAge ≥ 48h` vs the ~41h redelivery envelope); NATS users/grants are hand-written per cell — how five consumers shipped without `$JS.ACK` grants (<issue id="33e005d5-f925-4d4a-b46c-d423ec5ac549" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1224/five-webhooks-github-v1-consumers-lack-an-explicit-dollarjsack-publish">COR-1224</issue>); monitors are hand-added per durable, so a consumer can ship unmonitored; deploys race the shared fleet branch with no ordering guard (a prod schema rollback already happened, <issue id="fbd6173d-349e-42f7-9a38-856d62fa4ef6" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1046/deploy-pipeline-race-out-of-order-promotedeploy-lets-an-older-build">COR-1046</issue>); and the cell layer has zero fault-injection coverage — NATS is exempt in Antithesis, so every NATS failure mode has been discovered in production.

## Proposed solution

* **Admission control, three arms:** stream/consumer-CR invariant checks (maxAge vs ladder, DLQ pairing, limits); a NACK CR safety lint (require `preventDelete` + full-mirror specs, ban `inactiveThreshold`, block server-immutable edits, unique (stream, durable) per cluster); import-boundary lint — raw JetStream calls legal only inside go-nuts, ratcheted (grandfathered list only shrinks, named owner).
* promote↔deploy ordering gate (<issue id="fbd6173d-349e-42f7-9a38-856d62fa4ef6" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1046/deploy-pipeline-race-out-of-order-promotedeploy-lets-an-older-build">COR-1046</issue>); strict up-to-date status checks on entire-api.
* Missing monitors: OTLP export failure (<issue id="715d583f-81ab-4119-b9ea-8606e8c10216" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1085/no-monitor-on-otlp-metric-export-failure-delta-temporality-makes-a">COR-1085</issue>), entire-core log indexing (<issue id="b3e73f21-f13e-45e4-b769-b7ae67b6b913" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1083/entire-core-logs-are-not-indexed-in-datadog">COR-1083</issue>), gateway 5xx (<issue id="209bcc59-9c5f-4907-a21d-2e1659431707" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1099/gateway-generated-5xx-are-invisible-no-envoy-telemetry-and-app-side">COR-1099</issue>); runner_work monitors as GA gate.
* **Generate** NATS users, publish grants, and per-durable ack-floor monitors from the fleet Consumer CRs — the <issue id="33e005d5-f925-4d4a-b46c-d423ec5ac549" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1224/five-webhooks-github-v1-consumers-lack-an-explicit-dollarjsack-publish">COR-1224</issue> class can't recur through this path.
* Fault injection to the cell layer: NATS as a fault target, entire-api in the Antithesis SUT; first chaos run exercises a NATS partition against a live consumer.

    "description": "## Problem

Every NATS correctness fix this month landed in the app where it bit, and the bug class resurfaced in the next app: Term-without-settle was fixed three times (<issue id="96688401-2b2d-48dd-8a77-a4400bd1bb45" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1492/entire-search-exhausted-ref-events-are-termed-which-does-not-settle">ENT-1492</issue> → <issue id="61e680fd-b8da-4226-8d21-e703b0482d29" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1525/ci-webhooks-the-outbound-dispatcher-still-terms-poison-ref-events-on">ENT-1525</issue> → <issue id="2e3ba22f-563d-407f-a1c0-28e470b8fe06" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1496/entire-search-lifecycle-consumer-still-terms-exhausted-events-same-ent">ENT-1496</issue> still open); five consumers were missing `$JS.ACK` grants (<issue id="33e005d5-f925-4d4a-b46c-d423ec5ac549" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1224/five-webhooks-github-v1-consumers-lack-an-explicit-dollarjsack-publish">COR-1224</issue>); an app backoff config silently overriding AckWait caused a 48h indexer backlog. {"id":"ENT-1496","title":"entire-search: lifecycle consumer still Terms exhausted events (same ENT-1492 bug, no DLQ)","description":"## Context

<issue id="96688401-2b2d-48dd-8a77-a4400bd1bb45" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1492/entire-search-exhausted-ref-events-are-termed-which-does-not-settle">ENT-1492</issue> replaced `Term()` with dead-letter-then-Ack on the **ref** consumer (`search-indexer-refs` on `repo_refs_v1`), because Term does not settle a message on NATS 2.14.2 — it pins the durable's ack floor until StreamMaxAge and silently discards the event.

The **lifecycle** consumer (`resource_lifecycle_v1.repo.deleted` → Turbopuffer namespace delete, <issue id="0b0713a3-819c-4ae5-a541-e84544314a27" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1001/semantic-search-handle-account-deletion">ENT-1001</issue>) shares the exact same worker/`settleFailure` code path in `internal/consumer/consumer.go` and was deliberately left on the legacy Term fallback (`settleTerminal` with no DLQ configured), because:

* `repo_refs_dlq_v1` and the `repo.refs.dlq.v1.>` publish grant are named for and scoped to ref events; folding lifecycle poison into it would muddy the stream contract
* lifecycle events are rare (repo deletions only) and the consumer is kill-switch-guarded (`NATS_LIFECYCLE_ENABLED`)

So the latent bug remains there: a lifecycle event that exhausts its 7 deliveries (or fails parse / permanently) is Term'd → ack floor pins until `resource_lifecycle_v1`'s maxAge (96h prod) → and the namespace cleanup is silently dropped, leaving the deleted repo's `v4-{repoULID}` Turbopuffer namespace (and its indexed content) in place.

## Fix options

1. Dedicated `resource_lifecycle_dlq_v1`-style stream + grant + `WithDeadLetter` wiring (the full <issue id="96688401-2b2d-48dd-8a77-a4400bd1bb45" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1492/entire-search-exhausted-ref-events-are-termed-which-does-not-settle">ENT-1492</issue> pattern) — probably overkill for the volume
2. A reconcile/sweep that re-derives pending namespace deletions from the system of record, making a dropped event self-healing — then exhausted events can simply Ack
3. Term→Ack with a loud error log (settles reliably, no floor pin; trades the wedged-floor alert for a logged drop)

Note the code fallback in `Consumer.settleTerminal` already logs Term errors instead of discarding them, and every settle log line carries `stream_seq`, so triage is better than it was pre-<issue id="96688401-2b2d-48dd-8a77-a4400bd1bb45" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1492/entire-search-exhausted-ref-events-are-termed-which-does-not-settle">ENT-1492</issue> regardless.

Residual-data angle: a dropped `repo.deleted` cleanup is a data-retention issue, not just an indexing gap — worth weighing when prioritizing.","priority":{"value":4,"name":"Low"},"url":"https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1496/entire-search-lifecycle-consumer-still-terms-exhausted-events-same-ent","gitBranchName":"nodo/ent-1496-entire-search-lifecycle-consumer-still-terms-exhausted","createdAt":"2026-08-04T22:44:21.629Z","updatedAt":"2026-08-12T09:15:44.237Z","archivedAt":null,"completedAt":null,"startedAt":null,"canceledAt":null,"dueDate":null,"slaStartedAt":null,"slaMediumRiskAt":null,"slaHighRiskAt":null,"slaBreachesAt":null,"status":"Backlog","statusType":"backlog","labels":["Backend","Bug"],"attachments":[],"documents":[],"stateHistory":[{"state":{"id":"8e117581-93c5-4ca8-b53b-8fc6d2c7510f","name":"Backlog","type":"backlog"},"startedAt":"2026-08-04T22:44:21.629Z","endedAt":null}],"releases":[],"createdBy":"Evis Drenova","createdById":"bd1c458e-3bb3-4d0c-8ad7-e36f19afc156","project":"Entire Search","projectId":"fa9553ac-b2e9-4642-8ee4-56262ee9aca0","team":"Entire","teamId":"832db0be-d9d8-45dc-9774-7f35babe62c0","relations":{"blocks":[],"blockedBy":[],"relatedTo":[{"id":"ENT-1492","title":"entire-search: exhausted ref events are Termed, which does not settle them — dead-letter and Ack instead"},{"id":"ENT-1001","title":"[semantic-search] handle account deletion"},{"id":"ENT-1601","title":"Track A — Stall-proofing: the poison-message remedy lands in go-nuts (wk 1–3, ~11 pd)"},{"id":"COR-1252","title":"NATS robustness & standardization: stop fixing per-app, enforce per-layer"},{"id":"ENT-1525","title":"ci-webhooks: the outbound dispatcher still Terms poison ref events on repo_refs_v1 (same ENT-1492 bug, and the DLQ grant is missing)"}],"duplicateOf":null}}

{"id":"ENT-1625","title":"entire-search: "checkpoints not ready" is treated as a failure — hydration lag burns the retry ladder and leaves a permanent index gap","description":"## Symptom

`summarizeCheckpointResults` classifies a checkpoint whose hydration/metadata isn't ready yet as a **failure**. It is a *not yet* condition, and treating it as failure costs a permanent hole in the search index.

Confirmed in prod on 2026-08-13 (P2 `[search eks-prod-us-east-2] ref event permanently dropped`, repo `01KZR413REBVRF8ZQTXFVT2W2H` = `GoodnotesGlobal/goodnotes-frontend-entire-checkpoints`, us jurisdiction). Checkpoints `9c9250171eb0` and `a7f968a7a324` are **not in the index and nothing will put them there** short of a manual backfill.

## Evidence

`@error` was byte-identical on all five deliveries:

```
2/11 checkpoints not ready (hydration/metadata), re-queuing: 9c9250171eb0, a7f968a7a324
```

Per-attempt counters, also identical every time:

| field | value |
| -- | -- |
| `checkpoint_count` | 11 |
| `total_indexed` | 35 |
| `not_ready` | **2** |
| `index_failures` | 0 |
| `transcript_failures` | 0 |

Window: first delivery 10:48:12 UTC → dead-lettered 11:33:16 UTC (**45m04s**, `@attempts: 5`, `settle: dead_lettered`, `stream_seq: 3365017`). DLQ capture itself worked correctly per <issue id="96688401-2b2d-48dd-8a77-a4400bd1bb45" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1492/entire-search-exhausted-ref-events-are-termed-which-does-not-settle">ENT-1492</issue> — `Nats-Dlq-Reason: max_deliveries`, 1 message on `repo_refs_dlq_v1` (`aws-us-east-2`).

The repo was healthy before and after (four later events, all `not_ready: 0`), so this was a **transient hydration lag that outlived a fixed timer** — not a poison checkpoint.

## Mechanism — three separate defects

**1. Wrong granularity.** `requeueError` (`internal/handler/handler.go:1830`) returns a whole-event failure if *any* checkpoint is not ready. The 9 healthy checkpoints indexed successfully (35 vectors) on **every one of the 5 attempts** and were then discarded anyway. Same work done 5×, kept 0×.

**2. Wrong budget.** `notReady` is a bare `fmt.Errorf`, so it takes the generic retry path and spends the ladder that exists for *transient errors*. Nothing bounds hydration latency, so the budget is unrelated to what it's waiting on. Note <issue id="205b99bd-a2c8-4ed8-8d26-6bb9f8e4f992" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1601/track-a-stall-proofing-the-poison-message-remedy-lands-in-go-nuts-wk-1">ENT-1601</issue> does **not** relieve this — under the new server-owned ladder dead-letter lands at t+42m (`consumerBackoff`, `internal/consumer/consumer.go:658`), so this same event would still be dropped. And `consumerMaxTimeToDeadLetter = 45m` is now a startup invariant ("a future ladder that would take longer cannot start at all"), which deliberately closes "just extend the ladder" as an option.

**3. Wrong finality — this is the part that loses data.** Ref events carry explicit `old_target`→`new_target`, and each event starts where the previous one ended, so a dead-lettered range is never revisited. Verified from the logs:

| event | range | outcome |
| -- | -- | -- |
| dropped | `50abddff…` → `15922546…` | 2 checkpoints never indexed |
| next (12:24 UTC) | `15922546…` → `ea8c4624…` | clean |
| next (12:26 UTC) | `ea8c4624…` → `2ba01bb6…` | clean |

Contiguous but **disjoint** — the live path structurally cannot heal the gap. The monitor text agrees ("nothing will retry them automatically"). There is also no product-side signal that those two checkpoints aren't searchable; they silently aren't.

## Why this is not <issue id="99260cc2-5e54-4b5b-999d-5620d8da339e" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1408/search-increment-indexing-ent-1390-drops-self-healing-a-transcript">ENT-1408</issue>

<issue id="99260cc2-5e54-4b5b-999d-5620d8da339e" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1408/search-increment-indexing-ent-1390-drops-self-healing-a-transcript">ENT-1408</issue> is chunk-level *inside* a checkpoint — `stub_reason=transcript_absent`, increment offsets skipping a slice. This is event-level: the whole ref range is discarded before those code paths matter. Our logs show `transcript_failures: 0`. Same theme (self-healing lost), different code, different fix. Related, not duplicate.

## Fix shape

The codebase already contains the right precedent. `TranscriptPendingError` is typed and routed **deliberately outside** `jsconsumer.Retry` (`internal/consumer/consumer.go:375`) — capped and ACKed terminally rather than dead-lettered, on the reasoning that "a transcript may appear later." Hydration-not-ready wants the same treatment:

1. Type it (e.g. `HydrationPendingError`) so the consumer can give it a disposition of its own instead of the generic error ladder.
2. Re-queue only the not-ready subset, so completed checkpoints commit instead of being thrown away and redone.
3. Decide the terminal behaviour explicitly: either a long/unbounded pending track, or — if it must give up — have the dead-letter enqueue a backfill for the dropped range. The runbook already asserts the work is re-derivable from the repo's refs, so this is automatable rather than a human step.

## Recovery still outstanding

Repo `01KZR413REBVRF8ZQTXFVT2W2H` needs a backfill for ref update `50abddffec3f9486eafa8e83db8040370b3f2535` → `15922546819b8281601652ed2fe49c9edaa6c58d`. Not yet done.

## Notes picked up while investigating

* **Repeat offender overlap.** A 14-day census of `@not_ready:>0` found repo `01KWHDFJ0C575CRVF18DPVSQW0` hitting this same condition 5× on 2026-08-06 (it recovered, 0 drops). {"id":"COR-1224","title":"Five webhooks_github_v1 consumers lack an explicit $JS.ACK publish grant","description":"Found while rolling NATS to 2.14.4 for <issue id="f73ee309-c4d3-47fb-af75-0dcc23f7d31a" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1223/upgrade-nats-when-the-upstream-jetstream-oversized-record-fix-is">COR-1223</issue>. **Pre-existing, unrelated to that upgrade** — the roll only exposed it.

Fix is up as <pull-request id="6e3d27b9-35fc-46bf-93bb-198dae97f494" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/review/REDACTED">entirehq/fleet#4249</pull-request>.

## The bug

Five users consume `webhooks_github_v1` but have no `$JS.ACK.webhooks_github_v1.>` publish grant in `apps/nats/base/helmrelease.yaml`. They rely on `allow_responses`, which covers only **one** reply within **\~2m** of delivery.

An ack issued outside that window is rejected with `Publish Violation`. A rejected ack leaves the message **unsettled**, so it redelivers and the work repeats. On a poison message it pins the consumer's ack floor — the same failure mode <issue id="61e680fd-b8da-4226-8d21-e703b0482d29" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1525/ci-webhooks-the-outbound-dispatcher-still-terms-poison-ref-events-on">ENT-1525</issue> and <issue id="96688401-2b2d-48dd-8a77-a4400bd1bb45" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1492/entire-search-exhausted-ref-events-are-termed-which-does-not-settle">ENT-1492</issue> were filed for on other streams.

## How it surfaced

A NATS pod restart reliably pushes acks past the `allow_responses` window. Rolling `eks-prod-us-east-2` on 2026-08-10 produced three violations in 90 seconds:

```
15:03:38  webhook-forwarder  Publish Violation  $JS.ACK.webhooks_github_v1...
15:04:43  core-fanout        Publish Violation  $JS.ACK.webhooks_github_v1...
15:04:44  fanout             Publish Violation  $JS.ACK.webhooks_github_v1...
```

## Scope is wider than what logged

Auditing the ACLs against the stream's live consumer list:

| User | Consumes stream | Had ACK grant |
| -- | -- | -- |
| `webhook-forwarder` | yes | **no** |
| `fanout` | yes | **no** |
| `core-fanout` | yes | **no** |
| `meta-fanout` | yes | **no** |
| `trails-fanout` | yes (2 durables) | **no** |
| `entire-core-global` | yes | yes |

`meta-fanout` and `trails-fanout` carry the same latent gap and merely happened to ack inside the window. `entire-search` also holds the grant, with a comment giving this exact reasoning — so this is a **known pattern that five users were missed by**, not a new decision.

It only manifests in `eks-prod-us-east-2` because that is where `webhooks_github_v1` has real traffic; the staging copies are idle, which is why the earlier staging and regional-prod rolls were silent.

## Impact so far: none

All eight consumers settled at `pending=0`, `redelivered=0`, ack floors at the stream head. The denied acks were retried inside a fresh window. This is a latent correctness gap, not an active incident — but it will recur on every NATS restart, and it is exactly the shape that turns a poison message into a stuck consumer.

## Worth considering beyond the fix

The five grants close the immediate gap, but the underlying pattern is that `allow_responses` gets used as an implicit ack grant and silently expires under load or restart. A broader audit — every user that subscribes a stream and acks it, checked for a matching `$JS.ACK.<stream>.>` — would find whether other streams carry the same gap. `webhooks_github_v1` is simply the one with enough traffic and enough consumers to reveal it.

## Note for whoever looks next

The server logs this as `Publish Violation`, **not** `Permissions Violation`. Grepping for the latter matches nothing and reads as a clean result — that is why this was nearly missed. {"id":"COR-1270","title":"webhook-forwarder and fanout run a 41h orphaned BackOff ladder no code declares (live ENT-1535, prod)","description":"## What was found

Measured 2026-08-14 during Track D's loop-1 pre-flight, via `natsctl -- consumer info webhooks_github_v1 <durable> --json` on **prod us-east-2** and **staging us-west-2** (identical on both):

| durable | code declares | server actually stores | real envelope |
| -- | -- | -- | -- |
| `webhook-forwarder` | no `BackOff`, client `NakWithDelay(30s)` | `backoff: [30s, 2m, 10m, 1h, 4h, 12h, 24h]` | **41h12m30s** |
| `fanout-us-east-2` / `fanout-us-west-2` | no `BackOff`, client `NakWithDelay(30s)` | same 7 rungs | **41h12m30s** |
| `core-fanout` | no `BackOff` | absent | 3m30s — agrees |
| `meta-fanout` | no `BackOff` | absent | 3m30s — agrees |
| `trails-fanout-push` | no `BackOff` | absent | 3m30s — agrees |
| `trails-fanout-pull-request` | no `BackOff` | absent | 3m30s — agrees |

Two of the seven `webhooks_github_v1` consumers carry a server-side redelivery ladder that **no source file declares**, alongside a client-side `NakWithDelay(30s)`. That is mixed ownership — the <issue id="57d2a8d9-c2a6-49c4-8014-8a67857ef1b0" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1535/entire-search-the-ent-1492-dlq-doesnt-prevent-the-stall-a-poison-ref">ENT-1535</issue> defect — live in production.

Because the requested Nak delay equals `BackOff[0]` (both 30s), the server's stretch term is zero on the first rung and redeliveries then follow the **server** ladder exactly. So the real give-up envelope is **41h12m30s**, against `cmd/webhook-forwarder/forwarder.go:48-52`, which states: *"No* `nats.BackOff` *is set, so this is a free choice — not clamped to a schedule."*

## How it got there

`consumerMaxDeliver`'s own comment names the mechanism without drawing the conclusion: *"dropping* `nats.BackOff` *is tolerated (BackOff is not part of that comparison)."* It is tolerated by nats.go's `checkConfig`, which is exactly why the ladder survived its deletion from the source — legacy `PullSubscribe` **binds** to an existing durable and never updates it. So a ladder removed from code stays on the server forever.

The four durables that never carried a ladder never acquired an orphan. This is a history artefact, not a config decision — nobody chose 41 hours.

## Why it matters, independent of Track D

A delivery that keeps failing (entire-web 5xx, network error) holds the `webhooks_github_v1` **ack floor for up to 41 hours**. That stream is interest-retention with seven consumers, and a pinned floor is the <issue id="57d2a8d9-c2a6-49c4-8014-8a67857ef1b0" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1535/entire-search-the-ent-1492-dlq-doesnt-prevent-the-stall-a-poison-ref">ENT-1535</issue>/Aug 5–6 shape: the stall signal cannot distinguish one pinned message from a throughput collapse.

It is a **stall, not a loss**: 41h12m30s < the stream's 96h `maxAge`, so the delivery still reaches DLQ capture on delivery 8.

**Second finding — nothing observes this today.** The only per-consumer monitor on this stream (`monitor_ingest_consumer_backlog.tf`) fires on `num_pending + num_ack_pending > 5000` sustained over 20m — a *volume* signal, sized for the 2026-06-01 orphaned-durable starvation. A single message pinning the floor for 41h leaves `num_ack_pending` at 1 and never trips it. Unlike `repo_refs_v1`, `webhooks_github_v1` has **no ack-floor-age monitor at all**, so this behaviour is not merely undocumented — it is unmeasured.

## Proposed work

1. **Decide the intended envelope.** Options span 3m30s (a declared flat 30s ladder), ~42m (the entire-search shape `[5m, 5m, 5m, 12m, 15m]`), and ~4h (bounded but patient). The real question is how long an entire-web outage should be absorbed automatically versus dead-lettered for manual replay — `webhooks_github_dlq` retains 7 days in prod, and replay is a manual `mirrorctl` operation.
2. **Make it declared, not inherited.** Whichever envelope is chosen, it has to be written where the code says it is. Reconciling an existing durable's `BackOff` needs `CreateOrUpdateConsumer` (the modern client) — which is precisely what the Track D migration of these two loops does, so the fix and the migration can be the same change if the timing suits.
3. **Close the observability gap** — an ack-floor-age monitor on `webhooks_github_v1`, sized under whatever envelope is chosen.

## Relationship to Track D

Found by <issue id="3b85cbc3-db3f-422f-acf9-aa89bc5e47c8" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1254/track-d-consumer-standardization-jsconsumer-everywhere-durables-as">COR-1254</issue>'s pre-flight and it changes that plan (loop 2 and loop 9 are no longer envelope-preserving migrations — see the correction on mirror-pipeline trail #100), but it is **not** created by the migration and should not wait on it. The migration is the natural vehicle for item 2; items 1 and 3 stand on their own.
