{"id":"COR-1046","title":"Deploy pipeline race: out-of-order promote/deploy lets an older build overwrite a newer one (rolled back the ENT-1231 schema in prod+staging)","description":"entiredb's Main workflow promotes/deploys whatever build finishes CI last, not the newest commit — two adjacent merges can land out of order and roll the fleet pin backwards.

**Incident (2026-07-23, \~06:08–07:00 UTC):**

* 05:43 Main starts for `3fc2552` (parent commit); 05:49 Main starts for `7553eef` (<issue id="6d58017a-c47a-4279-8c9e-9de3c6e487a1" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1231/migrate-the-collaborative-trail-body-editor-editor-documents-durable">ENT-1231</issue> SA-grant schema change, child commit)
* `7553eef`'s core deploy+promote finished FIRST (fleet pins 06:00/06:02); its pods wrote the new SpiceDB schema and the reconciler granted `platform#svc_editor_sync` in every region
* `3fc2552`'s (older!) deploy+promote finished second (fleet pins 06:06/06:08) — rolling core BACK to pre-schema code in staging AND prod
* Every rolled-back core then error-looped `SchemaService/WriteSchema` (~14/min, all regions): the old schema write would delete `svc_editor_sync`, which now has a tuple under it — `INVALID_ARGUMENT`, permanently (code rollback cannot fix it; the tuple persists)
* No user-facing authz impact (SpiceDB serves the stored schema); core's schema/grant reconciliation was dead until re-pinned
* Recovery: re-ran `promote-entire-core` + `deploy-entire-core` on the `7553eef` run → fleet PR #3570 (prod, merged 06:49) + deploy pin (staging, 06:56); reused the original image digest, no rebuild

**Fix ideas:** promote/deploy jobs should refuse to write a fleet pin whose source commit is an ancestor of the currently-pinned one (git ancestry check in the resolve step), or serialize fleet writes per app by commit order via a concurrency group keyed to the app with cancel-in-progress semantics that favor the newer commit.

Schema-change deploys make this race *sticky* (the SpiceDB tuple-under-relation guard turns a transient rollback into a permanent error loop) — worth fixing before more `core/authz/schema.go` changes land.

Found while shipping <issue id="6d58017a-c47a-4279-8c9e-9de3c6e487a1" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1231/migrate-the-collaborative-trail-body-editor-editor-documents-durable">ENT-1231</issue>. As of Aug 17: the foundational fix shipped, but the standardization program is still early. I would not call COR-1252 done.

| Track | State | Reality |
|---|---|---|
| A — stall-proofing | Done | go-nuts retry discipline and real-broker tests merged; first entire-search adopter promoted |
| B — alert routing | Canceled | Re-homed outside this program; underlying routing gap remains |
| D — migrations | In Progress | Bootstrap merged; first of 11 durable migrations is still a draft |
| E — guardrails | Backlog | Admission lint, generated grants/monitors, and NATS chaos work have not started |

What shipped:

- go-nuts retry/DLQ/floor telemetry: [#14](https://github.com/entireio/go-nuts/pull/14).
- Real-broker semantic suite: [#15](https://github.com/entireio/go-nuts/pull/15), [#16](https://github.com/entireio/go-nuts/pull/16).
- entire-search adoption: [#178](https://github.com/entirehq/entire-search/pull/178). Its staging deployment and production promotion succeeded, and the generated Fleet promotion [#4436](https://github.com/entirehq/fleet/pull/4436) merged. I did not re-check actual pod reconciliation or post-rollout production behavior.
- Runbook and monitor changes: Fleet [#4398](https://github.com/entirehq/fleet/pull/4398), Infra [#1167](https://github.com/entirehq/infra/pull/1167).
- Track D bootstrap/harness: mirror-pipeline [#245](https://github.com/entirehq/mirror-pipeline/pull/245).

The immediate work item is mirror-pipeline [#246](https://github.com/entirehq/mirror-pipeline/pull/246): open draft, green CI, clean merge state, no formal reviews. It is the first actual consumer migration; roughly ten durable migrations remain afterward. Nothing newer is linked, and activity stopped on Aug 14.

Important scope drift:

- Consumer CR ownership was parked after the canary analysis found bind-only ordering and `InactiveThreshold` blockers. COR-1252 and COR-1254 still describe CR-managed durables as the plan, so their descriptions are stale.
- The enforcing floor breaker did not ship operationally: it is observe-only, its soak never started, and enforce-or-delete remains undecided.
- The live poison-message conformance canary was canceled, leaving the end-to-end DLQ path unproven in a live cell.
- Track E’s “generate grants and monitors from Consumer CRs” now needs redesign or parking.

Known residual risks include [COR-1270](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1270) — a high-priority live 41-hour orphaned ladder — and [ENT-1496](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1496), the lifecycle consumer’s remaining bare-Term behavior. The non-lossy quarantine tool was canceled, so a capture-defeating stall still falls back to lossy `stream rmm`.

Bottom line: one strong library/adopter slice is in production desired state; the “stop fixing per-app” outcome is not yet achieved. The critical path is review/merge #246, burn down the remaining consumers, then rewrite Track E around the non-CR paved road. M3 remains recorded for Oct 14 and M4 for Oct 30, but the umbrella has no due date or current health signal.

---
name: live-pr-review-entire
description: Review a live PR or branch change in the entire repo family when the user says "review this change", "review this PR", "review again", or asks whether it is shippable.
argument-hint: "[repo-or-pr-context]"
user-invocable: false
allowed-tools:
  - Read
  - Grep
  - Bash
---

# live-pr-review-entire

Use this when the task is a real review of a live artifact in `entiredb`, `mirror-pipeline`, `fleet`, `git-sync`, or a task-area clone. Do not use it for implementation-only asks unless the user explicitly wants findings first.

## When to use

Triggers:

1. The user says `review this change`, `review this PR`, `re-review`, `check again`, or asks whether something is shippable.
2. The checkout may be ambiguous: GitHub PR, local branch diff, staged diff, or a throwaway clone.
3. Correctness may depend on adjacent contracts like Fleet manifests, JetStream authz, companion repos, or CI state.

Non-goals:

1. Do not start coding fixes unless the user asks for them.
2. Do not summarize the PR description as if that were the review.

## Inputs / context to gather

1. Confirm the actual repo and review surface first.
   - `pwd`
   - `git status --short --branch`
   - `git remote -v`
   - If the current directory is not a repo, look for the nested checkout that is.
2. Identify the authoritative artifact.
   - GitHub PR: `gh pr view ... --json ...`, `gh pr diff ...`
   - Local branch: compare `origin/main...HEAD` vs `main...HEAD` only after confirming which base is real
   - Staged or unstaged review: inspect both before assuming the branch diff is enough
3. Gather adjacent contracts only when the runtime path crosses boundaries.
   - Fleet manifests / kustomize renders
   - Companion repo code paths
   - CI or check status when the user asks

## Procedure

1. Establish the review surface before reading much code.
   - Confirm PR number, base, head SHA, branch name, changed files, and whether the local checkout matches it.
   - If the repo uses `entire://` remotes or a shallow clone, prefer explicit `gh ... -R ...` and GitHub metadata over assumptions from local refs.
   - If the custom remote will not resolve `pull/<n>/head`, fetch the PR head directly from GitHub into an isolated local ref or disposable worktree before deep reading.
   - If GitHub reports `mergeStateStatus=DIRTY` or `mergeable=CONFLICTING`, refresh the live base ref (`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/git/ref/heads/<base> --jq .object.sha`) before finalizing so you do not anchor conclusions to a stale branch point.
2. Read the diff and touched files, then inspect the smallest adjacent contract surface that can invalidate the review.
   - Examples: authz grants, stream ownership, filter subjects, telemetry queries, companion error contracts, or shared validators/helpers that fan out into create/delete/manage flows.
   - For delete/teardown work, trace both sides of the terminal transition: whether decommissioned resources are still routable for cleanup, and whether an event/outbox is acknowledged or a durable tombstone/reconciler remains after publish.
3. Run the narrowest meaningful validation.
   - Go: touched-package tests first; use broader tests only if the environment supports them.
   - Manifests: `kustomize build` or `kubectl kustomize`.
   - CI: `gh pr checks` when the user asks or when local validation is incomplete.
4. Report findings in severity order with concrete file anchors and explicit validation boundaries.
   - If no findings, say so directly and include residual risk or static-only caveats.
5. If the user asks for re-review, repeat from the current head SHA instead of relying on the earlier conclusion.
   - If they say they added a commit or ask to "re-pull from the branch", run a fresh `git fetch origin` (or the repo-appropriate fetch), re-pin `gh pr view` metadata, and confirm the new head SHA before keeping or changing the verdict.

## Efficiency plan

1. Cache the PR metadata, head SHA, and chosen review base early so you do not rediscover them.
2. Use `rg` to find exact symbols, stream names, filter subjects, or error strings from the diff before opening many files.
3. Stop expanding adjacent checks once the governing contract is confirmed.
4. If sandbox failures are clearly environmental, pivot to narrower validation or note the boundary instead of retrying the same command repeatedly.
5. If the branch moves mid-review, stop re-reading old conclusions and refresh only the metadata, diff base, and touched validation set for the new head.
6. If existing review comments or Bugbot feedback could overlap your findings, fetch them directly with `gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/pulls/<pr>/comments --paginate` and treat them as clues, not as substitutes for your own validation.

## Pitfalls and fixes

1. Symptom: `gh api ...?ref=...` fails in zsh.
   Fix: quote the path containing `?ref=`.
2. Symptom: `origin/main...HEAD` is misleading or empty.
   Fix: confirm the real PR base from GitHub metadata or fetch the base commit first.
3. Symptom: the current directory is not a repo.
   Fix: find the nested checkout and review there.
4. Symptom: `kustomize` is missing.
   Fix: try `kubectl kustomize`.
5. Symptom: `git fetch origin pull/<n>/head` or equivalent PR-ref fetches fail on an `entire://` remote.
   Fix: fetch from `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>.git` into an isolated ref or worktree, then review from there.
6. Symptom: Go/mise validation reports package or stat-cache permission errors, or parallel commands contaminate each other.
   Fix: use an isolated cache per command, e.g. `env GOCACHE=/private/tmp/<run>-gocache GOFLAGS=-mod=vendor go test -race -count=1 ./...`, and serialize affected Go commands.
7. Symptom: Go tests fail on localhost DB or listener setup inside the sandbox, for example `listen tcp6 [::1]:0: bind: operation not permitted` from `httptest`.
   Fix: rerun in a bind-capable context when possible, or narrow the test target and report the limitation as environmental.
8. Symptom: the user says they added a commit after you've already inspected files.
   Fix: treat the earlier read as stale, fetch the branch again, re-pin the PR head SHA, and only then finalize the review.
9. Symptom: the PR is already dirty/conflicting and the local diff still looks reviewable.
   Fix: refresh the live base SHA first; the old branch point may no longer represent the effective review delta.
10. Symptom: a validator change looks narrowly scoped in the diff, but the behavior impact is wider.
   Fix: trace all call sites of shared helpers like `validate()` before calling the change safe.
11. Symptom: teardown publishes a lifecycle event and then deletes its durable intent.
    Fix: inspect the publisher's delivery semantics and the downstream consumers. A best-effort/swallowed publish error needs acknowledged delivery, an outbox, or a tombstone/reconciler before the source anchor is removed.
12. Symptom: a delete intent is claimable after cluster decommission but cleanup cannot build its bridge.
    Fix: do not treat the resulting unknown-cluster error as success; preserve teardown routing or prevent decommission until pending/provisioned intents drain.
13. Symptom: an embedded NATS test reports `embedded nats server not ready in time` in the sandbox.
    Fix: loopback binding may be blocked; rerun in a bind-capable context and state the environmental boundary rather than treating it as a code failure.
14. Symptom: operator recovery infers a message was not acknowledged because `AckFloor` did not pass it.
    Fix: `AckFloor` is contiguous, not per-message evidence. Advancement is positive evidence; non-advancement is uncertain until consumer-specific evidence confirms the state. Never recommend destructive global stream deletion from the floor alone.
15. Symptom: code/docs treat `Ack`/`Term` returning nil as confirmed settlement.
    Fix: `$JS.ACK` authorization failure can surface asynchronously while the floor stays pinned. Require async-error monitoring and `$JS.ACK.>` permission, or use `DoubleAck` when confirmation is essential.
16. Symptom: a retry change assumes JetStream `BackOff` delays a plain `Nak()`.
    Fix: BackOff controls acknowledgement-timeout redelivery; plain NAK is immediate and `NakWithDelay` is client-timed. For a server-owned ladder, leave transient failures untouched and prove timing against a real broker.
17. Symptom: a destructive NATS quarantine drill accepts a URL merely containing `localhost` or `127.0.0.1`.
    Fix: hostname substring checks can accept a production port-forward or `localhost.example.com`; require a drill-created marker and independently verify the endpoint before deletion/recreation.

## Verification checklist

1. The final review names the exact artifact reviewed: PR number or branch, head SHA, and scope.
2. Findings, if any, are tied to concrete files or contracts.
3. The answer states what validation actually ran and what remained static-only.
4. Re-reviews explicitly confirm the new head state instead of repeating the old verdict.
5. If the branch moved during the review, the final answer names the refreshed head SHA and separates local validation from any still-pending GitHub checks.

Entire-Checkpoint: a9e49119f687","messageHeadline":"fix(natstest): shut the embedded server down when readiness times out","oid":"5de888fb84409aa7981e67777ed917c440516d8e"},{"authoredDate":"2026-08-14T14:19:32Z","authors":[{"email":"andrea@entire.io","id":"MDQ6VXNlcjgyOTE3OA==","login":"nodo","name":"Andrea Nodari"},{"email":"noreply@anthropic.com","id":"MDQ6VXNlcjgxODQ3","login":"claude","name":"Claude Opus 5 (1M context)"}],"committedDate":"2026-08-14T14:19:32Z","messageBody":"…(COR-1254 loop 1)

Loop 1 of Track D. The cross-region resource_lifecycle_v1 fan moves off its
hand-rolled PullSubscribe/Fetch(1) loop onto jsconsumer.Run + Process, and its
redelivery ladder moves server-side. Same durable name, so no recreation and no
redelivery storm; behaviour is preserved except where noted below.

WHAT MOVES

- jsconsumer.Run + Process replace the subscribe/backoff loop, the Fetch loop, the
  shutdown-error classification and the span prologue. MaxMessages 1 preserves the
  Fetch(1) pacing: AckWait runs from server delivery into the client buffer, not
  from callback dispatch, so anything queued behind a slow fan would age
  unprocessed.
- The ladder is now the durable's. lifecycleBackOff derives consumerFailureDelay
  x (consumerMaxDeliver-1) from the two constants rather than restating them, so
  the numbers that must agree cannot drift. The app's disposition for a failed fan
  is DO NOTHING — the ack timeout brings the delivery back on that ladder. A
  client NakWithDelay beside a server ladder is the ENT-1535 defect (the server
  stretches each NAK by the BackOff increments, so redeliveries follow neither);
  a plain Nak would redeliver immediately and skip the ladder.
- Every field CreateOrUpdateConsumer sends is now stated, because a field omitted
  in code is not "unchanged on the durable" — it is reset to a default.

WHAT DOES NOT MOVE

Give-up semantics. No Term path, no Retry, no DLQ: the event is republished
verbatim so nothing about it can be permanently unprocessable, and
resource_lifecycle_v1 is limits-retention — it holds every event for its full max
age whatever this consumer does, so the replay path is the source stream. Adding
capture would need a DLQ stream and a meta-fanout publish grant that do not exist.

InactiveThreshold stays unset, and now says so explicitly. The 2026-06-01 reaping
valve is for interest streams where an abandoned durable pins deliveries for ALL
consumers; on limits retention an idle durable pins nothing. All seven cells carry
no threshold today and none is added.

The timing envelope is unchanged — 8 deliveries, give up at t+3m30s — which the
pre-flight is what licenses claiming: snapshots of all 7 cells showed this durable
has NO server-side backoff, so the effective ladder really was the client's flat
30s. (webhook-forwarder and fanout are NOT like this; they carry an undeclared 41h
ladder, COR-1270. Loop 2 cannot make this claim.)

ONE DELIBERATE CONFIG CHANGE

MaxAckPending 65536 -> 1000. The 65536 in all seven cells was never chosen:
nats.go's legacy PullSubscribe copies its own client-side subscription-channel
capacity into the server config. jsconsumer sends the field on every start, so
leaving it zero would have rewritten all seven silently; this makes it a recorded
decision instead. Generous either way at a one-message prefetch.

TWO KNOWN DELTAS

- /readyz is narrower. The old loop held a `subscribed` bool set after each
  successful PullSubscribe, so a RETRYABLE boot failure (stream absent, no
  responders) also read NotReady. jsconsumer.Run exposes no start-success signal,
  so Ready() now reports only that the configuration was accepted — which does
  cover this migration's likeliest failure, an immutable-field disagreement. In
  exchange Run recreates a consume loop that closes mid-run, as the old outer loop
  did. Closing the gap needs go-nuts to expose readiness from Run; recorded beside
  the Runner.Drain and FloorMonitor-attach gaps entire-search #131 logged.
- The fan-failure log drops redeliver_in and gains max_deliver. The app no longer
  schedules the redelivery, so printing a delay would be a claim about someone
  else's config — true only while the two agree, which is the drift this track
  exists to remove. Position in the ladder is what a responder can act on; the
  ladder is on the durable.

outcome=nak is kept verbatim on the metric: dashboards key on it and its meaning
is unchanged (this delivery failed and will come back). What changed is who
schedules the redelivery, which the metric never described.

The local ackableMsg seam and numDelivered helper are gone — jetstream.Msg is
already an interface, natsmsgtest.FakeMsg is the double, and backoff.NumDelivered
is the library's own reading of the delivery count.

broker-level evidence rather than fake-level. The existing unit tests answer what
the handler DOES — which disposition it chose. These answer what the broker does
about it, which the fakes cannot: they encode the same model as the code, so a
belief held wrongly in both places produces a green test.

Three broker tests, one per load-bearing belief:

- StoredConfigIsTheRenderedConfig drives the REAL lifecycleConsumerConfig through

  the executable form of the pre-flight diff: against the 7-cell snapshot the
  intended delta is exactly two fields (the ladder appears, MaxAckPending becomes
  a chosen number) and everything else must land unchanged.
- FanFailure_IsRedeliveredByTheServerLadder pins the belief that replaced the
  client NakWithDelay: settle nothing, get the delivery back, paced by BackOff.
  The fixture ladder is SCALED to milliseconds and GROWING on purpose — on a flat
  ladder BackOff[0] equals AckWait, so the test would pass whether redelivery
  followed the ladder or merely the ack timeout, pinning nothing. Growing rungs

  |        8 | t+3m30s — give up            | t+3m30s — give up     |

maxAge to 6h, base is 96h), and against the rung-count/AckWait agreement rules.

Review finding on trail #102, and correct: documenting the readiness regression was
not the same as accepting it.

Ready() reflected only configRejected — set when jsconsumer.Run RETURNS, which it
does only for a permanently rejected config. Run retries everything else and logs a
warning per attempt, so through the outages a readiness gate exists for (stream not
provisioned yet, JetStream unreachable while the TCP connection is up: no
responders, meta-leader election, a CONSUMER.CREATE permission rejection surfacing
as a timeout) configRejected never flips and /readyz stayed green while nothing was
consumed.

I checked whether the pre-existing gate covered it. It does not:
natsregions.Health.Status() asks Local.IsConnected() only, so a live connection to a
JetStream that cannot answer passes it. And in lifecycleOnly mode this consumer is
the pod's SOLE readiness gate, so green there hides a real outage from anything
watching /readyz — exactly what the pre-migration `subscribed` bool did not do.

Ready() is now (config accepted) AND (durable reachable), the second refreshed by a
slow probe that lives exactly as long as the consume loop. Run joins it on the way
out, so no ConsumerInfo can be in flight on a connection the caller is about to
drain.

What the probe proves: the stream and durable exist and the JetStream API answered.
What it does not: that THIS process is the one consuming (replicas share the
durable), or that a delivery arrived. It is a strictly better proxy than
configRejected for every case above, and it starts false — so a pod is NotReady
until the first success, matching the old gate's boot behaviour.

races Run creating the durable, so a single 5s interval left a healthy pod NotReady
for seconds after it was already consuming — visible as a 5.10s test runtime, now
0.36s. It polls at 250ms until the first success, then settles to 5s, so a
sustained outage is not hammered with four ConsumerInfo requests a second at the
moment the server is already struggling.

directions on a broker with no stream provisioned (removing the probe leaves it
Ready and red), ProbeRunsUnderRun asserts Run actually starts the probe and joins it

how the wrong one gets built. The real fix is go-nuts exposing readiness from Run —

Entire-Checkpoint: 32f1d36c99ca","messageHeadline":"fix(meta-fanout): make /readyz track the durable, not just config acc…","oid":"92bcb7dd8de0aa6ea0a8d4d22a4fee3467000c08"},{"authoredDate":"2026-08-14T14:56:34Z","authors":[{"email":"andrea@entire.io","id":"MDQ6VXNlcjgyOTE3OA==","login":"nodo","name":"Andrea Nodari"},{"email":"noreply@anthropic.com","id":"MDQ6VXNlcjgxODQ3","login":"claude","name":"Claude Opus 5 (1M context)"}],"committedDate":"2026-08-14T14:56:34Z","messageBody":"…re failure-run telemetry

Two P2 review findings on trail #102, both correct.

1. THE PROBE JOIN DEADLOCKED ON A REJECTED CONFIG (lifecycle.go)

I registered `defer stopProbe()` and then `defer func(){ <-probeDone }()`. Defers
run LIFO, so the JOIN ran first and the cancel second — and the probe exits only
on its context. A Run that returned while the parent context was still alive (the
only such path: a permanently rejected config) therefore blocked in its own defer
until whole-app shutdown: goroutine leaked, the caller's lifecycleDone never
closed, and the probe kept polling — at the 250ms startup cadence if CONSUMER.INFO
never succeeded.

Now one defer that cancels THEN joins. The join is still required: an in-flight
ConsumerInfo must not outlive Run and land on a connection the caller is about to
drain.

TestLifecycleRun_ReturnsOnRejectedConfig covers it, with the parent context

migration's likeliest failure must page.

which is the same defect as no test — and it hid a wrong expectation, since the
rollout-ordering case swaps in the canonical message rather than prefixing the
caller's. Both fixed; the message is now asserted.

the modern-client migration has more than one adopter to generalise from — recorded

Two P2 review findings on trail #102 at 3765557.

1. THE FAST CADENCE COULD RESUME AFTER A POST-BIND LOSS

nextProbeInterval decided from the outcome plus a raw attempts-remaining counter,
and a success settled the interval without spending the budget. So a durable that
bound on its first probe kept ~19 unspent attempts, and a genuine loss inside the
following ~95s (19 spent one per 5s tick) returned 250ms — re-entering the fast
cadence to hammer a server that had just lost the durable. The comment three lines
above said that must never happen; the code did not implement it.

Every single-call assertion I had written passed, because the broken property is
about a SEQUENCE: end, and never resume. So the decision is now a small state
machine (probeCadence) whose observe(bound) ZEROES the budget on success rather than
leaving it to decay, and the test drives sequences — never-binds, binds-immediately-
then-loses, binds-mid-startup-then-loses. Verified it catches the bug: restoring the
non-zeroing branch fails with "a success must end the startup phase, not merely
pause it".

2. CANCELLING AN IN-FLIGHT PROBE LOGGED A FALSE ERROR ON EVERY ROLLOUT

Run cancels the probe context on the way out, so a CONSUMER.INFO in flight at that
moment returns context.Canceled. That value is not in the transient set, so it
reached Health as a fault:

  {"level":"ERROR","msg":"Lifecycle durable unreachable; reporting NotReady","error":"context canceled"}

Self-inflicted shutdown noise — precisely what natslog exists to remove (COR-1228:
57 ErrNoResponders in 83ms during a deploy, three false alerts in forty minutes) —
reintroduced by the probe added to report real outages.

Guarded narrowly: BOTH the parent context being done AND the error being
context.Canceled, the same discipline as nuts.IsShutdownFetchErr, which will only
call a drain benign when ctx is already done. A context.DeadlineExceeded from the
probe's own timeout leaves the parent alive and still reaches Health, as do
consumer-deletion and stream-missing errors. The test asserts both directions —
silence on a cancelled parent, and a complaint on a live one — so the guard cannot
be widened into swallowing real failures without going red. Verified: removing it
reproduces the exact ERROR record above.

Loop 1 of Track D. The cross-region resource_lifecycle_v1 fan moves off its
hand-rolled PullSubscribe/Fetch(1) loop onto jsconsumer.Run + Process, and its
redelivery ladder moves server-side. Same durable name, so no recreation and no
redelivery storm; behaviour is preserved except where noted below.

WHAT MOVES

- jsconsumer.Run + Process replace the subscribe/backoff loop, the Fetch loop, the
  shutdown-error classification and the span prologue. MaxMessages 1 preserves the
  Fetch(1) pacing: AckWait runs from server delivery into the client buffer, not
  from callback dispatch, so anything queued behind a slow fan would age
  unprocessed.
- The ladder is now the durable's. lifecycleBackOff derives consumerFailureDelay
  x (consumerMaxDeliver-1) from the two constants rather than restating them, so
  the numbers that must agree cannot drift. The app's disposition for a failed fan
  is DO NOTHING — the ack timeout brings the delivery back on that ladder. A
  client NakWithDelay beside a server ladder is the ENT-1535 defect (the server
  stretches each NAK by the BackOff increments, so redeliveries follow neither);
  a plain Nak would redeliver immediately and skip the ladder.
- Every field CreateOrUpdateConsumer sends is now stated, because a field omitted
  in code is not "unchanged on the durable" — it is reset to a default.

WHAT DOES NOT MOVE

Give-up semantics. No Term path, no Retry, no DLQ: the event is republished
verbatim so nothing about it can be permanently unprocessable, and
resource_lifecycle_v1 is limits-retention — it holds every event for its full max
age whatever this consumer does, so the replay path is the source stream. Adding
capture would need a DLQ stream and a meta-fanout publish grant that do not exist.

InactiveThreshold stays unset, and now says so explicitly. The 2026-06-01 reaping
valve is for interest streams where an abandoned durable pins deliveries for ALL
consumers; on limits retention an idle durable pins nothing. All seven cells carry
no threshold today and none is added.

The timing envelope is unchanged — 8 deliveries, give up at t+3m30s — which the
pre-flight is what licenses claiming: snapshots of all 7 cells showed this durable
has NO server-side backoff, so the effective ladder really was the client's flat
30s. (webhook-forwarder and fanout are NOT like this; they carry an undeclared 41h
ladder, COR-1270. Loop 2 cannot make this claim.)

ONE DELIBERATE CONFIG CHANGE

MaxAckPending 65536 -> 1000. The 65536 in all seven cells was never chosen:
nats.go's legacy PullSubscribe copies its own client-side subscription-channel
capacity into the server config. jsconsumer sends the field on every start, so
leaving it zero would have rewritten all seven silently; this makes it a recorded
decision instead. Generous either way at a one-message prefetch.

TWO KNOWN DELTAS

- /readyz is narrower. The old loop held a `subscribed` bool set after each
  successful PullSubscribe, so a RETRYABLE boot failure (stream absent, no
  responders) also read NotReady. jsconsumer.Run exposes no start-success signal,
  so Ready() now reports only that the configuration was accepted — which does
  cover this migration's likeliest failure, an immutable-field disagreement. In
  exchange Run recreates a consume loop that closes mid-run, as the old outer loop
  did. Closing the gap needs go-nuts to expose readiness from Run; recorded beside
  the Runner.Drain and FloorMonitor-attach gaps entire-search #131 logged.
- The fan-failure log drops redeliver_in and gains max_deliver. The app no longer
  schedules the redelivery, so printing a delay would be a claim about someone
  else's config — true only while the two agree, which is the drift this track
  exists to remove. Position in the ladder is what a responder can act on; the
  ladder is on the durable.

outcome=nak is kept verbatim on the metric: dashboards key on it and its meaning
is unchanged (this delivery failed and will come back). What changed is who
schedules the redelivery, which the metric never described.

The local ackableMsg seam and numDelivered helper are gone — jetstream.Msg is
already an interface, natsmsgtest.FakeMsg is the double, and backoff.NumDelivered
is the library's own reading of the delivery count.

The migration changed give-up semantics, so per the Track D rules it needs
broker-level evidence rather than fake-level. The existing unit tests answer what
the handler DOES — which disposition it chose. These answer what the broker does
about it, which the fakes cannot: they encode the same model as the code, so a
belief held wrongly in both places produces a green test.

Three broker tests, one per load-bearing belief:

- StoredConfigIsTheRenderedConfig drives the REAL lifecycleConsumerConfig through
  the real CreateOrUpdateConsumer and reads back what the server stored. This is
  the executable form of the pre-flight diff: against the 7-cell snapshot the
  intended delta is exactly two fields (the ladder appears, MaxAckPending becomes
  a chosen number) and everything else must land unchanged.
- FanFailure_IsRedeliveredByTheServerLadder pins the belief that replaced the
  client NakWithDelay: settle nothing, get the delivery back, paced by BackOff.
  The fixture ladder is SCALED to milliseconds and GROWING on purpose — on a flat
  ladder BackOff[0] equals AckWait, so the test would pass whether redelivery
  followed the ladder or merely the ack timeout, pinning nothing. Growing rungs
  mean the second gap can only come from BackOff[1]. Gap tolerances are half the
  distance to the nearest rival explanation (~0 for a plain Nak; rung1 for a
  ladder that does not advance), so the assertion cannot accept the behaviour it
  was written to reject.
- CleanFan_AdvancesTheAckFloor pins the success path on the floor itself, which is
  what every stall alert on these streams reads. FakeMsg can only show that Ack was
  called; a denied $JS.ACK publish returns no error at all (COR-1224), so "we
  called Ack" and "the message is settled" are different claims.

Plus the timing contract, validated by go-nuts' exported jsconsumer.Schedule
rather than by hand, rendering the before/after table for the trail:

  | delivery | before (client Nak, measured) | after (server ladder) |
  |        2 | t+30s                        | t+30s                 |
  |        8 | t+3m30s — give up            | t+3m30s — give up     |

checked against the TIGHTEST retention any cell gives the stream (staging trims
maxAge to 6h, base is 96h), and against the rung-count/AckWait agreement rules.

- recordingJS is unusable for the failure test — it records only SUCCESSFUL

durable), or that a delivery arrived. It is a strictly better proxy than
configRejected for every case above, and it starts false — so a pod is NotReady

races Run creating the durable, so a single 5s interval left a healthy pod NotReady

sustained outage is not hammered with four ConsumerInfo requests a second at the

Two P2 review findings on trail #102, both correct.

1. THE PROBE JOIN DEADLOCKED ON A REJECTED CONFIG (lifecycle.go)

I registered `defer stopProbe()` and then `defer func(){ <-probeDone }()`. Defers
run LIFO, so the JOIN ran first and the cancel second — and the probe exits only
on its context. A Run that returned while the parent context was still alive (the
only such path: a permanently rejected config) therefore blocked in its own defer
until whole-app shutdown: goroutine leaked, the caller's lifecycleDone never
closed, and the probe kept polling — at the 250ms startup cadence if CONSUMER.INFO
never succeeded.

Now one defer that cancels THEN joins. The join is still required: an in-flight
ConsumerInfo must not outlive Run and land on a connection the caller is about to
drain.

TestLifecycleRun_ReturnsOnRejectedConfig covers it, with the parent context
deliberately left alive because that is the condition the bug needed. The rejection
is the real-world one this migration risks — a durable pre-existing with an
immutable field set differently — and the broker supplies it verbatim: "ack policy
can not be updated" (err_code 10012). Verified it catches the bug: with the two
defers restored the test fails at its 20s guard; with the fix it returns in 0.04s.

2. SUSTAINED-OUTAGE TELEMETRY WAS LOST WITH natslog.Health

Adopting jsconsumer.Run dropped the old subscribe loop's natslog.Health
supervision, and Run is not an equivalent: it logs every retryable failure at WARN
indefinitely, with no escalation and no counter. So the five-minute warn->error
escalation and the restart-proof nats.consumer.recoverable_failures counter both
went away. That matters most in US/default mode, where readiness DELIBERATELY
excludes this consumer so a problem here cannot stall the live github_meta fan-out
— which means a stopped lifecycle fan there shows up only in telemetry, and the
telemetry had been removed.

The readiness probe is the programmatic signal Run does not expose, so it now
drives Health: SubscribeErr on a failed probe (the create/bind path, which absorbs
a slow JetStream API and a not-yet-provisioned stream), Recovered on success.

That required teaching natslog the modern client's errors first, and this is the
part worth review attention. nuts.IsTransientSubscribeErr keys on the LEGACY nats.*
values; the jetstream package defines its own distinct ones —
jetstream.ErrStreamNotFound is a *jsError carrying an APIError, not
nats.ErrStreamNotFound, so errors.Is finds neither across the two. Wiring the probe
in naively would have classified every rollout-ordering failure as a FAULT and
logged it at ERROR: the exact alert-eroding noise natslog exists to prevent
(COR-1228), introduced by the package meant to prevent it.

So SubscribeErr now also matches jetstream.ErrStreamNotFound (canonical
"Stream not yet present, retrying", warn forever, excluded from escalation), and
isTransientSubscribeErr extends the go-nuts predicate with ErrConsumerNotFound /
ErrConsumerDoesNotExist (a supervised runner recreates a missing durable, so this
is a race until escalation says otherwise) and ErrJetStreamNotEnabled (a 503 from a
server still starting). ErrConsumerCreate and ErrBadRequest stay at ERROR — the
migration's likeliest failure must page.

TestSubscribeErrClassifiesModernClientErrors is the modern half of the existing
severity table. Note on the fixture: its wantMsg column was initially never read,
which is the same defect as no test — and it hid a wrong expectation, since the
rollout-ordering case swaps in the canonical message rather than prefixing the
caller's. Both fixed; the message is now asserted.

This extension belongs in go-nuts beside the predicate it extends. Left here until
the modern-client migration has more than one adopter to generalise from — recorded
with the Runner.Drain / FloorMonitor-attach / Run-readiness follow-ups.

1. A MISSING DURABLE MEANT TWO THINGS AND I CLASSIFIED IT AS ONE

I demoted the modern ErrConsumerNotFound / ErrConsumerDoesNotExist to transient
inside natslog. That is right during the initial create race and wrong afterwards,
and natslog already had the contract I broke: nats.ErrConsumerDeleted stays at
ERROR because a durable that disappears is recreated from the stream's
DeliverPolicy, losing the cursor. For THIS consumer that is not abstract —
DeliverPolicy is all and resource_lifecycle_v1 retains up to 96h, so a recreate
re-fans the retained backlog cross-region, and the demotion would have let it
happen under generic warnings.

The distinction is not available from the error value, so it does not belong in a
predicate over error values. natslog goes back to keeping a missing consumer loud
(ErrJetStreamNotEnabled stays transient — a 503 from a server still starting), and
the PROBE makes the call, because only the probe knows which side of the first
successful bind it is on:

- before any bind + consumer missing -> debug, no failure run. Expected: Run is
  concurrently creating it and logs its own attempts.
- after a bind -> natslog.SubscribeErr, which is now ERROR for this class.
- everything else (no responders, timeouts, stream missing) -> SubscribeErr from
  the first attempt, so a real outage at boot still escalates after five minutes.

everBound is one-way on purpose: re-entering the startup posture after a real
disappearance would both silence it and hammer the server at the fast cadence.

Honest limit, stated in the code: at a 5s cadence this probe can miss a delete that
Run recreates before the next tick, so it is a backstop, not a detector. The
reliable signal is the runner's own recreate, which jsconsumer only logs.

It ended on the first success only, so a pod starting while the stream or the API
was unavailable never left it: four CONSUMER.INFO requests and — after the Health
wiring — four log lines per second, indefinitely. That contradicted the comment
directly above it and recreated the log-volume problem natslog exists to solve.

The phase is now bounded by attempts as well: 20 at 250ms (~5s, orders of magnitude
more than creating a durable takes), then the steady 5s cadence whether or not it
ever succeeded.

ON THE TESTS

The disappearance test asserts LOG LEVEL, not just the boolean, because the level is
what the finding was about — it deletes a bound durable under the consumer and
requires ERROR.

The burst test is worth noting: my first version re-implemented the cadence loop and
counted its own probes over 8 wall-clock seconds. It passed — and would have kept
passing with the bound deleted from production, which is the same defect as no test,
and slow as well as useless. The decision is now a pure function
(nextProbeInterval) that probeDurable actually calls, and the test drives that.
Verified it fails with the bound removed: "interval = 250ms, want the steady 5s".
Runtime 8.03s -> 0.00s.

Two P2 review findings on trail #102 at 3765557.

1. THE FAST CADENCE COULD RESUME AFTER A POST-BIND LOSS

nextProbeInterval decided from the outcome plus a raw attempts-remaining counter,
and a success settled the interval without spending the budget. So a durable that
bound on its first probe kept ~19 unspent attempts, and a genuine loss inside the
following ~95s (19 spent one per 5s tick) returned 250ms — re-entering the fast
cadence to hammer a server that had just lost the durable. The comment three lines
above said that must never happen; the code did not implement it.

Every single-call assertion I had written passed, because the broken property is
about a SEQUENCE: end, and never resume. So the decision is now a small state
machine (probeCadence) whose observe(bound) ZEROES the budget on success rather than
leaving it to decay, and the test drives sequences — never-binds, binds-immediately-
then-loses, binds-mid-startup-then-loses. Verified it catches the bug: restoring the
non-zeroing branch fails with "a success must end the startup phase, not merely
pause it".

2. CANCELLING AN IN-FLIGHT PROBE LOGGED A FALSE ERROR ON EVERY ROLLOUT

Run cancels the probe context on the way out, so a CONSUMER.INFO in flight at that
moment returns context.Canceled. That value is not in the transient set, so it
reached Health as a fault:

  {"level":"ERROR","msg":"Lifecycle durable unreachable; reporting NotReady","error":"context canceled"}

Self-inflicted shutdown noise — precisely what natslog exists to remove (COR-1228:
57 ErrNoResponders in 83ms during a deploy, three false alerts in forty minutes) —
reintroduced by the probe added to report real outages.

Guarded narrowly: BOTH the parent context being done AND the error being
context.Canceled, the same discipline as nuts.IsShutdownFetchErr, which will only
call a drain benign when ctx is already done. A context.DeadlineExceeded from the
probe's own timeout leaves the parent alive and still reaches Health, as do
consumer-deletion and stream-missing errors. The test asserts both directions —
silence on a cancelled parent, and a complaint on a live one — so the guard cannot
be widened into swallowing real failures without going red. Verified: removing it
reproduces the exact ERROR record above.

Loop 1 of Track D. The cross-region resource_lifecycle_v1 fan moves off its
hand-rolled PullSubscribe/Fetch(1) loop onto jsconsumer.Run + Process, and its
redelivery ladder moves server-side. Same durable name, so no recreation and no
redelivery storm; behaviour is preserved except where noted below.

WHAT MOVES

- jsconsumer.Run + Process replace the subscribe/backoff loop, the Fetch loop, the
  shutdown-error classification and the span prologue. MaxMessages 1 preserves the
  Fetch(1) pacing: AckWait runs from server delivery into the client buffer, not
  from callback dispatch, so anything queued behind a slow fan would age
  unprocessed.
- The ladder is now the durable's. lifecycleBackOff derives consumerFailureDelay
  x (consumerMaxDeliver-1) from the two constants rather than restating them, so
  the numbers that must agree cannot drift. The app's disposition for a failed fan
  is DO NOTHING — the ack timeout brings the delivery back on that ladder. A
  client NakWithDelay beside a server ladder is the ENT-1535 defect (the server
  stretches each NAK by the BackOff increments, so redeliveries follow neither);
  a plain Nak would redeliver immediately and skip the ladder.
- Every field CreateOrUpdateConsumer sends is now stated, because a field omitted
  in code is not "unchanged on the durable" — it is reset to a default.

WHAT DOES NOT MOVE

Give-up semantics. No Term path, no Retry, no DLQ: the event is republished
verbatim so nothing about it can be permanently unprocessable, and
resource_lifecycle_v1 is limits-retention — it holds every event for its full max
age whatever this consumer does, so the replay path is the source stream. Adding
capture would need a DLQ stream and a meta-fanout publish grant that do not exist.

InactiveThreshold stays unset, and now says so explicitly. The 2026-06-01 reaping
valve is for interest streams where an abandoned durable pins deliveries for ALL
consumers; on limits retention an idle durable pins nothing. All seven cells carry
no threshold today and none is added.

nats.go's legacy PullSubscribe copies its own client-side subscription-channel
capacity into the server config. jsconsumer sends the field on every start, so
leaving it zero would have rewritten all seven silently; this makes it a recorded
decision instead. Generous either way at a one-message prefetch.

  successful PullSubscribe, so a RETRYABLE boot failure (stream absent, no

  cover this migration's likeliest failure, an immutable-field disagreement. In

  did. Closing the gap needs go-nuts to expose readiness from Run; recorded beside
  the Runner.Drain and FloorMonitor-attach gaps entire-search #131 logged.

  schedules the redelivery, so printing a delay would be a claim about someone
  else's config — true only while the two agree, which is the drift this track
  exists to remove. Position in the ladder is what a responder can act on; the
  ladder is on the durable.

outcome=nak is kept verbatim on the metric: dashboards key on it and its meaning
is unchanged (this delivery failed and will come back). What changed is who
schedules the redelivery, which the metric never described.

The local ackableMsg seam and numDelivered helper are gone — jetstream.Msg is
already an interface, natsmsgtest.FakeMsg is the double, and backoff.NumDelivered
is the library's own reading of the delivery count.

not the same as accepting it.

Ready() reflected only configRejected — set when jsconsumer.Run RETURNS, which it
does only for a permanently rejected config. Run retries everything else and logs a
warning per attempt, so through the outages a readiness gate exists for (stream not
provisioned yet, JetStream unreachable while the TCP connection is up: no
responders, meta-leader election, a CONSUMER.CREATE permission rejection surfacing
as a timeout) configRejected never flips and /readyz stayed green while nothing was
consumed.

natsregions.Health.Status() asks Local.IsConnected() only, so a live connection to a
JetStream that cannot answer passes it. And in lifecycleOnly mode this consumer is
the pod's SOLE readiness gate, so green there hides a real outage from anything
watching /readyz — exactly what the pre-migration `subscribed` bool did not do.

Ready() is now (config accepted) AND (durable reachable), the second refreshed by a
slow probe that lives exactly as long as the consume loop. Run joins it on the way
out, so no ConsumerInfo can be in flight on a connection the caller is about to
drain.

What the probe proves: the stream and durable exist and the JetStream API answered.
What it does not: that THIS process is the one consuming (replicas share the
durable), or that a delivery arrived. It is a strictly better proxy than
configRejected for every case above, and it starts false — so a pod is NotReady
until the first success, matching the old gate's boot behaviour.

Two cadences, because startup and outage want opposite things. The first probe
races Run creating the durable, so a single 5s interval left a healthy pod NotReady
for seconds after it was already consuming — visible as a 5.10s test runtime, now
0.36s. It polls at 250ms until the first success, then settles to 5s, so a
sustained outage is not hammered with four ConsumerInfo requests a second at the
moment the server is already struggling.

directions on a broker with no stream provisioned (removing the probe leaves it
Ready and red), ProbeRunsUnderRun asserts Run actually starts the probe and joins it
(removing the goroutine leaves the helper tests passing and this one red).

and will want this shape, but inventing the shared abstraction from one example is
how the wrong one gets built. The real fix is go-nuts exposing readiness from Run —

Two P2 review findings on trail #102, both correct.

1. THE PROBE JOIN DEADLOCKED ON A REJECTED CONFIG (lifecycle.go)

I registered `defer stopProbe()` and then `defer func(){ <-probeDone }()`. Defers
run LIFO, so the JOIN ran first and the cancel second — and the probe exits only
on its context. A Run that returned while the parent context was still alive (the
only such path: a permanently rejected config) therefore blocked in its own defer
until whole-app shutdown: goroutine leaked, the caller's lifecycleDone never
closed, and the probe kept polling — at the 250ms startup cadence if CONSUMER.INFO
never succeeded.

Now one defer that cancels THEN joins. The join is still required: an in-flight
ConsumerInfo must not outlive Run and land on a connection the caller is about to
drain.

TestLifecycleRun_ReturnsOnRejectedConfig covers it, with the parent context
deliberately left alive because that is the condition the bug needed. The rejection
is the real-world one this migration risks — a durable pre-existing with an
immutable field set differently — and the broker supplies it verbatim: "ack policy
can not be updated" (err_code 10012). Verified it catches the bug: with the two
defers restored the test fails at its 20s guard; with the fix it returns in 0.04s.

2. SUSTAINED-OUTAGE TELEMETRY WAS LOST WITH natslog.Health

Adopting jsconsumer.Run dropped the old subscribe loop's natslog.Health
supervision, and Run is not an equivalent: it logs every retryable failure at WARN
indefinitely, with no escalation and no counter. So the five-minute warn->error
escalation and the restart-proof nats.consumer.recoverable_failures counter both
went away. That matters most in US/default mode, where readiness DELIBERATELY
excludes this consumer so a problem here cannot stall the live github_meta fan-out
— which means a stopped lifecycle fan there shows up only in telemetry, and the
telemetry had been removed.

The readiness probe is the programmatic signal Run does not expose, so it now
drives Health: SubscribeErr on a failed probe (the create/bind path, which absorbs
a slow JetStream API and a not-yet-provisioned stream), Recovered on success.

That required teaching natslog the modern client's errors first, and this is the
part worth review attention. nuts.IsTransientSubscribeErr keys on the LEGACY nats.*
values; the jetstream package defines its own distinct ones —
jetstream.ErrStreamNotFound is a *jsError carrying an APIError, not
nats.ErrStreamNotFound, so errors.Is finds neither across the two. Wiring the probe
in naively would have classified every rollout-ordering failure as a FAULT and
logged it at ERROR: the exact alert-eroding noise natslog exists to prevent
(COR-1228), introduced by the package meant to prevent it.

So SubscribeErr now also matches jetstream.ErrStreamNotFound (canonical
"Stream not yet present, retrying", warn forever, excluded from escalation), and
isTransientSubscribeErr extends the go-nuts predicate with ErrConsumerNotFound /
ErrConsumerDoesNotExist (a supervised runner recreates a missing durable, so this
is a race until escalation says otherwise) and ErrJetStreamNotEnabled (a 503 from a
server still starting). ErrConsumerCreate and ErrBadRequest stay at ERROR — the
migration's likeliest failure must page.

TestSubscribeErrClassifiesModernClientErrors is the modern half of the existing
severity table. Note on the fixture: its wantMsg column was initially never read,
which is the same defect as no test — and it hid a wrong expectation, since the
rollout-ordering case swaps in the canonical message rather than prefixing the
caller's. Both fixed; the message is now asserted.

This extension belongs in go-nuts beside the predicate it extends. Left here until
the modern-client migration has more than one adopter to generalise from — recorded
with the Runner.Drain / FloorMonitor-attach / Run-readiness follow-ups.

successful bind it is on:

- after a bind -> natslog.SubscribeErr, which is now ERROR for this class.
- everything else (no responders, timeouts, stream missing) -> SubscribeErr from
  the first attempt, so a real outage at boot still escalates after five minutes.

everBound is one-way on purpose: re-entering the startup posture after a real

directly above it and recreated the log-volume problem natslog exists to solve.

Two P2 review findings on trail #102 at 3765557.

1. THE FAST CADENCE COULD RESUME AFTER A POST-BIND LOSS

nextProbeInterval decided from the outcome plus a raw attempts-remaining counter,
and a success settled the interval without spending the budget. So a durable that
bound on its first probe kept ~19 unspent attempts, and a genuine loss inside the
following ~95s (19 spent one per 5s tick) returned 250ms — re-entering the fast
cadence to hammer a server that had just lost the durable. The comment three lines
above said that must never happen; the code did not implement it.

Every single-call assertion I had written passed, because the broken property is
about a SEQUENCE: end, and never resume. So the decision is now a small state
machine (probeCadence) whose observe(bound) ZEROES the budget on success rather than
leaving it to decay, and the test drives sequences — never-binds, binds-immediately-
then-loses, binds-mid-startup-then-loses. Verified it catches the bug: restoring the
non-zeroing branch fails with "a success must end the startup phase, not merely
pause it".

2. CANCELLING AN IN-FLIGHT PROBE LOGGED A FALSE ERROR ON EVERY ROLLOUT

Run cancels the probe context on the way out, so a CONSUMER.INFO in flight at that
moment returns context.Canceled. That value is not in the transient set, so it
reached Health as a fault:

  {"level":"ERROR","msg":"Lifecycle durable unreachable; reporting NotReady","error":"context canceled"}

Self-inflicted shutdown noise — precisely what natslog exists to remove (COR-1228:
57 ErrNoResponders in 83ms during a deploy, three false alerts in forty minutes) —
reintroduced by the probe added to report real outages.

Guarded narrowly: BOTH the parent context being done AND the error being
context.Canceled, the same discipline as nuts.IsShutdownFetchErr, which will only
call a drain benign when ctx is already done. A context.DeadlineExceeded from the
probe's own timeout leaves the parent alive and still reaches Health, as do
consumer-deletion and stream-missing errors. The test asserts both directions —
silence on a cancelled parent, and a complaint on a live one — so the guard cannot
be widened into swallowing real failures without going red. Verified: removing it
reproduces the exact ERROR record above.

221	// The redelivery ladder is the SERVER's: the durable carries [lifecycleBackOff],
   222	// and the app's disposition for a failed fan is to DO NOTHING — the delivery is
   223	// left for the ack timeout to bring back on that ladder. The two alternatives are
   224	// both wrong. A client-side NakWithDelay alongside a server ladder is the
   225	// ENT-1535 defect itself (the server stretches each NAK delay by the BackOff
   226	// increments, so redeliveries follow neither and the configured one becomes dead
   227	// config). A plain Nak redelivers immediately, skipping the ladder entirely.

   230	// nothing about it can be permanently unprocessable; and resource_lifecycle_v1 is
   231	// limits-retention, holding every event for its full max age whatever this
   232	// consumer does — so the replay path is the source stream, not a capture stream.
   233	// Adding one would need a DLQ stream and a meta-fanout publish grant that do not
   234	// exist; deliberately out of scope here.

   236		nc      *nats.Conn
   237		fanout  *lifecycleFanout
   238		metrics *metaFanoutMetrics
   239		durable string
   240		subject string

   242		// enqueuer + resolver drive the additive mirror.created → github_meta seed
   243		// (COR-717). Both nil leaves the consumer a pure cross-region fan (its
   244		// original behavior), so fan-only tests need not wire them.
   245		enqueuer backfillEnqueuer
   246		resolver mirrorResolver

   248		// health carries the failure-run supervision the hand-rolled subscribe loop
   249		// used to hold, now driven by the readiness probe rather than by Fetch errors:
   250		// warn while a failure is being absorbed, error once five minutes have passed
   251		// with no recovery, and the restart-proof recoverable_failures counter either
   252		// way. jsconsumer.Run has no equivalent — it warns per attempt, indefinitely —
   253		// so without this a sustained outage was indistinguishable from deploy churn.
   254		// Zero value is healthy and ready to use.
   255		health natslog.Health
   256	
   257		// configRejected records that [jsconsumer.Run] returned, which it does only
   258		// for a configuration the broker will never accept — never for a transient
   259		// failure it can retry. /readyz consults it, so a durable this deployment
   260		// cannot create reports NotReady rather than looking healthy while consuming
   261		// nothing. That is this migration's likeliest failure mode: an
   262		// immutable-field disagreement against the live consumer.
   263		//
   264		// On its own this covers only a PERMANENT rejection, which is not enough for
   265		// a readiness gate — hence durableBound below.
   266		configRejected atomic.Bool
   267	
   268		// durableBound is the liveness half of /readyz: whether this pod's durable can
   269		// actually be reached on the server right now, refreshed by a slow probe while
   270		// Run supervises the consume loop.
   271		//

   273		// every failure it can and logs a warning per attempt, so configRejected alone
   274		// would leave /readyz green through exactly the outages the gate is for: a
   275		// stream not provisioned yet, a JetStream API that is unreachable while the TCP
   276		// connection is up (no responders, meta-leader election, a CONSUMER.CREATE
   277		// permission rejection that manifests as a timeout). The pre-existing
   278		// natsregions health check does NOT cover those — it only asks IsConnected —

   280		// a green /readyz through such a window would hide a real outage. That is the
   281		// regression the pre-migration `subscribed` bool did not have.

   285		// shares the durable), or that a delivery arrived. It is a strictly better
   286		// proxy than configRejected for every case above, and it starts false so a pod
   287		// is NotReady until the first probe succeeds — matching the old gate's boot

   293		// extracted; left local until a second caller exists rather than inventing a

   300		// the startup posture after a real disappearance would both silence it and
   301		// hammer the server at the fast cadence when it is least able to answer.
   302		everBound atomic.Bool

   304		// probeStartupAttempts overrides lifecycleReadyProbeStartupAttempts. Zero uses
   305		// the constant; a test shrinks it so the never-created-after-the-budget path
   306		// can be driven in milliseconds rather than the five seconds the shipped value
   307		// takes. The only knob of its kind here, and it exists because that path is the

   322	// currently reachable. See the field docs for what each half does and does not
   323	// prove.

   329	// every redelivery consumerMaxDeliver allows.

   332	// must agree cannot drift — the durable's MaxDeliver, len(BackOff) under the
   333	// server's tail-repeat, and (for a consumer that has one) its Retry's MaxDeliver.

   335	// region, which does not get cheaper to wait out; MaxDeliver bounds the envelope.

   337		rungs := make([]time.Duration, consumerMaxDeliver-1)

   339			rungs[i] = consumerFailureDelay
   340		}
   341		return rungs
   342	}

   345	// the redeliver-in log line below reads its rungs, and the timing-contract test
   346	// validates it through jsconsumer.Schedule rather than restating the arithmetic.

   348		return jsconsumer.Schedule{
   349			ServerBackOff: lifecycleBackOff(),
   350			MaxDeliver:    consumerMaxDeliver,
   351			AckWait:       consumerAckWait,
   352		}
   353	}
   354	
   355	// lifecycleConsumerConfig is the durable's full configuration. Every field the
   356	// pre-migration PullSubscribe left implicit is stated, because
   357	// CreateOrUpdateConsumer sends them all: a field omitted here is not "unchanged
   358	// on the live durable", it is reset to a default.
   359	func lifecycleConsumerConfig(durable, subject string) jsconsumer.Config {
   360		return jsconsumer.Config{
   361			Stream:        lifecycleStream,
   362			Durable:       durable,
   363			FilterSubject: subject,
   364			AckWait:       consumerAckWait,
   365			MaxDeliver:    consumerMaxDeliver,
   366			BackOff:       lifecycleBackOff(),
   367			MaxAckPending: lifecycleMaxAckPending,
   368			// InactiveThreshold stays unset, deliberately. The 2026-06-01 safety
   369			// valve applies to interest-retention streams, where an abandoned durable
   370			// pins every subsequent delivery for ALL consumers until the stream's
   371			// maxAge; resource_lifecycle_v1 is limits-retention, so an idle durable
   372			// pins nothing and reaping it would only cost a cursor. The live durables
   373			// carry no threshold in any of the seven cells and none is added here.
   374			InactiveThreshold: 0,
   375			// One message client-side, preserving the pre-migration Fetch(1) pacing:
   376			// AckWait runs from server delivery into the buffer, not from callback
   377			// dispatch, so anything queued behind a slow fan would age unprocessed.
   378			MaxMessages: 1,
   379			SpanName:    "meta_fanout.lifecycle_fan", // preserve the existing span name verbatim
   380			Name:        "meta-fanout-lifecycle",
   381			Tracer:      otel.Tracer(tracerName),
   382		}
   383	}
   384	
   385	// Run consumes until ctx is cancelled, then joins the in-flight handler before
   386	// returning — so the caller may tear down what the handler uses (the remote
   387	// publish handles, the connection) the moment it returns.
   388	func (c *lifecycleConsumer) Run(ctx context.Context) {
   389		cfg := lifecycleConsumerConfig(c.durable, c.subject)
   390	
   391		// The readiness probe lives as long as the consume loop: derive a context so it
   392		// stops when Run returns, whether that is a cancelled parent or a rejected
   393		// config.
   394		probeCtx, stopProbe := context.WithCancel(ctx)
   395		probeDone := make(chan struct{})
   396		go func() {
   397			defer close(probeDone)
   398			c.probeDurable(probeCtx, cfg)
   399		}()
   400		// Cancel THEN join, in one defer. Two defers would run LIFO — the join first,
   401		// the cancel second — and the probe only exits on its context, so a Run that
   402		// returns while the parent context is still alive (a permanently rejected
   403		// config) would block here until whole-app shutdown, leaking the goroutine and
   404		// never closing the caller's done channel. Joining after the cancel is still
   405		// required: an in-flight ConsumerInfo must not outlive Run and land on a
   406		// connection the caller is about to drain.
   407		defer func() {
   408			stopProbe()
   409			<-probeDone
   410		}()
   411	
   412		if err := jsconsumer.Run(ctx, c.nc, cfg, func(msg jetstream.Msg) { c.handle(ctx, cfg, msg) }); err != nil {

   414			// everything it can. Surface it on /readyz and say so loudly — the pod is
   415			// alive and consuming nothing.
   416			c.configRejected.Store(true)

   418				slog.String("durable", c.durable), slog.String("subject", c.subject), slog.Any("error", err))
   419		}
   420	}

   422	// probeDurable keeps lifecycleConsumer.durableBound current until ctx is done. It
   423	// probes immediately, then on a ticker, so a pod does not sit NotReady for a whole
   424	// interval after a healthy start.
   425	//

   427	// against every cell's NATS, and /readyz is polled far more often than the answer
   428	// changes — so the probe is cached rather than run per request.

   430		js, err := jetstream.New(c.nc)

   442		// after it was already consuming.

   445		// success alone was wrong: a pod that starts while the stream or the JetStream
   446		// API is unavailable never succeeds, so it would sit at four ConsumerInfo
   447		// requests and four log lines per second indefinitely — recreating the
   448		// log-volume problem natslog exists to solve, and contradicting the very
   449		// comment that said a long outage would not be hammered.

   451		interval := lifecycleReadyProbeStartupInterval
   452		ticker := time.NewTicker(interval)

   456			// missing durable is only expected while jsconsumer.Run is still racing to
   457			// create it; once the budget is spent, a durable that never appeared is a
   458			// real outage and must reach Health like any other — otherwise "not created
   459			// yet" stays silent forever, which is the telemetry gap this probe exists to
   460			// close.

461			//
   462			// With the shipped constants that puts the first loud report at roughly ten
   463			// seconds after start: ~5s of grace (20 × 250ms), then the next probe on the
   464			// steady cadence. Deliberate — the alternative is either a fast cadence that
   465			// outlives the race it exists for, or a second knob to hurry the first
   466			// complaint, and ten seconds to notice a durable that will never appear is
   467			// well inside any window an operator cares about.
   468			inStartupGrace := !c.everBound.Load() && cadence.startupPending()
   469			bound := c.durableReachable(ctx, js, cfg, inStartupGrace)
   470			c.durableBound.Store(bound)
   471			if bound {
   472				c.everBound.Store(true)
   473			}
   474			if want := cadence.observe(bound); want != interval {
   475				interval = want
   476				ticker.Reset(interval)
   477			}
   478			select {
   479			case <-ctx.Done():
   480				return
   481			case <-ticker.C:
   482			}
   483		}
   484	}
   485	
   486	// probeCadence owns the interval between readiness probes, as a state machine
   487	// rather than a calculation, because the property that matters is about a SEQUENCE:
   488	// the fast startup phase must never resume once it has ended.
   489	//
   490	// A previous version computed the interval from the outcome and a raw
   491	// attempts-remaining counter. That satisfied every single-call assertion and still
   492	// broke the property: a success left the counter untouched, so a durable that bound
   493	// on its first probe kept ~19 unspent attempts, and a genuine post-bind loss inside
   494	// the following minute or two re-entered the 250ms cadence — hammering the server at
   495	// exactly the moment it was least able to answer, which is what the phase is
   496	// bounded to prevent. Ending the phase means ZEROING the budget, not decrementing
   497	// past it, and only a type that remembers can be asked whether it did.
   498	type probeCadence struct{ startupLeft int }
   499	
   500	func newProbeCadence(startupAttempts int) *probeCadence {
   501		return &probeCadence{startupLeft: startupAttempts}
   502	}
   503	
   504	// startupPending reports whether startup attempts remain — i.e. whether a missing
   505	// durable is still the expected startup race rather than a real absence.
   506	func (p *probeCadence) startupPending() bool { return p.startupLeft > 0 }
   507	
   508	// observe records a probe's outcome and returns the wait before the next one. A
   509	// success ends the startup phase permanently; otherwise the phase runs until its
   510	// budget is spent.
   511	func (p *probeCadence) observe(bound bool) time.Duration {
   512		if bound {
   513			p.startupLeft = 0
   514			return lifecycleReadyProbeInterval
   515		}
   516		if p.startupLeft > 0 {
   517			p.startupLeft--
   518		}
   519		if p.startupLeft == 0 {
   520			return lifecycleReadyProbeInterval
   521		}
   522		return lifecycleReadyProbeStartupInterval
   523	}
   524	
   525	// durableReachable reports whether the durable answers on the server, and routes
   526	// the outcome through natslog.Health. A bounded timeout of its own, so a probe
   527	// cannot hang past the interval and stall the readiness signal at a stale value.
   528	//
   529	// Health is what restores the supervision the hand-rolled loop had and
   530	// jsconsumer.Run does not provide: Run logs every retryable failure at WARN
   531	// forever, with no counter and no escalation, so a sustained outage looked exactly
   532	// like deploy churn. Routing the probe through Health brings back both halves —
   533	// the nats.consumer.recoverable_failures counter (restart-proof, for the
   534	// pods-cycling-faster-than-escalation case) and the return to ERROR level after
   535	// five minutes without recovery.
   536	//
   537	// This matters most where /readyz cannot help. In US/default mode the readiness
   538	// gate deliberately excludes this consumer, so that a problem here cannot stall
   539	// the live github_meta fan-out — which means a stopped lifecycle fan in US shows up
   540	// ONLY in telemetry. The probe is the signal; Health is what makes it page.
   541	func (c *lifecycleConsumer) durableReachable(ctx context.Context, js jetstream.JetStream, cfg jsconsumer.Config, inStartupGrace bool) bool {
   542		probeCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, lifecycleReadyProbeTimeout)
   543		defer cancel()

   546			// a request in flight at that moment comes back context.Canceled — which is
   547			// NOT in the transient set, so routing it to Health logged an ERROR on every

   550			// in forty minutes), reintroduced by the thing meant to report real outages.

   553			// Canceled. A context.DeadlineExceeded from this probe's own timeout leaves
   554			// the parent alive and still reaches Health, as do consumer-deletion and
   555			// stream-missing errors — the same discipline as nuts.IsShutdownFetchErr,

   703			// (`nats consumer info`).
   704			slog.WarnContext(ctx, "Lifecycle fan failed; will redeliver",

   727	// synthetic message with neither, in which case dedup is simply not applied.

   486	// probeCadence owns the interval between readiness probes, as a state machine
   487	// rather than a calculation, because the property that matters is about a SEQUENCE:
   488	// the fast startup phase must never resume once it has ended.
   489	//
   490	// A previous version computed the interval from the outcome and a raw
   491	// attempts-remaining counter. That satisfied every single-call assertion and still
   492	// broke the property: a success left the counter untouched, so a durable that bound
   493	// on its first probe kept ~19 unspent attempts, and a genuine post-bind loss inside
   494	// the following minute or two re-entered the 250ms cadence — hammering the server at
   495	// exactly the moment it was least able to answer, which is what the phase is
   496	// bounded to prevent. Ending the phase means ZEROING the budget, not decrementing
   497	// past it, and only a type that remembers can be asked whether it did.
   498	type probeCadence struct{ startupLeft int }
   499	
   500	func newProbeCadence(startupAttempts int) *probeCadence {
   501		return &probeCadence{startupLeft: startupAttempts}
   502	}
   503	
   504	// startupPending reports whether startup attempts remain — i.e. whether a missing
   505	// durable is still the expected startup race rather than a real absence.
   506	func (p *probeCadence) startupPending() bool { return p.startupLeft > 0 }
   507	
   508	// observe records a probe's outcome and returns the wait before the next one. A
   509	// success ends the startup phase permanently; otherwise the phase runs until its
   510	// budget is spent.
   511	func (p *probeCadence) observe(bound bool) time.Duration {
   512		if bound {
   513			p.startupLeft = 0
   514			return lifecycleReadyProbeInterval
   515		}

   517			p.startupLeft--
   518		}
   519		if p.startupLeft == 0 {
   520			return lifecycleReadyProbeInterval
   521		}
   522		return lifecycleReadyProbeStartupInterval
   523	}

   525	// durableReachable reports whether the durable answers on the server, and routes
   526	// the outcome through natslog.Health. A bounded timeout of its own, so a probe
   527	// cannot hang past the interval and stall the readiness signal at a stale value.
   528	//
   529	// Health is what restores the supervision the hand-rolled loop had and
   530	// jsconsumer.Run does not provide: Run logs every retryable failure at WARN
   531	// forever, with no counter and no escalation, so a sustained outage looked exactly
   532	// like deploy churn. Routing the probe through Health brings back both halves —
   533	// the nats.consumer.recoverable_failures counter (restart-proof, for the
   534	// pods-cycling-faster-than-escalation case) and the return to ERROR level after
   535	// five minutes without recovery.
   536	//
   537	// This matters most where /readyz cannot help. In US/default mode the readiness
   538	// gate deliberately excludes this consumer, so that a problem here cannot stall
   539	// the live github_meta fan-out — which means a stopped lifecycle fan in US shows up
   540	// ONLY in telemetry. The probe is the signal; Health is what makes it page.
   541	func (c *lifecycleConsumer) durableReachable(ctx context.Context, js jetstream.JetStream, cfg jsconsumer.Config, inStartupGrace bool) bool {
   542		probeCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, lifecycleReadyProbeTimeout)

   546			// a request in flight at that moment comes back context.Canceled — which is
   547			// NOT in the transient set, so routing it to Health logged an ERROR on every
   548			// rollout. That is the self-inflicted shutdown noise natslog exists to remove
   549			// (COR-1228: 57 ErrNoResponders in 83ms during a deploy, three false alerts
   550			// in forty minutes), reintroduced by the thing meant to report real outages.
   551			//
   552			// Deliberately narrow: BOTH the parent being done AND the error being
   553			// Canceled. A context.DeadlineExceeded from this probe's own timeout leaves
   554			// the parent alive and still reaches Health, as do consumer-deletion and
   555			// stream-missing errors — the same discipline as nuts.IsShutdownFetchErr,
   556			// which is only willing to call a drain benign when ctx is already done.
   557			if ctx.Err() != nil && errors.Is(err, context.Canceled) {

   561			}

   563			// probe loop knows which — hence inStartupGrace rather than a judgement from
   564			// the error value.
   565			//
   566			// Inside the grace it is the startup race with jsconsumer.Run creating the
   567			// durable: expected, Run logs its own attempts, and reporting it through
   568			// Health would manufacture a failure run out of normal boot.
   569			//

   571			// never got created (creation failing while INFO answers not-found), or it
   572			// disappeared after binding — which natslog keeps loud on purpose, because
   573			// the supervisor recreates it from the stream's DeliverPolicy (all), losing
   574			// the cursor and re-fanning whatever resource_lifecycle_v1 still retains, up

   577			//

   579			// recreates before the next tick, so it is a backstop rather than a
   580			// detector. The reliable signal is the runner's own recreate, which

   590			// stream not existing yet (rollout ordering, kept at warn however long it

   525	// durableReachable reports whether the durable answers on the server, and routes
   526	// the outcome through natslog.Health. A bounded timeout of its own, so a probe
   527	// cannot hang past the interval and stall the readiness signal at a stale value.
   528	//
   529	// Health is what restores the supervision the hand-rolled loop had and
   530	// jsconsumer.Run does not provide: Run logs every retryable failure at WARN
   531	// forever, with no counter and no escalation, so a sustained outage looked exactly
   532	// like deploy churn. Routing the probe through Health brings back both halves —
   533	// the nats.consumer.recoverable_failures counter (restart-proof, for the
   534	// pods-cycling-faster-than-escalation case) and the return to ERROR level after
   535	// five minutes without recovery.
   536	//
   537	// This matters most where /readyz cannot help. In US/default mode the readiness
   538	// gate deliberately excludes this consumer, so that a problem here cannot stall
   539	// the live github_meta fan-out — which means a stopped lifecycle fan in US shows up
   540	// ONLY in telemetry. The probe is the signal; Health is what makes it page.
   541	func (c *lifecycleConsumer) durableReachable(ctx context.Context, js jetstream.JetStream, cfg jsconsumer.Config, inStartupGrace bool) bool {
   542		probeCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, lifecycleReadyProbeTimeout)
   543		defer cancel()
   544		if _, err := js.Consumer(probeCtx, cfg.Stream, cfg.Durable); err != nil {
