            # one internal-tls cert whose DNS SAN is "entire-api", so a single
            # user covers them (verify_and_map keys on the DNS SAN, not the
            # SPIFFE URI). repo-activity ingests the inbound repo_refs_v1.> stream
            # and publishes user_activity_v1.> (forwarder) + repo_index_jobs.>
            # (ref-classify + the backfill command) or its bucketed successor
            # repo_index_jobs_v2.> (both, through the cutover), and drains a
            # dedicated repo_index_jobs_backfill.> stream for the batch backfill;
            # user-activity consumes user_activity_v1.>; the checkpoint-analysis
            # worker (COR-588) publishes + drains repo_checkpoint_analysis_jobs.>.
            # The streams
            # themselves are now provisioned declaratively by nack (see
            # apps/nats-streams), so $JS.API.> here covers only the
            # consumer-create calls (CreateOrUpdateConsumer) and their _INBOX.>
            # replies — not stream creation. Explicit $JS.ACK
            # grants are added ONLY for the long-running consumers — the ref
            # ingester, the chunked backfill page-walks (MaxAckPending =
            # INDEX_MAX_ACK_PENDING, durable-scoped, default 512) on the
            # dedicated repo_index_jobs_backfill.>
            # stream, and the checkpoint-analysis consumer (5m job timeout +
            # periodic InProgress heartbeats) — outlast the ~2m one-shot allow_responses
            # window (same reason mirror-worker / entire-search carry $JS.ACK
            # grants); the fast user_activity_v1 consumer's acks stay covered by
            # allow_responses. The unified api process itself uses no NATS.
            # (Inherited verbatim from the retired "activity" user — same subject
            # footprint, new workload identity.)
            - user: "entire-api"
              permissions:
                publish:
                  allow:
                    - "user_activity_v1.>"
                    - "repo_index_jobs.>"
                    - "repo_index_jobs_v2.>"
                    - "repo_index_jobs_backfill.>"
                    - "repo_checkpoint_analysis_jobs.>"
                    # COR-960: dead-letter capture for the four WorkQueue job
                    # streams above — a poison/exhausted job is republished to
                    # repo.jobs.dlq.v1.<stream>.<reason> (see
                    # apps/nats-streams/base/repo-jobs-dlq-v1.yaml) before the
                    # original is acked/deleted off the queue. Without this
                    # grant the DLQ publish is denied (async), the worker naks,
                    # and the job pins the queue forever.
                    - "repo.jobs.dlq.v1.>"
                    - "$JS.API.>"
                    - "$JS.ACK.repo_refs_v1.>"
                    - "$JS.ACK.repo_index_jobs.>"
                    - "$JS.ACK.repo_index_jobs_v2.>"
                    - "$JS.ACK.repo_index_jobs_backfill.>"
                    - "$JS.ACK.repo_checkpoint_analysis_jobs.>"
                    # Ack for the resource_lifecycle_v1 pull consumer below.
                    # Explicit (not allow_responses) because the /me reprocessing
                    # can outlast the ~2m one-shot window.
                    - "$JS.ACK.resource_lifecycle_v1.>"
                    # Publish here because entire-api broadcasts this subject
                    # cross-cell (the relay fans each toggle into every
                    # jurisdiction) — see repo-settings-v1.yaml. Also consumed below.
                    - "repo_settings.v1.>"
                    # Ack for the repo_settings_v1 durable consumer below.
                    # Explicit (not allow_responses) because a settings-
                    # convergence redelivery can outlast the ~2m one-shot window.
                    - "$JS.ACK.repo_settings_v1.>"
                    # Publish-only (RFD-023): the repo-activity trails relay
                    # (internal/trailsrelay) drains trails_outbox and publishes
                    # each event into this cell's LOCAL trail_events_v1 stream —
                    # cell-local, no cross-cell fan-out. entire-api does NOT
                    # consume trail events (no subscribe/$JS.ACK grant); the
                    # future edge/BFF consumer gets its own user. Each publish's
                    # PubAck is the server's reply on the existing _INBOX.> reply
                    # subject under allow_responses — no ack grant needed.
                    # See apps/nats-streams/base/trail-events-v1.yaml.
                    - "trail_events_v1.>"
                    # Ack/Nak/Term for the placement-scoped Trails secondary-
                    # event consumer. Explicit because delayed Naks may outlive
                    # allow_responses' one-shot reply permission.
                    - "$JS.ACK.trail_forge_events_v1.>"
                    # runner-machine (ENT-1182). The runner Deployment shares
                    # this identity — same internal-tls cert, DNS SAN
                    # "entire-api" — so its work queue rides this user, not a
                    # new one. `runner launch` publishes the provision message
                    # and the consumer republishes follow-up kinds
                    # (prompt/poll/snapshot) on the same prefix; subject shape
                    # is runner_work_v1.<repoId>.<kind>.
                    - "runner_work_v1.>"
                    # Dead-letter capture. deadLetterFailingRun republishes a
                    # poison/exhausted job to runner.work.dlq.v1.<reason>
                    # BEFORE terming the original — a DELIBERATELY separate
                    # stream from repo_jobs_dlq_v1 (design §1, "don't overload
                    # repo_jobs_dlq_v1"). Without this grant the DLQ publish is
                    # denied asynchronously, exactly as the repo.jobs.dlq.v1
                    # comment above describes: the job is termed with no record.
                    - "runner.work.dlq.v1.>"
                    # Ack/Nak/Term for BOTH runner durables, and this one is
                    # load-bearing rather than belt-and-braces. The poll
                    # consumer is deliberately unbounded (pollMaxDeliver = -1)
                    # and NakWithDelays every 5s against a 30-minute
                    # deadline_at — ~360 redeliveries per run, each far beyond
                    # allow_responses' ~2m one-shot window. Same rationale the
                    # ref-ingester / backfill / checkpoint-analysis grants above
                    # give, but with a much wider margin.
                    - "$JS.ACK.runner_work_v1.>"
                subscribe:
                  allow:
                    - "repo_refs_v1.>"
                    - "user_activity_v1.>"
                    - "repo_index_jobs.>"
                    - "repo_index_jobs_v2.>"
                    - "repo_index_jobs_backfill.>"
                    - "repo_checkpoint_analysis_jobs.>"
                    # COR-960: crash/orphan backstop — the exhaust reaper
                    # (internal/jobsdlq) queue-subscribes to each job stream's
                    # MAX_DELIVERIES advisories (queue <consumer>-exhaust-reaper)
                    # to dead-letter and DeleteMsg jobs the in-band give-up path
                    # missed (mirrors the mirror-worker grant above). Wildcard
                    # over the consumer token, one line per stream — a stream
                    # token wildcard would not cross the _backfill suffix.
                    - "$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MAX_DELIVERIES.repo_index_jobs.>"
                    - "$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MAX_DELIVERIES.repo_index_jobs_v2.>"
                    - "$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MAX_DELIVERIES.repo_index_jobs_backfill.>"
                    - "$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MAX_DELIVERIES.repo_checkpoint_analysis_jobs.>"
                    # entire-api consumes these lifecycle subtypes: the two
                    # identity arms (/me author-attribution reprocessing), the
                    # repo arm (repos-table seeding from provisioning), the
                    # user arm (account-deletion purge of the activity stores),
                    # the mirror arm (the gated mirrorlifecycle consumer, bound
                    # once CONSUME_MIRROR_LIFECYCLE is enabled), the native mirror
                    # arm (placement seed + native-primary activation), and the
                    # repo_group arm (the processing-primary signal — COR-1001's
                    # repogroupprimary consumer records entire-core's elected
                    # processing primary per group; bound unconditionally, so this
                    # grant must exist before that entire-api deploy).
                    - "resource_lifecycle_v1.github_handle.*"
                    - "resource_lifecycle_v1.verified_email.*"
                    - "resource_lifecycle_v1.repo.*"
                    - "resource_lifecycle_v1.user.*"
                    - "resource_lifecycle_v1.mirror.*"
                    - "resource_lifecycle_v1.native_mirror.*"
                    - "resource_lifecycle_v1.repo_group.*"
                    # This cell's own durable repo_settings_v1 consumer binds its
                    # jurisdiction subject (repo_settings.v1.<ownJur>) to converge
                    # cross-cell settings toggles into the local placement.
                    - "repo_settings.v1.>"
                    # The shared entire-api identity exists in every cell; the
                    # repo-activity durable itself filters this broad grant to
                    # exact trail_forge.v1.<jurisdiction>.<cluster> subjects.
                    - "trail_forge.v1.>"
                    # runner-machine (ENT-1182): the two kind-filtered durables
                    # on runner_work_v1 — runner-work-consumer
                    # (provision/prompt/snapshot) and runner-poll-consumer
                    # (poll). Split because a JetStream WorkQueue stream rejects
                    # two consumers with overlapping filter subjects. One grant
                    # covers both; each durable's own filter narrows it.
                    #
                    # No MAX_DELIVERIES advisory subscribe, unlike the three job
                    # streams above: the runner dead-letters in-band via
                    # deadLetterFailingRun and has no internal/jobsdlq-style
                    # exhaust reaper, so there is no advisory listener to grant.
                    - "runner_work_v1.>"
                    - "_INBOX.>"
                allow_responses: true
            # entire-api-refevents — subscribe-only identity for the live
            # ref-events SSE endpoint (GET /repos/{repo_id}/refs/events,
            # internal/refstream.Subscribe): read-only on repo_refs_v1, no
            # publish/ack rights, deliberately narrower than the shared
            # entire-api user above (which the api process's regular workers
            # use and which carries much broader publish/$JS.API grants this
            # feature has no need for). Live in every cell as of the prod
            # rollout: the cert presenting this identity is minted from
            # apps/entire-api/base/internal-tls-refevents.yaml, so every cluster
            # running entire-api maps to this user. Whether the api actually
            # subscribes is the per-cell REF_EVENTS_STREAM_ENABLED flag in each
            # entire-api overlay, not this grant.
            - user: "entire-api-refevents"

                    - "repo_refs_v1.>"
                    - "_INBOX.>"

            # entire-api-runner-launch — API-only identity for
            # internal/runner.LaunchRun. JetStream PublishMsg sends to the
            # initial provision subject and receives its PubAck on an _INBOX
            # reply; it does not publish later work kinds, create consumers, or
            # acknowledge work, so this user intentionally has no $JS.API.> or
            # $JS.ACK.runner_work_v1.> grant.
            # The base Certificate/mount is safe in every cell; only the
            # royalcanin overlay enables RUNNER_LAUNCH_ENABLED.
            - user: "entire-api-runner-launch"
              permissions:
                publish:
                  allow:
                    - "runner_work_v1.*.provision"
                subscribe:
                  allow:
                    - "_INBOX.>"
                allow_responses: true
    # podTemplate.merge.spec.volumes / container.merge.volumeMounts are NOT
    # added for nats-server-tls — the chart auto-mounts via config.tls.secretName.
    # Adding them here replaces the chart's default volumes (config ConfigMap +
    # pid emptyDir), which is what broke the previous PR — see fleet#304.
    podTemplate:
      merge:
        spec:
          topologySpreadConstraints:
            - maxSkew: 1
              topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
              # DoNotSchedule: quorum safety beats schedulability. With
              # ScheduleAnyway, a drain or consolidation could re-pack two of
              # the three JetStream peers into one AZ, and a later single-AZ
              # outage would then take 2/3 peers — cluster-wide quorum loss
              # for every R3 stream. With the hard constraint, if an AZ is
              # unavailable the displaced pod stays Pending while the two
              # remaining peers hold quorum from distinct AZs — strictly
              # better than co-locating quorum members.
              whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
              labelSelector:
                matchLabels:
                  app.kubernetes.io/name: nats
          securityContext:
            runAsUser: 1000
            runAsGroup: 1000
            fsGroup: 1000
            runAsNonRoot: true
            seccompProfile:
              type: RuntimeDefault
    container:
      merge:
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: 100m
            memory: 512Mi
          limits:
            cpu: 500m
            # Sized against max_payload 40 MiB (see config.merge above; PR
            # #2431's own note said to watch the old 1Gi limit after that
            # bump). A burst of large webhook deliveries holds several
            # in-flight copies per message — publish buffer, route fan-out to
            # both JetStream followers, and per-durable delivery on the
            # 7-consumer webhooks_github_v1 interest stream (trails-fanout adds
            # two event-specific durables) — so 1Gi left
            # ~25x payload of headroom for everything including the filestore
            # cache. OOM-killing NATS pods is a quorum risk (2 of 3 OOMs =
            # cluster down), so give the server real headroom instead.
            memory: 2Gi
        securityContext:
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          capabilities:
            drop:
              - ALL
    natsBox:
      # Disabled. The natsio/nats-box:0.19.3 image has an entrypoint that
      # tries `cd /root` regardless of $HOME, which fails under PodSecurity
      # restricted (forces runAsUser=1000). The container CrashLoopBackOff's
      # and blocks Helm's --wait on the whole HelmRelease upgrade.
      #
      # Tried so far without success:
      #   - #315: add restricted-compliant securityContext (got past PSA
      #     admission, pod scheduled, container started)
      #   - #316: set HOME=/tmp via env (didn't help — `cd /root` is
      #     hardcoded somewhere in the image entrypoint or chart args,
      #     ignores $HOME)
      #
      # Not on the critical path — natsBox is for ad-hoc debugging. Run
      # ad-hoc with `kubectl run` instead:
      #
      #   kubectl run -it --rm nats-debug -n nats --image=natsio/nats-box:0.19.3 \
      #     --overrides='{"spec":{"securityContext":{"runAsUser":1000,...}, ...}}'
      #
      # Or revisit by debugging the entrypoint (probably needs a chart args
      # override to skip the cd-into-$HOME setup).
      enabled: false
    reloader:
      # The chart's reloader auto-watches any volumeMount with a prefix in
      # `natsVolumeMountPrefixes` (default `/etc/`). Since the chart mounts
      # the TLS secret under /etc/nats-certs/, the reloader picks up
      # cert-manager renewals automatically — no extraConfigs needed.
      merge:
        securityContext:
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          capabilities:
            drop:
              - ALL
    # prometheus-nats-exporter sidecar — scrapes the local NATS server's
    # monitor port (8222) and re-exposes /varz, /connz, /routez, /subz,
    # and /jsz=all as Prometheus metrics on port 7777. The otel-collector
    # gateway scrapes 7777 directly (see
    # infrastructure/controllers/otel-collector/helmrelease-gateway.yaml).
    promExporter:
      enabled: true
      merge:
        securityContext:
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          runAsNonRoot: true
          runAsUser: 1000
          capabilities:
            drop:
              - ALL

20	1. The user says `review this change`, `review this PR`, `re-review`, `check again`, or asks whether something is shippable.
    21	2. The checkout may be ambiguous: GitHub PR, local branch diff, staged diff, or a throwaway clone.
    22	3. Correctness may depend on adjacent contracts like Fleet manifests, JetStream authz, companion repos, or CI state.
    23	
    24	Non-goals:
    25	
    26	1. Do not start coding fixes unless the user asks for them.
    27	2. Do not summarize the PR description as if that were the review.
    28	
    29	## Inputs / context to gather
    30	
    31	1. Confirm the actual repo and review surface first.
    32	   - `pwd`
    33	   - `git status --short --branch`
    34	   - `git remote -v`
    35	   - If the current directory is not a repo, look for the nested checkout that is.
    36	2. Identify the authoritative artifact.
    37	   - GitHub PR: `gh pr view ... --json ...`, `gh pr diff ...`
    38	   - Local branch: compare `origin/main...HEAD` vs `main...HEAD` only after confirming which base is real
    39	   - Staged or unstaged review: inspect both before assuming the branch diff is enough
    40	3. Gather adjacent contracts only when the runtime path crosses boundaries.
    41	   - Fleet manifests / kustomize renders
    42	   - Companion repo code paths
    43	   - CI or check status when the user asks
    44	
    45	## Procedure
    46	
    47	1. Establish the review surface before reading much code.
    48	   - Confirm PR number, base, head SHA, branch name, changed files, and whether the local checkout matches it.
    49	   - If the repo uses `entire://` remotes or a shallow clone, prefer explicit `gh ... -R ...` and GitHub metadata over assumptions from local refs.
    50	   - If the custom remote will not resolve `pull/<n>/head`, fetch the PR head directly from GitHub into an isolated local ref or disposable worktree before deep reading.
    51	   - If GitHub reports `mergeStateStatus=DIRTY` or `mergeable=CONFLICTING`, refresh the live base ref (`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/git/ref/heads/<base> --jq .object.sha`) before finalizing so you do not anchor conclusions to a stale branch point.
    52	2. Read the diff and touched files, then inspect the smallest adjacent contract surface that can invalidate the review.
    53	   - Examples: authz grants, stream ownership, filter subjects, telemetry queries, companion error contracts, or shared validators/helpers that fan out into create/delete/manage flows.
    54	   - For delete/teardown work, trace both sides of the terminal transition: whether decommissioned resources are still routable for cleanup, and whether an event/outbox is acknowledged or a durable tombstone/reconciler remains after publish.
    55	3. Run the narrowest meaningful validation.
    56	   - Go: touched-package tests first; use broader tests only if the environment supports them.
    57	   - Manifests: `kustomize build` or `kubectl kustomize`.
    58	   - CI: `gh pr checks` when the user asks or when local validation is incomplete.
    59	4. Report findings in severity order with concrete file anchors and explicit validation boundaries.
    60	   - If no findings, say so directly and include residual risk or static-only caveats.
    61	5. If the user asks for re-review, repeat from the current head SHA instead of relying on the earlier conclusion.
    62	   - If they say they added a commit or ask to "re-pull from the branch", run a fresh `git fetch origin` (or the repo-appropriate fetch), re-pin `gh pr view` metadata, and confirm the new head SHA before keeping or changing the verdict.
    63	
    64	## Efficiency plan
    65	
    66	1. Cache the PR metadata, head SHA, and chosen review base early so you do not rediscover them.
    67	2. Use `rg` to find exact symbols, stream names, filter subjects, or error strings from the diff before opening many files.
    68	3. Stop expanding adjacent checks once the governing contract is confirmed.
    69	4. If sandbox failures are clearly environmental, pivot to narrower validation or note the boundary instead of retrying the same command repeatedly.
    70	5. If the branch moves mid-review, stop re-reading old conclusions and refresh only the metadata, diff base, and touched validation set for the new head.
    71	6. If existing review comments or Bugbot feedback could overlap your findings, fetch them directly with `gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/pulls/<pr>/comments --paginate` and treat them as clues, not as substitutes for your own validation.
    72	
    73	## Pitfalls and fixes
    74	
    75	1. Symptom: `gh api ...?ref=...` fails in zsh.
    76	   Fix: quote the path containing `?ref=`.
    77	2. Symptom: `origin/main...HEAD` is misleading or empty.
    78	   Fix: confirm the real PR base from GitHub metadata or fetch the base commit first.
    79	3. Symptom: the current directory is not a repo.
    80	   Fix: find the nested checkout and review there.
    81	4. Symptom: `kustomize` is missing.
    82	   Fix: try `kubectl kustomize`.
    83	5. Symptom: `git fetch origin pull/<n>/head` or equivalent PR-ref fetches fail on an `entire://` remote.
    84	   Fix: fetch from `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>.git` into an isolated ref or worktree, then review from there.
    85	6. Symptom: Go/mise validation reports package or stat-cache permission errors, or parallel commands contaminate each other.

     7	# Live review of mirror-pipeline PR #246 found a race, then two additional readiness issues
     8	
     9	Rollout context: The user asked “review this change” and later “anything else other than this?” for `/Users/nodo/work/tasks/track-d-consumer-std/mirror-pipeline`. Review was review-only, with live GitHub SHA pinning and adjacent Fleet/NATS contract inspection.
    10	
    11	## Task 1: Review lifecycle consumer migration
    12	
    13	Outcome: partial
    14	
    15	Preference signals:
    16	- The user asked only “review this change” and expected a complete correctness/risk review rather than edits -> future reviews should inspect the live diff, surrounding runtime contracts, validate behavior, and remain review-only unless editing is explicitly requested.
    17	
    18	Key steps:
    19	- Reviewed branch `nodo/cor-1254-loop1-lifecycle-jsconsumer` against `main` (`1b24bd6`), initially at `92bcb7d`, PR #246.
    20	- Inspected `jsconsumer` retry/readiness semantics, lifecycle code, real-broker tests, Fleet NATS grants, and stream configuration.
    21	- Verified the migration’s intended behavior: server-owned BackOff ladder, unsettled failed deliveries, explicit consumer configuration, durable reachability readiness probe, and correct `$JS.ACK.resource_lifecycle_v1.>` / `$JS.API.>` permissions.
    22	- Found a P1 race in the new test: `lifecycle_broker_test.go:616` polled `bytes.Buffer.String()` while a probe goroutine wrote logs through slog.
    23	- Focused package tests passed normally, but `go test -race` failed; GitHub CI independently reported the same race.
    24	- The race was fixed in commit `3765557`, using a mutex-protected buffer and record-specific JSON assertions; live CI then passed.
    25	
    26	Failures and how to do differently:
    27	- Do not treat normal tests or local race runs as sufficient when a test captures process-wide logging asynchronously; use synchronized capture and validate the intended record, not raw shared output.
    28	- Keep committed PR state separate from uncommitted checkout work. The checkout later contained an uncommitted readiness/cadence change that was not part of the reviewed head.
    29	
    30	Reusable knowledge:
    31	- `jsconsumer.Run` owns retry supervision and returns only for permanent configuration errors; readiness must not rely only on `Run` returning.
    32	- For this lifecycle fan, failed fanout must leave the JetStream message unsettled so the durable BackOff ladder controls redelivery; plain `Nak` is immediate and `NakWithDelay` conflicts with server BackOff.
    33	- Real-broker tests are required to prove stored consumer configuration, server redelivery timing, and AckFloor advancement; fakes only prove disposition calls.
    34	- Fleet’s `meta-fanout` identity already has the required `resource_lifecycle_v1.>` subscribe/publish, `$JS.ACK.resource_lifecycle_v1.>`, and `$JS.API.>` grants.
    35	
    36	References:
    37	- PR: `https://github.com/entirehq/mirror-pipeline/pull/246`
    38	- Initial blocking finding: `cmd/meta-fanout/lifecycle_broker_test.go:616`; CI run `31814070684`.
    39	- Fix commit: `3765557 test(meta-fanout): synchronize the captured log buffer; assert on records, not raw text`.
    40	
    41	## Task 2: Additional review sweep
    42	
    43	Outcome: partial
    44	
    45	Preference signals:
    46	- The user asked “anything else other than this?” -> future follow-up reviews should re-pin the current head and independently sweep for additional correctness, lifecycle, shutdown, telemetry, and cross-system issues rather than merely restating the known finding.
    47	
    48	Key steps:
    49	- Re-reviewed live head `3765557`; PR was clean/mergeable and CI green.
    50	- Found two additional P2 issues on that head:
    51	  1. After a successful readiness probe, the startup-attempt budget remained nonzero. A later post-bind probe failure could re-enter the 250ms cadence and hammer JetStream during an outage. Uncommitted `probeCadence` work in the checkout appeared to address this, but was not yet in the PR.
    52	  2. Canceling an in-flight `CONSUMER.INFO` probe returns `context.Canceled`, which `durableReachable` passed to `natslog.SubscribeErr`, producing a false ERROR during shutdown. A targeted probe reproduced: `{"level":"ERROR","msg":"Lifecycle durable unreachable; reporting NotReady","error":"context canceled"}`.
    53	- No other actionable issues were found in retry disposition, consumer configuration, readiness semantics, or Fleet ACLs.
    54	
    55	Failures and how to do differently:
    56	- A stateful sequence property cannot be safely tested with a stateless helper that only receives the current outcome and a raw counter. The startup phase must be explicitly terminated after success and never resumed; a stateful cadence object/test should encode that invariant.
    57	- Treat self-cancellation (`context.Canceled` / `context.DeadlineExceeded` when the parent context is already canceled) as shutdown noise, while preserving real timeout, missing-consumer, and deletion signals.
    58	
    59	Reusable knowledge:
    60	- Readiness probes need separate state for “ever bound” and “startup grace still active.” Missing durable before first bind is expected; missing durable after binding is operationally significant because recreation can replay retained events.
    61	- The probe’s fast startup cadence must be one-way: first success or budget exhaustion transitions permanently to the steady interval.
    62	
    63	References:
    64	- Live reviewed head: `3765557cd7ff5ef53e806fdcdbbf4497428f9596`.
    65	- Additional cadence issue: `cmd/meta-fanout/lifecycle.go` `probeDurable` / `nextProbeInterval` logic.
    66	- Additional shutdown issue: `cmd/meta-fanout/lifecycle.go` `durableReachable`; reproduced with `context.Canceled`.
    67	- Checkout had uncommitted `cmd/meta-fanout/lifecycle.go` cadence work; it was not reviewed as part of PR head.

Commands are run outside the sandbox if they are approved by the user, or match an existing rule that allows it to run unrestricted. The command string is split into independent command segments at shell control operators, including but not limited to:

Request changes. I found one P2 correctness issue at head `2f0b483f`; the head remained stable through review.

### Finding — retry exhaustion now happens earlier

The migration changes when the retry timer begins:

- Previously: fan work completed, then `NakWithDelay(30s)` started the delay.
- Now: JetStream’s 30-second `BackOff` begins at message delivery, overlapping fan processing.

Fan-out is sequential across three remotes, each with a five-second timeout ([fan loop](https://github.com/entirehq/mirror-pipeline/blob/2f0b483fd622a6d3333eba164ef29e491c7d2947/cmd/meta-fanout/lifecycle.go#L133-L156), [publish timeout](https://github.com/entirehq/mirror-pipeline/blob/2f0b483fd622a6d3333eba164ef29e491c7d2947/cmd/meta-fanout/lifecycle.go#L191-L197)). Failed attempts are intentionally left unsettled for server redelivery ([failure path](https://github.com/entirehq/mirror-pipeline/blob/2f0b483fd622a6d3333eba164ef29e491c7d2947/cmd/meta-fanout/lifecycle.go#L688-L714)).

A real-broker diagnostic measured the difference with a 400ms handler and one-second delay:

- Old client-owned delay: `1.402s`
- New server-owned delay: `1.002s`

In production, one timed-out remote shortens the eight-delivery recovery window by roughly 35 seconds; three timeouts can shorten it by roughly 1m45s. Because there is no terminal DLQ, earlier exhaustion can turn a recoverable regional outage into missed fan-out requiring manual replay.

The timing tests currently compare only configured delays and use an immediately failing publisher, so they cannot detect this change ([timing assertion](https://github.com/entirehq/mirror-pipeline/blob/2f0b483fd622a6d3333eba164ef29e491c7d2947/cmd/meta-fanout/lifecycle_timing_test.go#L20-L61), [broker fixture](https://github.com/entirehq/mirror-pipeline/blob/2f0b483fd622a6d3333eba164ef29e491c7d2947/cmd/meta-fanout/lifecycle_broker_test.go#L141-L163)).

Either preserve the old wall-clock recovery window, or explicitly accept and document the shorter envelope and add a slow-handler real-broker test.

Validation otherwise looks good: focused race tests passed, touched package tests passed, `diff --check` is clean, CI is green, and Fleet’s current lifecycle/JetStream permissions cover the new consumer. The earlier race, readiness-cadence, and shutdown-log findings are fixed.

Failed attempts are intentionally left unsettled for server redelivery ([failure path](https://github.com/entirehq/mirror-pipeline/blob/2f0b483fd622a6d3333eba164ef29e491c7d2947/cmd/meta-fanout/lifecycle.go#L688-L714)).

A real-broker diagnostic measured the difference with a 400ms handler and one-second delay:

- Old client-owned delay: `1.402s`
- New server-owned delay: `1.002s`

In production, one timed-out remote shortens the eight-delivery recovery window by roughly 35 seconds; three timeouts can shorten it by roughly 1m45s. Because there is no terminal DLQ, earlier exhaustion can turn a recoverable regional outage into missed fan-out requiring manual replay.

The timing tests currently compare only configured delays and use an immediately failing publisher, so they cannot detect this change ([timing assertion](https://github.com/entirehq/mirror-pipeline/blob/2f0b483fd622a6d3333eba164ef29e491c7d2947/cmd/meta-fanout/lifecycle_timing_test.go#L20-L61), [broker fixture](https://github.com/entirehq/mirror-pipeline/blob/2f0b483fd622a6d3333eba164ef29e491c7d2947/cmd/meta-fanout/lifecycle_broker_test.go#L141-L163)).

Either preserve the old wall-clock recovery window, or explicitly accept and document the shorter envelope and add a slow-handler real-broker test.

Validation otherwise looks good: focused race tests passed, touched package tests passed, `diff --check` is clean, CI is green, and Fleet’s current lifecycle/JetStream permissions cover the new consumer. The earlier race, readiness-cadence, and shutdown-log findings are fixed.

241-- A floor-age monitor must distinguish idle caught-up consumers from pending stalls, disarm cached stall state after consumer-info poll errors, and clear per-message failure clocks after ordinary successful settlement. Enforce `RecoverBy` at the runtime quarantine decision, not solely during construction validation. [Task 2]
242-
243-## Failures and how to do differently
244-
245-- Symptom: a refreshed PR carries an older review finding. Cause: the branch moved. Fix: re-pin the head before reusing a finding; here `0819499` fixed the original final-ack classification. [Task 1]
246:- Symptom: retry code assumes BackOff slows an explicit NAK, or tests only a fake disposition call. Cause: the mechanism and test oracle are wrong. Fix: leave transient failures untouched for AckWait/BackOff and prove timing with an embedded real broker. [Task 1]
247-- Symptom: recovery guidance says a target is stranded because AckFloor did not advance. Cause: it treats a contiguous watermark as per-message proof. Fix: call non-advancement uncertain and never prescribe destructive global stream deletion without additional consumer-specific evidence. [Task 1]
248-- Symptom: a stationary floor ages new work, stale poll data triggers enforcement, or recovered work is immediately quarantined. Cause: consumer-global snapshots and failure clocks outlive the evidence they represent. Fix: require fresh healthy observations, separate idle from pending state, and clear/scope failure state on successful processing. [Task 2]
249-- Symptom: terminal DLQ capture failure is reported as `OutcomeRetried`. Cause: final `MaxDeliver` NAK has no reserved broker delivery. Fix: reserve a delivery budget, use durable retry/outbox handling, or report explicit stranded/manual recovery; do not claim a retry that cannot occur. [Task 2]
250:- Symptom: comments still describe plain-Nak/NakWithDelay after the implementation uses `awaitRedelivery`. Fix: update public docs and migration tests with the actual server-owned AckWait/BackOff model. [Task 1][Task 2]
251-

1062-
1063:- For mirror-pipeline Datadog checks, start with service labels `mirror-worker`, `core-fanout`, `fanout`, and `meta-fanout`; `mirror-worker` was the fastest path to real failure signal here [Task 1]
1064-- `mirror.sync.completed{outcome:nak|term}` is the high-signal failure metric; `outcome:raced` is intentionally excluded from the sync-failure monitor and should not be treated as equivalent to a real failure [Task 1]

mirror-pipeline — the service whose whole job is consuming JetStream — has **zero** `jsconsumer` adopters; every fetch loop is hand-rolled. That's the failure class behind the 48h backlog (an app backoff config silently overriding AckWait) and it means no consumer inherits library fixes (circuit breaker, DLQ capture, telemetry). Consumer config is imperative, per-app, undiffable, and identical across cells whether that fits or not.

## Proposed solution

* **Harden go-nuts first:** reject invalid configs at startup (backoff ladder > AckWait unrepresentable; DLQ policy required; no bare `Term()`); add bind-only mode (+ dev mode for local/CI); publish stream contracts as a module so `refevents`-style hand copies die.
* **Migrate one loop at a time** (<issue id="e9af1b79-ed6c-49fc-99c6-b90d4bc6f045" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1009/go-nuts-phase-5-migrate-remaining-consumeadmin-surfaces-to-the-modern">COR-1009</issue> ph. 5): mirror-pipeline's 4 loops, then entiredb `permssweep`, entire-api `ingest`/`analysis`.
* **Per loop, durables become fleet-managed NACK** `Consumer` **CRs** (extends nats-streams "Option A"): snapshot `nats consumer info -j`, author a full-mirror CR (`preventDelete: true`, explicit `ackPolicy`, `ackWait = backoff[0]`, live maxAckPending/maxWaiting stated), canary-adopt verifying ack floor/delivery counts unchanged, then switch the app to bind-only in the same change (single-writer rule). Go/no-go checkpoint after the first canary durable; fallback is app-owned consumers with library validation.
* Durable advisory capture for the live index queue (<issue id="5f90e18b-2788-40fa-bd86-8c63cd86aff5" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-997/durable-advisory-capture-for-job-stream-dead-lettering-close-the-repo">COR-997</issue>).

{"comments":[{"id":"c459872d-079d-43a9-80c0-84112a0f6f88","body":"**Migration kickoff approved (2026-08-14, Andrea, after orchestrator review of the phase-0 analysis).** Full phase-0 read-out: 4 loops resolve to **11 durables ≈ 12 PRs**, one trail per consumer; Retry/DLQ adoption on exactly the 5 durables where DLQ + grant + enablement pre-exist; the other 6 keep designed give-ups (KV fail-index + rekick, workqueue TermOnExhaustion, retention-backed silent drop). Order: PR-0 (go-nuts bump + embedded-broker harness + shared Schedule conformance helper) → meta-fanout-lifecycle → webhook-forwarder (Shape A) → engine switch (default off) → the rest, lowest risk first; cmd/worker last.

**Decisions of record:**
1. **Class rule — long-running handlers cannot use server-owned ladders:** server normalization forces `ackWait = backoff[0]`, and `KeepInProgress` caps heartbeat extension at ~5×AckWait, so a fast first rung starves handlers whose work time ≫ rung (cmd/worker: 30m syncs vs a 2m30s cap). Such consumers keep **single-owner client scheduling**, validated by `jsconsumer.Schedule` (empty violations). Mixed ownership remains forbidden — that was the ENT-1535 defect; pure client ownership is not.
2. **Exit criterion amended:** "0 hand-rolled fetch loops **except cmd/fanout's two pooled consumers**" — jsconsumer's serial Consume + prefetch-discarding Stop cannot host the 8-worker pools without duplicate git syncs (1s dedup window on mirror_git_v1). Follow-up: go-nuts `Runner.Drain` + pool-friendly consume — to be bundled in one future go-nuts session with the breaker enforce-or-delete and the contracts module.
3. **Engine switch approved** (per-consumer, default off, preserves merge-by-merge staging observation) with its deletion as a **ticketed** final PR.
4. **Binding per-PR requirements:** stored-vs-rendered `nats consumer info -j` diff (staging + prod) in every trail body — `CreateOrUpdateConsumer` writes fields the legacy client never sent (zero MaxAckPending → server default 1000; immutable-field disagreement → fatal on rollout); monitor/runbook text deltas ride **in the same PR** as any give-up semantics change (the MAX_DELIVERIES/MSG_TERMINATED advisory backstops go quiet under capture-then-Ack); cmd/worker's PR carries a test pinning `MaxDeliver × syncTimeout + scheduled waits < mirror_git_v1 maxAge` (measured worst case 5h04m vs 6h — the margin must not erode without a red test).
5. Trails-fanout 24h/72h InactiveThreshold divergence: normalize or document, own commit, written rationale.

Also corrected from phase-0 measurement: InactiveThreshold reliance is **6 of 11 durables** (webhooks_github_v1 consumers + forwarder + trails-fanouts), not "every fanout loop"; and the migration *deletes* the `ensureInactiveThreshold` read-modify-write hack (legacy PullSubscribe ignored the field), slightly cheapening CR-reactivation precondition #2.","createdAt":"2026-08-14T11:35:09.876Z","updatedAt":"2026-08-14T11:35:09.779Z","parentId":null,"resolvedAt":null,"quotedText":null,"author":{"id":"76f6927c-ac03-4620-9454-a3acd751fbd7","name":"Andrea Nodari"},"onBehalfOf":null},{"id":"9984f248-a47b-4b4a-8b51-8c8a565adcff","body":"**CR half PARKED (decision, Andrea, 2026-08-14).** Track D continues as the library-migration track only (jsconsumer + server-owned ladders, one trail per consumer, COR-1009 ph. 5); no NACK Consumer CRs will be authored. The canary session was closed without pushing its branch — the CR artifact was deliberately not preserved; the knowledge that matters (canary verdict, field-manual corrections, the two structural blockers, durable-selection rationale) is recorded in the comment above and suffices to re-author in ~an hour if this resumes.

**Reactivation preconditions, all three, before any CR work restarts:**
1. go-nuts **bind-only mode shipped** (Start must stop writing BackOff, or CR-owned ladders flap forever — the ordering blocker).
2. mirror-pipeline's **InactiveThreshold reliance redesigned** (a CR permanently defeats the reaping safety valve from the 2026-06-01 incident).
3. A **concrete need** that per-repo validation can't meet: per-cell ladder divergence, or fleet-central merge-time validation demonstrably missed something that CI-per-repo (exported `jsconsumer.Schedule` in each app's gate) could not catch.

What the program loses meanwhile, accepted: merge-time fleet-central timing validation, E7's generation-from-CRs (E7 to be re-shaped around per-repo declarations or parked in turn), per-cell ladder overlays. Consequence for Track E noted on COR-1255's thread by reference here.","createdAt":"2026-08-14T11:03:47.816Z","updatedAt":"2026-08-14T11:03:47.738Z","parentId":null,"resolvedAt":null,"quotedText":null,"author":{"id":"76f6927c-ac03-4620-9454-a3acd751fbd7","name":"Andrea Nodari"},"onBehalfOf":null},{"id":"bdd8dda5-7243-4bbc-8580-e05332cd0de5","body":"**Canary verdict (2026-08-14, staging canary session — deliverable authored, deliberately not run/applied).** Chosen durable: `ci-webhooks-inbound` on `ci_webhooks_inbound_v1`, staging us-west-2 (staging-only by construction, sole consumer, Limits retention, boring traffic, app half already a jsconsumer adopter). Full-mirror CR + verification plan complete on local branch `nodo/cor-1254-consumer-cr-canary` (commit `84fd5f5`, **unpushed**). Zero Consumer CRs exist in any cluster.

**Field-manual corrections (verified against installed CRD / nack 0.23.0 / jsm.go 0.4.1 / nats-server 2.14.4):**
- The field is **`spec.backoff`, all-lowercase** — `backOff:` is *silently pruned* by the API server; `kubeconform -strict` is the only guard.
- Adoption-merge has three field classes: CRD-defaulted (always sent), unconditionally-sent-as-zero, sent-only-if-set (omission retains). Danger is not uniform: `ackPolicy`/`deliverPolicy`/`replayPolicy`/`maxWaiting` are immutable-on-update and **fail loudly, durable untouched**; **`ackWait` is the sole silent catastrophe** (mutable, CRD default 1ns).
- nack runs pedantic **unconditionally** (hardcoded), so `ackWait == backoff[0]` is server-enforced.
- `preventDelete` protects the durable, not its config; reverting a CR change does not un-apply it.

**Two structural blockers for CR adoption beyond the canary:**
1. **CR-owned ladders are ordering-blocked on bind-only:** jsconsumer `Start` always writes `BackOff`, so an app with a nil ladder *clears* a CR-owned ladder on every start and nack restores it ~1 min later — permanent config flapping. Bind-only mode (D0, not yet built) must exist before any ladder-carrying CR.
2. **mirror-pipeline durables are not adoptable:** every fanout loop (a) relies on server-side `InactiveThreshold` reaping (24–72h) as the safety valve from the 2026-06-01 interest-stream incident — a Consumer CR defeats it, nack recreating the reaped durable within ~1 min and restoring the interest pin permanently; and (b) schedules redelivery client-side (NakWithDelay 30s×7), so a CR would mirror server config while the real timing contract lives in the app, invisible to the E1 lint. Loops must migrate to jsconsumer + server ladders FIRST; CRs, if ever, come after.

Side-finding to triage separately: `meta-fanout-backfill` (github_meta_backfill) has a `/readyz` coupling that fails latently at the next rollout.

**Sequencing consequence regardless of park/proceed: the original "CR + bind-only per loop in one change" recipe inverts — library migration first, CRs second.** Parking decision + branch preservation pending Andrea.","createdAt":"2026-08-14T10:32:44.752Z","updatedAt":"2026-08-14T10:32:44.729Z","parentId":null,"resolvedAt":null,"quotedText":null,"author":{"id":"76f6927c-ac03-4620-9454-a3acd751fbd7","name":"Andrea Nodari"},"onBehalfOf":null},{"id":"bcfdf8ad-96f7-40e0-b93a-31d1f300409b","body":"**Ladder-ownership decision affecting all Track D CRs (2026-08-12, Andrea): Consumer CRs carry the redelivery ladder (`backOff`) — the server/CR is the single owner; apps plain-Nak.** Full rationale on ENT-1601.

Consequences for this track:
- Full-mirror CRs include `backOff` (+ `ackWait = backoff[0]`, pedantic mode) — already implied by the field manual; now it is also *the* ladder, not a mirror of a client-side one.
- Migrating apps drop any client-side redelivery scheduling as part of their jsconsumer migration; go-nuts `Retry` provides capture-then-Ack, telemetry, and the observe soak only.
- Bind-only mode validates client-side expectations (`RecoverBy`, `FloorAge`, `MaxTimeToDeadLetter` arithmetic) against the durable's actual server ladder at startup — closed loop, no inference.
- Fleet CI admission (COR-1255) validates the complete timing contract from the CR alone using go-nuts' exported `jsconsumer.Schedule.Validate` — including the mixed-ownership violation, which must never pass review.
- The staging canary is unaffected (full-mirror already includes `backOff`); note the durable chosen should have a server-side ladder or none, and the CR mirrors reality either way.","createdAt":"2026-08-12T13:16:22.207Z","updatedAt":"2026-08-12T13:16:22.169Z","parentId":null,"resolvedAt":null,"quotedText":null,"author":{"id":"76f6927c-ac03-4620-9454-a3acd751fbd7","name":"Andrea Nodari"},"onBehalfOf":null}],"hasNextPage":false}

COR-1254 Track D — Consumer standardization: jsconsumer everywhere, durables as fleet Consumer CRs (wk 2–9, ~18 pd)

## Problem mirror-pipeline — the service whose whole job is consuming JetStream — has **zero** `jsconsumer` adopters; every fetch loop is hand-rolled. That's the failure class behind the 48h backlog (an app backoff config silently overriding AckWait) and it means no consumer inherits library fixes (circuit breaker, DLQ capture, telemetry). Consumer config is imperative, per-app, undiffable, and identical across cells whether that fits or not. ## Proposed solution * **Harden go-nuts first:** reject invalid configs at startup (backoff ladder > AckWait unrepresentable; DLQ policy required; no bare `Term()`); add bind-only mode (+ dev mode for local/CI); publish stream contracts as a module so `refevents`-style hand copies die. * **Migrate one loop at a time** ([COR-1009](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1009/go-nuts-phase-5-migrate-remaining-consumeadmin-surfaces-to-the-modern) ph. 5): mirror-pipeline's 4 loops, then entiredb `permssweep`, entire-api `ingest`/`analysis`. * **Per loop, durables become fleet-managed NACK** `Consumer` **CRs** (extends nats-streams "Option A"): snapshot `nats consumer info -j`, author a full-mirror CR (`preventDelete: true`, explicit `ackPolicy`, `ackWait = backoff[0]`, live maxAckPending/maxWaiting stated), canary-adopt verifying ack floor/delivery counts unchanged, then switch the app to bind-only in the same change (single-writer rule). Go/no-go checkpoint after the first canary durable; fallback is app-owned consumers with library validation. * Durable advisory capture for the live index queue ([COR-997](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-997/durable-advisory-capture-for-job-stream-dead-lettering-close-the-repo)). **Exit:** 0 hand-rolled fetch loops; 0 app-side create/update calls; legacy consume-surface list empty; migrated durables are fleet CRs with delivery state untouched.

COR-1254 Track D — Consumer standardization: jsconsumer everywhere, durables as fleet Consumer CRs (wk 2–9, ~18 pd)

## Problem mirror-pipeline — the service whose whole job is consuming JetStream — has **zero** `jsconsumer` adopters; every fetch loop is hand-rolled. That's the failure class behind the 48h backlog (an app backoff config silently overriding AckWait) and it means no consumer inherits library fixes (circuit breaker, DLQ capture, telemetry). Consumer config is imperative, per-app, undiffable, and identical across cells whether that fits or not. ## Proposed solution * **Harden go-nuts first:** reject invalid configs at startup (backoff ladder > AckWait unrepresentable; DLQ policy required; no bare `Term()`); add bind-only mode (+ dev mode for local/CI); publish stream contracts as a module so `refevents`-style hand copies die. * **Migrate one loop at a time** ([COR-1009](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-1009/go-nuts-phase-5-migrate-remaining-consumeadmin-surfaces-to-the-modern) ph. 5): mirror-pipeline's 4 loops, then entiredb `permssweep`, entire-api `ingest`/`analysis`. * **Per loop, durables become fleet-managed NACK** `Consumer` **CRs** (extends nats-streams "Option A"): snapshot `nats consumer info -j`, author a full-mirror CR (`preventDelete: true`, explicit `ackPolicy`, `ackWait = backoff[0]`, live maxAckPending/maxWaiting stated), canary-adopt verifying ack floor/delivery counts unchanged, then switch the app to bind-only in the same change (single-writer rule). Go/no-go checkpoint after the first canary durable; fallback is app-owned consumers with library validation. * Durable advisory capture for the live index queue ([COR-997](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-997/durable-advisory-capture-for-job-stream-dead-lettering-close-the-repo)). **Exit:** 0 hand-rolled fetch loops; 0 app-side create/update calls; legacy consume-surface list empty; migrated durables are fleet CRs with delivery state untouched.

The cross-region resource_lifecycle_v1 fan moves off its hand-rolled PullSubscribe/Fetch(1) loop onto jsconsumer.Run + Process, and its redelivery ladder moves server-side. Same durable name, so no recreation and no redelivery storm; behaviour is preserved except where noted below. WHAT MOVES - jsconsumer.Run + Process replace the subscribe/backoff loop, the Fetch loop, the shutdown-error classification and the span prologue. MaxMessages 1 preserves the Fetch(1) pacing: AckWait runs from server delivery into the client buffer, not from callback dispatch, so anything queued behind a slow fan would age unprocessed. - The ladder is now the durable's. lifecycleBackOff derives consumerFailureDelay x (consumerMaxDeliver-1) from the two constants rather than restating them, so the numbers that must agree cannot drift. The app's disposition for a failed fan is DO NOTHING — the ack timeout brings the delivery back on that ladder. A client NakWithDelay beside a server ladder is the ENT-1535 defect (the server stretches each NAK by the BackOff increments, so redeliveries follow neither); a plain Nak would redeliver immediately and skip the ladder. - Every field CreateOrUpdateConsumer sends is now stated, because a field omitted in code is not "unchanged on the durable" — it is reset to a default. WHAT DOES NOT MOVE Give-up semantics. No Term path, no Retry, no DLQ: the event is republished verbatim so nothing about it can be permanently unprocessable, and resource_lifecycle_v1 is limits-retention — it holds every event for its full max age whatever this consumer does, so the replay path is the source stream. Adding capture would need a DLQ stream and a meta-fanout publish grant that do not exist. InactiveThreshold stays unset, and now says so explicitly. The 2026-06-01 reaping valve is for interest streams where an abandoned durable pins deliveries for ALL consumers; on limits retention an idle durable pins nothing. All seven cells carry no threshold today and none is added. The timing envelope is unchanged — 8 deliveries, give up at t+3m30s — which the pre-flight is what licenses claiming: snapshots of all 7 cells showed this durable has NO server-side backoff, so the effective ladder really was the client's flat 30s. (webhook-forwarder and fanout are NOT like this; they carry an undeclared 41h ladder, COR-1270. Loop 2 cannot make this claim.) ONE DELIBERATE CONFIG CHANGE MaxAckPending 65536 -> 1000. The 65536 in all seven cells was never chosen: nats.go's legacy PullSubscribe copies its own client-side subscription-channel capacity into the server config. jsconsumer sends the field on every start, so leaving it zero would have rewritten all seven silently; this makes it a recorded decision instead. Generous either way at a one-message prefetch. TWO KNOWN DELTAS - /readyz is narrower. The old loop held a `subscribed` bool set after each successful PullSubscribe, so a RETRYABLE boot failure (stream absent, no responders) also read NotReady. jsconsumer.Run exposes no start-success signal, so Ready() now reports only that the configuration was accepted — which does cover this migration's likeliest failure, an immutable-field disagreement. In exchange Run recreates a consume loop that closes mid-run, as the old outer loop did. Closing the gap needs go-nuts to expose readiness from Run; recorded beside the Runner.Drain and FloorMonitor-attach gaps entire-search #131 logged. - The fan-failure log drops redeliver_in and gains max_deliver. The app no longer schedules the redelivery, so printing a delay would be a claim about someone else's config — true only while the two agree, which is the drift this track exists to remove. Position in the ladder is what a responder can act on; the ladder is on the durable. outcome=nak is kept verbatim on the metric: dashboards key on it and its meaning is unchanged (this delivery failed and will come back). What changed is who schedules the redelivery, which the metric never described. The local ackableMsg seam and numDelivered helper are gone — jetstream.Msg is already an interface, natsmsgtest.FakeMsg is the double, and backoff.NumDelivered is the library's own reading of the delivery count. The existing unit tests answer what the handler DOES — which disposition it chose. These answer what the broker does about it, which the fakes cannot: they encode the same model as the code, so a belief held wrongly in both places produces a green test. Three broker tests, one per load-bearing belief: - StoredConfigIsTheRenderedConfig drives the REAL lifecycleConsumerConfig through the real CreateOrUpdateConsumer and reads back what the server stored. This is the executable form of the pre-flight diff: against the 7-cell snapshot the intended delta is exactly two fields (the ladder appears, MaxAckPending becomes a chosen number) and everything else must land unchanged. - FanFailure_IsRedeliveredByTheServerLadder pins the belief that replaced the client NakWithDelay: settle nothing, get the delivery back, paced by BackOff. The fixture ladder is SCALED to milliseconds and GROWING on purpose — on a flat ladder BackOff[0] equals AckWait, so the test would pass whether redelivery followed the ladder or merely the ack timeout, pinning nothing. Growing rungs mean the second gap can only come from BackOff[1]. Gap tolerances are half the distance to the nearest rival explanation (~0 for a plain Nak; rung1 for a ladder that does not advance), so the assertion cannot accept the behaviour it was written to reject. - CleanFan_AdvancesTheAckFloor pins the success path on the floor itself, which is what every stall alert on these streams reads. FakeMsg can only show that Ack was called; a denied $JS.ACK publish returns no error at all (COR-1224), so "we called Ack" and "the message is settled" are different claims. Plus the timing contract, validated by go-nuts' exported jsconsumer.Schedule rather than by hand, rendering the before/after table for the trail: | delivery | before (client Nak, measured) | after (server ladder) | | 2 | t+30s | t+30s | | 8 | t+3m30s — give up | t+3m30s — give up | checked against the TIGHTEST retention any cell gives the stream (staging trims maxAge to 6h, base is 96h), and against the rung-count/AckWait agreement rules. Two notes on the fixtures themselves: - recordingJS is unusable for the failure test — it records only SUCCESSFUL publishes, so its count reads zero however many times the fan was attempted. Caught by the assertion failing; a local failingJS counts attempts instead. - the arrival timestamp is taken at delivery but published to the channel only after the handler returns. Sending first let the test collect its last arrival while that delivery's fan was still in flight, and assert on a count that had not happened yet. Verified stable across -count=3 and under -race. Ready() reflected only configRejected — set when jsconsumer.Run RETURNS, which it does only for a permanently rejected config. Run retries everything else and logs a warning per attempt, so through the outages a readiness gate exists for (stream not provisioned yet, JetStream unreachable while the TCP connection is up: no responders, meta-leader election, a CONSUMER.CREATE permission rejection surfacing as a timeout) configRejected never flips and /readyz stayed green while nothing was consumed. I checked whether the pre-existing gate covered it. It does not: natsregions.Health.Status() asks Local.IsConnected() only, so a live connection to a JetStream that cannot answer passes it. And in lifecycleOnly mode this consumer is the pod's SOLE readiness gate, so green there hides a real outage from anything watching /readyz — exactly what the pre-migration `subscribed` bool did not do. Ready() is now (config accepted) AND (durable reachable), the second refreshed by a slow probe that lives exactly as long as the consume loop. Run joins it on the way out, so no ConsumerInfo can be in flight on a connection the caller is about to drain. What the probe proves: the stream and durable exist and the JetStream API answered. What it does not: that THIS process is the one consuming (replicas share the durable), or that a delivery arrived. It is a strictly better proxy than configRejected for every case above, and it starts false — so a pod is NotReady until the first success, matching the old gate's boot behaviour. Two cadences, because startup and outage want opposite things. The first probe races Run creating the durable, so a single 5s interval left a healthy pod NotReady for seconds after it was already consuming — visible as a 5.10s test runtime, now 0.36s. It polls at 250ms until the first success, then settles to 5s, so a sustained outage is not hammered with four ConsumerInfo requests a second at the moment the server is already struggling. Two tests, and each fails for a different deletion: FollowsTheDurable asserts both directions on a broker with no stream provisioned (removing the probe leaves it Ready and red), ProbeRunsUnderRun asserts Run actually starts the probe and joins it (removing the goroutine leaves the helper tests passing and this one red). Left local to lifecycle.go rather than extracted: loops 2+ each have a /readyz gate and will want this shape, but inventing the shared abstraction from one example is how the wrong one gets built. The real fix is go-nuts exposing readiness from Run — recorded beside the Runner.Drain and FloorMonitor-attach gaps from entire-search #131. THE PROBE JOIN DEADLOCKED ON A REJECTED CONFIG (lifecycle.go) I registered `defer stopProbe()` and then `defer func(){ <-probeDone }()`. Defers run LIFO, so the JOIN ran first and the cancel second — and the probe exits only on its context. A Run that returned while the parent context was still alive (the only such path: a permanently rejected config) therefore blocked in its own defer until whole-app shutdown: goroutine leaked, the caller's lifecycleDone never closed, and the probe kept polling — at the 250ms startup cadence if CONSUMER.INFO never succeeded. Now one defer that cancels THEN joins. The join is still required: an in-flight ConsumerInfo must not outlive Run and land on a connection the caller is about to drain. TestLifecycleRun_ReturnsOnRejectedConfig covers it, with the parent context deliberately left alive because that is the condition the bug needed. The rejection is the real-world one this migration risks — a durable pre-existing with an immutable field set differently — and the broker supplies it verbatim: "ack policy can not be updated" (err_code 10012). Verified it catches the bug: with the two defers restored the test fails at its 20s guard; with the fix it returns in 0.04s. 2. SUSTAINED-OUTAGE TELEMETRY WAS LOST WITH natslog.Health Adopting jsconsumer.Run dropped the old subscribe loop's natslog.Health supervision, and Run is not an equivalent: it logs every retryable failure at WARN indefinitely, with no escalation and no counter. So the five-minute warn->error escalation and the restart-proof nats.consumer.recoverable_failures counter both went away. That matters most in US/default mode, where readiness DELIBERATELY excludes this consumer so a problem here cannot stall the live github_meta fan-out — which means a stopped lifecycle fan there shows up only in telemetry, and the telemetry had been removed. The readiness probe is the programmatic signal Run does not expose, so it now drives Health: SubscribeErr on a failed probe (the create/bind path, which absorbs a slow JetStream API and a not-yet-provisioned stream), Recovered on success. That required teaching natslog the modern client's errors first, and this is the part worth review attention. nuts.IsTransientSubscribeErr keys on the LEGACY nats.* values; the jetstream package defines its own distinct ones — jetstream.ErrStreamNotFound is a *jsError carrying an APIError, not nats.ErrStreamNotFound, so errors.Is finds neither across the two. Wiring the probe in naively would have classified every rollout-ordering failure as a FAULT and logged it at ERROR: the exact alert-eroding noise natslog exists to prevent (COR-1228), introduced by the package meant to prevent it. So SubscribeErr now also matches jetstream.ErrStreamNotFound (canonical "Stream not yet present, retrying", warn forever, excluded from escalation), and isTransientSubscribeErr extends the go-nuts predicate with ErrConsumerNotFound / ErrConsumerDoesNotExist (a supervised runner recreates a missing durable, so this is a race until escalation says otherwise) and ErrJetStreamNotEnabled (a 503 from a server still starting). ErrConsumerCreate and ErrBadRequest stay at ERROR — the migration's likeliest failure must page. TestSubscribeErrClassifiesModernClientErrors is the modern half of the existing severity table. Note on the fixture: its wantMsg column was initially never read, which is the same defect as no test — and it hid a wrong expectation, since the rollout-ordering case swaps in the canonical message rather than prefixing the caller's. Both fixed; the message is now asserted. This extension belongs in go-nuts beside the predicate it extends. Left here until the modern-client migration has more than one adopter to generalise from — recorded with the Runner.Drain / FloorMonitor-attach / Run-readiness follow-ups. A MISSING DURABLE MEANT TWO THINGS AND I CLASSIFIED IT AS ONE I demoted the modern ErrConsumerNotFound / ErrConsumerDoesNotExist to transient inside natslog. That is right during the initial create race and wrong afterwards, and natslog already had the contract I broke: nats.ErrConsumerDeleted stays at ERROR because a durable that disappears is recreated from the stream's DeliverPolicy, losing the cursor. For THIS consumer that is not abstract — DeliverPolicy is all and resource_lifecycle_v1 retains up to 96h, so a recreate re-fans the retained backlog cross-region, and the demotion would have let it happen under generic warnings. The distinction is not available from the error value, so it does not belong in a predicate over error values. natslog goes back to keeping a missing consumer loud (ErrJetStreamNotEnabled stays transient — a 503 from a server still starting), and the PROBE makes the call, because only the probe knows which side of the first successful bind it is on: - before any bind + consumer missing -> debug, no failure run. Expected: Run is concurrently creating it and logs its own attempts. - after a bind -> natslog.SubscribeErr, which is now ERROR for this class. - everything else (no responders, timeouts, stream missing) -> SubscribeErr from the first attempt, so a real outage at boot still escalates after five minutes. everBound is one-way on purpose: re-entering the startup posture after a real disappearance would both silence it and hammer the server at the fast cadence. Honest limit, stated in the code: at a 5s cadence this probe can miss a delete that Run recreates before the next tick, so it is a backstop, not a detector. The reliable signal is the runner's own recreate, which jsconsumer only logs. 2. THE FAST STARTUP PHASE WAS UNBOUNDED It ended on the first success only, so a pod starting while the stream or the API was unavailable never left it: four CONSUMER.INFO requests and — after the Health wiring — four log lines per second, indefinitely. That contradicted the comment directly above it and recreated the log-volume problem natslog exists to solve. The phase is now bounded by attempts as well: 20 at 250ms (~5s, orders of magnitude more than creating a durable takes), then the steady 5s cadence whether or not it ever succeeded. ON THE TESTS The disappearance test asserts LOG LEVEL, not just the boolean, because the level is what the finding was about — it deletes a bound durable under the consumer and requires ERROR. The burst test is worth noting: my first version re-implemented the cadence loop and counted its own probes over 8 wall-clock seconds. It passed — and would have kept passing with the bound deleted from production, which is the same defect as no test, and slow as well as useless. The decision is now a pure function (nextProbeInterval) that probeDurable actually calls, and the test drives that. Verified it fails with the bound removed: "interval = 250ms, want the steady 5s". Runtime 8.03s -> 0.00s. Gate: build, vet, go mod tidy -diff, git diff --check, gofmt -s, go test ./..., go test -race -count=2, golangci-lint (0 issues) — all clean. The quiet branch keyed on !everBound alone, so a durable that is never created — creation failing while CONSUMER.INFO answers not-found — stayed at debug forever: no counter, no escalation, and in US/default mode readiness deliberately excludes this consumer, so nothing else would have reported it either. Exactly the gap the probe was added to close, still open. The startup budget now governs the grace as well as the cadence. The loop computes inStartupGrace (never bound AND attempts remaining) and passes it in, so durableReachable no longer infers the situation from the error value — which it cannot, since the same ErrConsumerNotFound means "racing the create" or "will never appear" depending only on how long it has been true. Outside the grace, both remaining cases are loud: never created, or disappeared after binding. was_bound distinguishes them in the log; severity is the same because both need somebody to look. Operator-visible latency, now stated in the code: with the shipped constants the first loud report lands ~10s after start (~5s of grace, then the next steady probe). The alternatives were a fast cadence outliving the race it exists for, or a second knob to hurry the first complaint; ten seconds to notice a durable that will never appear is well inside any window that matters. ON THE TEST The reviewer's point that the old test could not reach this path was exact: it set everBound by hand. The new one drives the real probeDurable loop and never touches everBound. probeStartupAttempts is the one seam — zero uses the shipped constant — because the path needs the budget to expire, and at 20 × 250ms that is five seconds of test per assertion. Two setup mistakes worth recording, both caught by the test failing rather than by review: - I first ran it against a broker with NO stream. That yields ErrStreamNotFound, which already reaches Health as the canonical rollout-ordering line — a different path entirely, and the assertion never matched. The finding's scenario needs the stream present and the durable absent. - Verified it catches the bug: with the grace unbounded again it fails with "a durable that was never created stayed quiet past the startup budget; nothing entered natslog.Health". The interleaving needs a write and a poll to land together, which CI's scheduling produced and mine did not. captureLogs now returns a mutex-guarded buffer. Verified both directions: removing the mutex reproduces "WARNING: DATA RACE" locally on the focused test, restoring it passes at -race -count=3, and the full -race suite CI runs is clean. Fixing that surfaced a second, quieter problem in the same assertions. captureLogs replaces the PROCESS-WIDE default logger, so a parallel test's output lands in the same buffer — and the assertions searched the raw text for `"level":"ERROR"` anywhere in it. Both were passing for reasons that had nothing to do with the behaviour under test. Assertions now parse the captured JSON, find the record whose msg is the probe's own line, and read the level off THAT record. THE FAST CADENCE COULD RESUME AFTER A POST-BIND LOSS nextProbeInterval decided from the outcome plus a raw attempts-remaining counter, and a success settled the interval without spending the budget. So a durable that bound on its first probe kept ~19 unspent attempts, and a genuine loss inside the following ~95s (19 spent one per 5s tick) returned 250ms — re-entering the fast cadence to hammer a server that had just lost the durable. The comment three lines above said that must never happen; the code did not implement it. Every single-call assertion I had written passed, because the broken property is about a SEQUENCE: end, and never resume. So the decision is now a small state machine (probeCadence) whose observe(bound) ZEROES the budget on success rather than leaving it to decay, and the test drives sequences — never-binds, binds-immediately- then-loses, binds-mid-startup-then-loses. Verified it catches the bug: restoring the non-zeroing branch fails with "a success must end the startup phase, not merely pause it". 2. CANCELLING AN IN-FLIGHT PROBE LOGGED A FALSE ERROR ON EVERY ROLLOUT Run cancels the probe context on the way out, so a CONSUMER.INFO in flight at that moment returns context.Canceled. That value is not in the transient set, so it reached Health as a fault: {"level":"ERROR","msg":"Lifecycle durable unreachable; reporting NotReady","error":"context canceled"} Self-inflicted shutdown noise — precisely what natslog exists to remove (COR-1228: 57 ErrNoResponders in 83ms during a deploy, three false alerts in forty minutes) — reintroduced by the probe added to report real outages. Guarded narrowly: BOTH the parent context being done AND the error being context.Canceled, the same discipline as nuts.IsShutdownFetchErr, which will only call a drain benign when ctx is already done. A context.DeadlineExceeded from the probe's own timeout leaves the parent alive and still reaches Health, as do consumer-deletion and stream-missing errors. The test asserts both directions — silence on a cancelled parent, and a complaint on a live one — so the guard cannot be widened into swallowing real failures without going red. The comment three lines above said that must never happen; the code did not implement it. Every single-call assertion I had written passed, because the broken property is about a SEQUENCE: end, and never resume. So the decision is now a small state machine (probeCadence) whose observe(bound) ZEROES the budget on success rather than leaving it to decay, and the test drives sequences — never-binds, binds-immediately- then-loses, binds-mid-startup-then-loses. content.text:
I recommend accepting the clock-origin change and making it explicit. Keep the server-owned `30s × 7`, eight-delivery ladder.

Exact wall-clock preservation is incompatible with this migration:

- Restoring `NakWithDelay` recreates mixed ownership.
- Sending `InProgress` after failure is client scheduling disguised as a heartbeat.
- Increasing the rung to 45 seconds only approximates today’s three-region topology and unnecessarily slows fast failures.

I would add one corrective commit to this trail:

- Replace “timing envelope unchanged” with “scheduled ladder unchanged; wall-clock recovery window is shorter by handler time.”
- Fix `timingcontract` terminology so its `t+` values are clearly scheduled offsets, not guaranteed delivery timestamps.
- Add a slow-failure real-broker test proving the 30-second server clock starts at delivery.
- Record the operational delta: current production handler bound is approximately 15 seconds, so the eighth attempt moves from `3m30s–5m15s` previously to approximately `3m30s`.
- State that no existing monitor or runbook encodes the old wall-clock value, so no companion configuration change is required.

I would not expand the ladder or add a DLQ in this PR. Those are policy changes, whereas this trail should establish one honest, server-owned timing model. After that corrective commit passes CI, I’d consider the trail code-ready.

Author: Andrea Nodari <andrea@entire.io>
Commit: Andrea Nodari <andrea@entire.io>

    test(meta-fanout): state the server retry clock honestly
    
    Keep the lifecycle durable's server-owned 30s x 7 ladder and make the accepted clock-origin delta explicit: client NakWithDelay started after handler completion, while JetStream BackOff starts at delivery and overlaps handler work.
    
    The shared timing renderer now labels its values as scheduled offsets rather than wall-clock guarantees. A slow failing publisher against the embedded broker proves the second delivery follows the server deadline, not handler duration plus the rung.
    
    With the current three production remotes and a five-second publish timeout per remote, the legacy eighth delivery ranged from roughly 3m30s to 5m15s. The migrated scheduled eighth delivery is t+3m30s; no existing monitor or runbook encodes the older wall-clock range.

2f0b483fd622a6d3333eba164ef29e491c7d2947
fix(meta-fanout): end the startup phase permanently on bind; don't page on our own shutdown

Two P2 review findings on trail #102 at 3765557.

1. THE FAST CADENCE COULD RESUME AFTER A POST-BIND LOSS

nextProbeInterval decided from the outcome plus a raw attempts-remaining counter,
and a success settled the interval without spending the budget. So a durable that
bound on its first probe kept ~19 unspent attempts, and a genuine loss inside the
following ~95s (19 spent one per 5s tick) returned 250ms — re-entering the fast
cadence to hammer a server that had just lost the durable. The comment three lines
above said that must never happen; the code did not implement it.

Every single-call assertion I had written passed, because the broken property is
about a SEQUENCE: end, and never resume. So the decision is now a small state
machine (probeCadence) whose observe(bound) ZEROES the budget on success rather than
leaving it to decay, and the test drives sequences — never-binds, binds-immediately-
then-loses, binds-mid-startup-then-loses. Verified it catches the bug: restoring the
non-zeroing branch fails with "a success must end the startup phase, not merely
pause it".

2. CANCELLING AN IN-FLIGHT PROBE LOGGED A FALSE ERROR ON EVERY ROLLOUT

Run cancels the probe context on the way out, so a CONSUMER.INFO in flight at that
moment returns context.Canceled. That value is not in the transient set, so it
reached Health as a fault:

  {"level":"ERROR","msg":"Lifecycle durable unreachable; reporting NotReady","error":"context canceled"}

Self-inflicted shutdown noise — precisely what natslog exists to remove (COR-1228:
57 ErrNoResponders in 83ms during a deploy, three false alerts in forty minutes) —
reintroduced by the probe added to report real outages.

Guarded narrowly: BOTH the parent context being done AND the error being
context.Canceled, the same discipline as nuts.IsShutdownFetchErr, which will only
call a drain benign when ctx is already done. A context.DeadlineExceeded from the
probe's own timeout leaves the parent alive and still reaches Health, as do
consumer-deletion and stream-missing errors. The test asserts both directions —
silence on a cancelled parent, and a complaint on a live one — so the guard cannot
be widened into swallowing real failures without going red. Verified: removing it
reproduces the exact ERROR record above.

Gate: build, vet, go mod tidy -diff, git diff --check, gofmt -s, go test ./...,
go test -race ./... (full suite, as CI runs it), golangci-lint (0 issues) — all
clean.

item.stdout:
Attach an existing agent session that wasn't captured by hooks.

This creates a checkpoint from the session's transcript and links it to the
last commit. Use this when hooks failed to fire or weren't installed when
the session started, or to attach a research session.

If the last commit already has a checkpoint, the session is added to it.
Otherwise a new checkpoint is created.

Use --review to tag the attached session as an agent review. The
first user prompt in the transcript is recorded as the review prompt.
Pass --skills to declare which skills were actually run; omit to
attach a review without a declared skills list.

Works with any registered agent, including external agents enabled via
external_agents in settings. Run 'entire agent list' to see the full list.

If --agent doesn't locate a transcript, Entire auto-detects the agent from
the transcript and prints the detected agent name.

Usage:
  entire session attach <session-id> [flags]

Flags:
  -a, --agent string     Agent that created the session (see 'entire agent list' for registered agents, including external) (default "claude-code")
  -f, --force            Skip confirmation and amend the last commit with the checkpoint trailer (best-effort; if the amend fails the checkpoint is still created and the trailer is printed for manual paste)
  -h, --help             help for attach
      --review           Tag the attached session as an agent review
      --skills strings   Optional: declare which review skills were run in this session. Only used with --review
Install hooks for the specified agent in this repository.

  entire agent add claude-code
  entire agent add gemini

      --agent-help-skill entire agent-help   Install the stable Entire agent-help skill (points agents at entire agent-help)
      --force                                Reinstall hooks even if already present
  -h, --help                                 help for add
      --local-dev                            Install hooks in local-dev mode
      --search-skill                         Install the optional Entire search skill
